If not separable, it never converges (cycles). Equivalent to SGD on the loss max(0, −t·(wᵀx)) with lr 1.

Worked example (AND gate). Points (0,0),(0,1),(1,0) → −1, (1,1) → +1; start w=(0,0), b=0; update when t·score ≤ 0. Running it: converges after 9 passes (the last is a clean pass) to w=(3,2), b=−4. Check: (1,1)→3+2−4=1>0 ✓; (1,0)→−1, (0,1)→−2, (0,0)→−4 ✓. XOR (labels +,−,−,+ on the corners) is not linearly separable ⇒ never converges.

docs.title: 5. Training
docs.text: Cycle through data, update on mistakes; shuffle each epoch. Cost O(n·p) per epoch, memory O(p). Stop when an epoch has no mistakes or at max_iter. Not scale-invariant in speed (mistake bound depends on R), so standardize.

docs.title: 6. Evolution & trade-offs
docs.text: Step Gain Cost Perceptron → logistic regression Probabilities, convex smooth loss, converges on non-separable data Needs gradient/loss Perceptron → averaged/voted Better generalization, reduces order dependence Slight overhead Perceptron → SVM Max-margin solution, kernels Optimization cost Single layer → MLP Non-linear boundaries Needs backprop, non-convex

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: teaching, streaming/online learning with cheap updates, very large sparse problems (e.g. structured prediction in NLP with averaged perceptron). Avoid: non-separable data, when you need probabilities or margins — use logistic regression or SVM.

docs.title: 8. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Trivial, online, mistake-driven (updates only on errors), fast. − Result depends on data order, no margin maximization, no probabilities, no convergence on non-separable data.

docs.title: 9. Hyperparameters
docs.text: max_iter, eta0 (scaling only matters with a nonzero initial w), penalty/alpha (regularization), shuffle, early_stopping, class_weight, averaging.

docs.title: 10. Implementation
docs.text:
class Perceptron_:
    def fit(self, X, y, epochs=50):
        s = 2*y - 1; A = np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X]; w = np.zeros(A.shape[1])
        for e in range(epochs):
            errs = 0
            for a, t in zip(A, s):
                if t*(a@w) <= 0: w += t*a; errs += 1
            if errs == 0: break
        self.w = w; return self
Library: sklearn.linear_model.Perceptron (SGD-based) or SGDClassifier(loss="perceptron").

docs.title: 11. Evaluation & results
docs.text: Breast cancer, scaled, 5-fold CV: accuracy 0.967, AUC 0.993 (logistic 0.979 / 0.995) — close, as expected on near-separable data. From-scratch version: test acc 0.944 vs logistic 0.958 on one split (single-split difference, not a significant gap). AUC for a perceptron uses its raw score, which is not a probability.

docs.title: 12. Comparison
docs.text: Learns the same family of boundaries as logistic/linear SVM; differs only in loss (0-1-like mistake loss vs log vs hinge). Prefer logistic/SVM in production.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why can't a perceptron learn XOR? XOR is not linearly separable; one hyperplane can't split it. Add a hidden layer or features like x₁x₂.
  • Guarantee? Finite mistakes if separable, bound (R/γ)².
  • Difference to logistic regression? Hard threshold, mistake-driven updates, no probabilities.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Show the mistake bound empirically; implement the averaged perceptron; map XOR with feature x₁x₂ and re-train.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Rosenblatt (1958) Psychological Review; Minsky & Papert (1969); Freund & Schapire (1999) "Large margin classification using the perceptron algorithm."

docs.title: Chapter 2.3 — Naive Bayes
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 2.2 · Next 2.4 LDA/QDA · Priority 🟠 · Code: classification_scratch.py, classification_family.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Generative probabilistic classifier using Bayes' rule with a "naive" conditional-independence assumption. Classic for text (spam, topic), also fast baselines for high-dimensional data.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Bayes' theorem (1763; Laplace); used for text categorization from the early 1960s (Maron 1961); popularised by spam filtering (Graham 2002 "A Plan for Spam"); Domingos & Pazzani (1997) explained why NB classifies well even when independence is false (it needs correct ranking of class posteriors, not correct probabilities). Direct predecessor idea: full Bayes classifier (intractable in many dimensions) → NB factorization → TAN / Bayesian networks (Ch 3.5) relax independence.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Score each class by prior × product of how typical each feature is for that class. Pick the highest. Why "naive": features are assumed independent given the class, so the joint likelihood factors into one-dimensional pieces — easy to estimate even with few samples in many dimensions.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text:
P(c|x) ∝ P(c) Π_j P(x_j|c); prediction argmax_c [log P(c) + Σ_j log P(x_j|c)] (logs avoid underflow). Variants: Gaussian (x_j|c ~ 𝒩(μ_cj, σ²_cj)), Multinomial (word counts: θ_cj = (N_cj+α)/(N_c+α·V)), Bernoulli (word presence/absence), Complement NB (imbalanced text), Categorical. Laplace/Lidstone smoothing α>0 prevents zero probability for unseen words (equivalent to a Dirichlet prior, MAP).

Worked example (spam). P(spam)=0.4. "free": appears in 50% of spam, 5% of ham; "meeting": 5% of spam, 40% of ham. Email contains both. Spam score 0.4×0.5×0.05 = 0.010; ham score 0.6×0.05×0.40 = 0.012. Posterior spam = 0.010/0.022 = 0.4545 → classified ham, with probability only ~45% spam. Note how two moderately strong cues cancel; if "meeting" were absent from the model, spam would win. Independence assumption consequence: two highly correlated words both counted ⇒ evidence double-counted ⇒ overconfident probabilities (often near 0/1) even when ranking is fine.

docs.title: 5. Training & prediction
docs.text: Training = counting (one pass), O(n·p); closed-form MLE; no iterations, trivially online/incremental (partial_fit) and parallel. Prediction O(p·C). Memory O(p·C).

docs.title: 6. Evolution
docs.text: Step Improvement Cost Full Bayes → NB Tractable Independence assumption NB → TAN / Bayesian networks Model dependencies Structure learning NB → logistic regression Discriminative; same linear form for NB in log-space but weights fit jointly Slower to train, better with large n NB features → TF-IDF + linear / transformers Context, long-range semantics Heavier Ng & Jordan (2001): NB reaches its (higher) asymptotic error faster than logistic regression, so it can win on very small data while logistic wins as n grows.

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: tiny labeled sets, very high-dimensional sparse data, need training in seconds, streaming/online, text baselines, as a sanity benchmark. Avoid: strongly correlated features where calibrated probabilities matter, numeric features with non-Gaussian shapes (Gaussian NB), interactions mattering, final-accuracy-critical tasks where discriminative models are available.

docs.title: 8. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Extremely fast, tiny data requirement, handles many features, simple, interpretable log-odds per word. − Independence assumption, poor probability calibration, zero-frequency problem (fix with smoothing), Gaussian assumption.

docs.title: 9. Hyperparameters
docs.text: alpha (smoothing; 1 = Laplace; tune on CV, often smaller works better for text), var_smoothing (GaussianNB, adds to variances), priors / fit_prior, binarize (Bernoulli), norm (Complement).

docs.title: 10. Implementation
docs.text:
From scratch (Gaussian NB, see classification_scratch.py): 

mu  = np.array([X[y==k].mean(0) for k in classes]); var = np.array([X[y==k].var(0)+1e-9 for k in classes])
ll  = -0.5*(np.log(2*np.pi*var)[None] + (X[:,None,:]-mu[None])**2/var[None]).sum(2) + np.log(priors)
pred = classes[ll.argmax(1)]
Library: 
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB, MultinomialNB
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
text_clf = make_pipeline(CountVectorizer(), MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0))

docs.title: 11. Evaluation & results (measured)
docs.text: Breast cancer (5-fold CV): GaussianNB acc 0.939, AUC 0.989 (logistic 0.979 / 0.995) — ranks well, slightly lower accuracy. From-scratch Gaussian NB: 0.909 on one test split. Text, 4 categories of 20-newsgroups (headers/footers/quotes removed, test set): MultinomialNB 0.842, TF-IDF+Logistic 0.844, TF-IDF+LinearSVC 0.858 — NB is essentially tied with far less training time.

docs.title: 12. Case study
docs.text: Spam/topic filter: CountVectorizer → MultinomialNB trains in milliseconds and is a legitimate production baseline; inspect feature_log_prob_ to list top words per class for explanation. Recalibrate (isotonic/Platt) if probabilities feed decisions.

docs.title: 13. Comparison & decision
docs.text: Little data/text/speed → NB. More data, want better accuracy/calibration → logistic regression or linear SVM on TF-IDF. Context-heavy language tasks → fine-tuned transformers (Ch 5.4, 6.2).

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why does NB work despite false independence? Classification needs correct arg-max of posteriors; errors from dependence often affect all classes similarly.
  • Zero-frequency problem? A word unseen in a class zeros the product; fix with additive smoothing.
  • Generative vs discriminative? NB models P(x|c)P(c); logistic regression models P(c|x) directly.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Reproduce the spam calculation with α-smoothed counts; compare NB and logistic learning curves as n grows; check calibration of NB with a reliability curve.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Domingos & Pazzani (1997) Machine Learning; McCallum & Nigam (1998) multinomial vs Bernoulli NB for text; Manning, Raghavan & Schütze, Introduction to Information Retrieval (Ch 13, free); sklearn Naive Bayes guide.

docs.title: Chapter 2.4 — Linear & Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (LDA / QDA)
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 2.3 · Next 2.5 k-NN · Priority 🟡 · Code: classification_family.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Generative classifiers that model each class as a Gaussian. LDA shares one covariance across classes (linear boundary); QDA gives each class its own (quadratic boundary). LDA also acts as a supervised dimensionality reducer.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Fisher (1936) "The use of multiple measurements in taxonomic problems" (iris data): find the projection that maximizes between-class over within-class scatter. Rao (1948) extended to multiple classes; the Bayes/Gaussian derivation gives the same direction under equal covariances. Later: regularized discriminant analysis (Friedman 1989), shrinkage covariance (Ledoit–Wolf 2004), sparse LDA. Relationship to logistic regression: same linear form of log-odds, different estimation (generative vs discriminative, Efron 1975).

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Fit a bell-shaped cloud to each class. A new point belongs to whichever cloud makes it most probable (weighted by class frequency). Shared shape ⇒ boundary is a straight line; separate shapes ⇒ curved.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text:
Class density p(x|k)=𝒩(μ_k, Σ_k), prior π_k. Discriminant: δ_k(x) = log π_k + log p(x|k). - LDA (Σ_k=Σ): δ_k(x) = xᵀΣ⁻¹μ_k − ½μ_kᵀΣ⁻¹μ_k + log π_k — linear in x. - QDA: adds −½log|Σ_k| − ½(x−μ_k)ᵀΣ_k⁻¹(x−μ_k) — quadratic. - Fisher view: maximize J(w)=wᵀS_B w / wᵀS_W w; at most min(K−1, p) discriminant directions. - Parameter count: LDA ≈ Kp + p(p+1)/2; QDA ≈ Kp + K·p(p+1)/2 ⇒ QDA needs far more data. Assumptions: Gaussian classes; common covariance (LDA); no singular covariances.

Worked example (1-D). Class means 0 and 4, shared variance σ²=1. Equal priors ⇒ boundary at the midpoint 2. Priors 0.8 (class 0) / 0.2 (class 1): x* = (μ₀+μ₁)/2 + σ²/(μ₁−μ₀)·ln(π₀/π₁) = 2 + (1/4)ln 4 = 2.347 — the boundary shifts toward the rarer class, so more space goes to the common class.

docs.title: 5. Training
docs.text: Closed form: estimate class means, pooled covariance, priors. O(np² + p³). Solvers: svd (default, stable), lsqr/eigen (support shrinkage). Prediction O(pK).

docs.title: 6. Evolution & trade-offs
docs.text: Method Gain Cost Naive Bayes → LDA Models feature correlations Estimates covariance (p² params) LDA → QDA Class-specific shapes, curved boundary Many parameters, unstable when n small QDA/LDA → Regularized DA / shrinkage Stable covariance when p ~ n Tuning LDA → logistic regression Fewer assumptions, robust to non-Gaussian Slower fit LDA → kernel/flexible DA, SVM Non-Gaussian, nonlinear More tuning

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: small samples with roughly Gaussian classes, multi-class problems (compact, fast), dimensionality reduction before another classifier, interpretable discriminant axes, low-latency scoring. Avoid: heavy-tailed/multimodal classes, categorical features, p ≥ n without shrinkage, QDA with scarce data.

docs.title: 8. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Closed form, fast, multiclass-native, low variance (LDA), built-in projection. − Gaussian assumption, sensitive to outliers, singular covariance with collinearity (QDA fails), shared-covariance assumption.

docs.title: 9. Hyperparameters
docs.text: LDA: solver, shrinkage ('auto' Ledoit–Wolf or float 0–1), priors, n_components (projection), tol. QDA: reg_param (blend toward identity), priors.

docs.title: 10. Implementation
docs.text:
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis as LDA, QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis as QDA
lda  = LDA(solver="lsqr", shrinkage="auto")        # stable when p is large relative to n
qda  = QDA(reg_param=0.1)
Z = LDA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X, y)         # supervised projection
From scratch: pooled covariance Σ = Σ_k (n_k−1)Σ̂_k/(n−K); compute δ_k(x) and take argmax.

docs.title: 11. Evaluation & results (measured)
docs.text: Breast cancer, 5-fold CV: LDA acc 0.954 (AUC 0.990); QDA with reg_param=0.1 acc 0.956 (AUC 0.989). Default QDA failed to fit (covariance matrix of class 0 is not full rank) because the 30 features are strongly collinear — the textbook QDA failure; regularization fixed it. Moons dataset (nonlinear): LDA 0.852 vs logistic 0.854 vs RBF-SVC 0.932 — LDA's linear boundary can't bend.

docs.title: 12. Comparison
docs.text: Close in accuracy to logistic regression when classes are near-Gaussian; logistic wins as data departs from Gaussianity. LDA wins on tiny samples or when you want a projection. In practice: LDA as baseline/feature extractor, not the final model.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• LDA vs PCA? PCA is unsupervised (max variance); LDA uses labels (max class separation). Max K−1 components.
  • LDA vs logistic regression? Same linear log-odds; LDA estimates generatively under Gaussian assumptions, logistic discriminatively.
  • When does QDA beat LDA? Clearly different class covariances and plenty of data per class.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Derive the Fisher criterion solution; plot LDA projection of iris; compare LDA with shrinkage vs without as p→n.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Fisher (1936) Annals of Eugenics; Friedman (1989) "Regularized discriminant analysis"; ESL Ch 4.3; Ledoit & Wolf (2004).

docs.title: Chapter 2.5 — k-Nearest Neighbors & Nearest Centroid
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 2.4 · Next 2.6 SVM · Priority 🟠 · Code: classification_family.py, classification_scratch.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Instance-based (lazy, non-parametric) classifier/regressor: predict from the labels of the k most similar training points. "Customers like you bought X."

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Fix & Hodges (1951) introduced nearest-neighbor discrimination; Cover & Hart (1967) proved the 1-NN asymptotic error is at most twice the Bayes-optimal error. Efficiency: k-d trees (Bentley 1975), ball trees, LSH and modern ANN (HNSW, Malkov & Yashunin 2016; FAISS) powering vector search and RAG (Ch 6.4). Nearest Centroid (Rocchio/“Tibshirani's shrunken centroids”) is the compressed, parametric cousin.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text:
Look at your neighbors and vote. Small k ⇒ jagged, memorizing; large k ⇒ smooth, blurry. 

 k=1 : boundary follows every point (high variance)     k=large : boundary smooth (high bias)

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text:
Distance (Minkowski) d(x,x') = (Σ|x_j−x'_j|^q)^{1/q} (q=2 Euclidean, q=1 Manhattan), or cosine. Prediction: classification ŷ = argmax_c Σ_{i∈N_k(x)} w_i 1[y_i=c]; regression: (weighted) mean. Weights w_i = 1/d_i optional. Curse of dimensionality: in high dimensions distances concentrate (nearest and farthest become similar), neighbors stop being meaningful; need exponentially more data. Feature scaling is essential. Assumes: similar inputs ⇒ similar outputs in the chosen metric; meaningful distance; enough local density.

Worked example. 1-D training: x=1(A), 2(A), 3(B), 6(B), 7(B). Query 2.6: distances 1.6, 0.6, 0.4, 3.4, 4.4. k=1 → nearest is x=3 → B. k=3 → neighbors {3(B), 2(A), 1(A)} → A wins 2–1 → A. Prediction flips with k: that's the bias–variance dial.

docs.title: 5. Training & prediction
docs.text: "Training" stores the data (O(1) compute, O(np) memory). Prediction brute force O(n p) per query; k-d/ball trees help in low dimension (<~20); ANN indexes give sub-linear search for embeddings with approximate recall. Scale features; consider PCA/metric learning first.

docs.title: 6. Evolution
docs.text: Step Improvement Cost 1-NN → k-NN Noise robustness Choose k Weighted k-NN, kernel regression (Nadaraya–Watson) Closer points matter more Bandwidth Brute force → trees → ANN (HNSW/IVF/PQ) Speed Approximate answers, index memory k-NN → Nearest Centroid One prototype per class, tiny model Assumes compact classes Learned metrics / embeddings (NCA, Siamese, contrastive) Meaningful distance for images/text Training needed

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: small/medium data, low dimension, few features that are all meaningful, quick baseline, non-linear boundary without training, recommendation/retrieval over embeddings, anomaly detection via distance. Avoid: high-dimensional raw features, large n with strict latency (without ANN), many irrelevant features, imbalanced classes (majority swamps), when probabilities must be calibrated.

docs.title: 8. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • No training, naturally multiclass, flexible boundary, simple to explain ("here are the 5 similar cases"), asymptotically near-optimal. − Slow, memory-hungry predictions, sensitive to scaling/irrelevant features/noise, curse of dimensionality, poor extrapolation.

docs.title: 9. Hyperparameters
docs.text: n_neighbors (k; use odd for binary; tune by CV), weights (uniform/distance), metric/p, algorithm (auto/kd_tree/ball_tree/brute), leaf_size.

docs.title: 10. Implementation
docs.text:
From scratch (brute force): 

d = ((Xq[:,None,:] - Xtr[None])**2).sum(2)            # squared Euclidean, shape (nq, n)
idx = np.argsort(d, 1)[:, :k]
pred = (ytr[idx].mean(1) >= .5).astype(int)           # binary majority vote
Library: 
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier, NearestCentroid
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
knn = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=15, weights="distance"))

docs.title: 11. Evaluation & results (measured)
docs.text: Breast cancer 5-fold CV: scaled k-NN(5) acc 0.965 vs 0.932 unscaled (scaling matters); NearestCentroid 0.931. Moons (nonlinear, noise 0.25): train vs CV accuracy by k: | k | train | CV | |---|---|---| | 1 | 1.000 | 0.908 | | 5 | 0.950 | 0.926 | | 15 | 0.940 | 0.944 | | 50 | 0.936 | 0.932 | | 200 | 0.860 | 0.832 | k=1 memorizes (train 1.0), k=200 underfits. k-NN(15) beat every linear model on moons (0.944 vs ~0.85).

docs.title: 12. Case study
docs.text: Content-based "similar items": embed products, index with FAISS/HNSW, return top-k with cosine distance; evaluate with recall@k against exact search and online CTR. For tabular classification use it as a baseline against boosted trees.

docs.title: 13. Comparison
docs.text: vs SVM-RBF: similar flexibility but SVM stores only support vectors and trains a margin. vs trees: trees ignore irrelevant features; k-NN does not. vs logistic: k-NN handles nonlinearity but lacks parametric compactness.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why scale features? Distances are dominated by large-range features.
  • k too small / too large? Overfit / underfit.
  • Curse of dimensionality? Points become equidistant, neighbors uninformative.
  • Inference cost? O(n·p) naive per query; use ANN indexes.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Add irrelevant noise features and watch accuracy fall; implement distance-weighted k-NN; benchmark exact vs HNSW recall/latency.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Cover & Hart (1967) "Nearest neighbor pattern classification"; Malkov & Yashunin (2016) HNSW; ESL Ch 13; FAISS documentation.

docs.title: Chapter 2.6 — Support Vector Machines (Linear, Kernel, SVR)
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 2.5 · Next 3.1 Decision Trees · Priority 🟠 · Code: classification_family.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Margin-maximizing classifier/regressor. Finds the separating hyperplane with the widest gap; with kernels it separates non-linear data. SVR applies the idea to regression.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Vapnik & Chervonenkis: statistical learning theory, VC dimension, optimal hyperplane (1960s–70s) → Boser, Guyon & Vapnik (1992) kernel trick → Cortes & Vapnik (1995) soft margin ("support-vector networks") → SVR (Drucker et al. 1997), SMO training (Platt 1998), LIBSVM (Chang & Lin). Dominated classification in the late 1990s–2000s (text, bioinformatics, digits) until large-scale deep learning and boosting took over. Relation to perceptron: both linear separators; SVM picks the unique max-margin one.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text:
Among all separating lines, pick the one with the widest "street" between classes. Only the points on the curbs (support vectors) matter; the rest could be deleted without changing the model. 

   + +   |      margin = 2/‖w‖
  + +  --|-- ← support vectors on the margin
        ---|
   - -   |  -
Kernel trick: map to a higher-dimensional feature space where a line works, without ever computing the mapping.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text:
Hard margin: min ½‖w‖² s.t. y_i(wᵀx_i+b) ≥ 1. Soft margin: min ½‖w‖² + C Σξ_i s.t. y_i(wᵀx_i+b) ≥ 1−ξ_i, ξ_i≥0 ⇔ minimize hinge loss Σ max(0, 1−y_i f(x_i)) + (1/2C)‖w‖². Dual: max Σα_i − ½ΣΣ α_iα_j y_iy_j K(x_i,x_j) s.t. 0≤α_i≤C, Σα_iy_i=0; prediction f(x)=Σ α_i y_i K(x_i,x)+b over support vectors (α_i>0). Kernels: linear xᵀx'; polynomial (γxᵀx'+r)^d; RBF exp(−γ‖x−x'‖²); Mercer condition = PSD kernel matrix. SVR: ε-insensitive loss max(0,|y−f|−ε). Assumes: scale-sensitive; margin is a meaningful notion; kernel suits the data.

Worked example (hard margin). Points x=−1 (class −), x=+1 (class +), 1-D. Constraints: w·(−1)+b ≤ −1, w·1+b ≥ 1 ⇒ minimal |w|=1, b=0, margin width 2/|w|=2; both points are support vectors. Adding a far point at x=3 (+) changes nothing (not a support vector). Kernel example: 1-D data − at x=0, + at x=−2 and +2 isn't linearly separable, but mapping φ(x)=x² gives −→0, +→4, separable at 2.

docs.title: 5. Training
docs.text: Convex quadratic program. SMO/libsvm: O(n²)–O(n³) time, O(n²) kernel cache; prediction O(#SV·p). Linear SVM via liblinear/SGD scales O(n·p). Rule of thumb: kernel SVM comfortable up to ~tens of thousands of rows; beyond that use linear SVM, kernel approximation (Nystroem, random Fourier features) or other models. Scale features. SVC probabilities (Platt scaling, 5-fold internally) are costly and approximate.

docs.title: 6. Evolution
docs.text: Step Gain Cost Perceptron → hard-margin SVM Unique max-margin solution, generalization bound Needs separability → soft margin (C) Handles noise Tune C → kernel SVM Non-linear boundaries Quadratic+ scaling, kernel tuning → SVR, one-class SVM Regression, novelty detection — → Linear SVM at scale (liblinear, Pegasos) Millions of sparse features Linear boundary SVM → boosted trees/deep nets Better on large/structured data Different tuning/compute

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: small–medium n, high-dimensional features (text with linear SVM), clean margin, need nonlinear boundary with strong regularization control. Avoid: very large n (kernel), heavy noise/overlap without careful C, need for calibrated probabilities, many categorical features, interpretability needs.

docs.title: 8. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Strong generalization in high dimension, convex (global optimum), sparse solution (support vectors), flexible kernels. − Slow on big data, needs scaling and tuning (C, γ), no native probabilities, opaque kernel models.

docs.title: 9. Hyperparameters
docs.text: C (↑ narrower margin, fewer violations, overfit risk), kernel, gamma (RBF width; ↑ = wigglier boundary, overfit; scale default = 1/(p·Var(X))), degree/coef0 (poly), epsilon (SVR tube), class_weight, tol. Tune C and γ on a log grid.

docs.title: 10. Implementation
docs.text:
from sklearn.svm import SVC, LinearSVC, SVR
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC())
gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, {"svc__C": [.1,1,10,100], "svc__gamma": [1e-3,1e-2,1e-1,1]}, cv=5).fit(X, y)
lin = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LinearSVC())      # n large / sparse text
From scratch: sub-gradient descent on hinge loss (Pegasos): if y(w·x)<1: w ← (1−ηλ)w + ηyx else w ← (1−ηλ)w.

docs.title: 11. Evaluation & results (measured)
docs.text: Breast cancer, 5-fold CV: LinearSVC acc 0.968 (AUC 0.993); RBF SVC 0.977 (AUC 0.996); grid search best C=100, γ=0.001 → 0.981 (CV-selected on the same folds, so slightly optimistic; use nested CV for an honest figure). Over-flexible RBF (C=1000, γ=1) collapses to 0.631 ≈ majority baseline (0.627): memorized training data. Moons: RBF-SVC 0.932 vs LinearSVC 0.856. Fit time on synthetic 20-feature data (seconds): n=2k / 8k / 16k → Logistic 0.01/0.02/0.06, GaussianNB 0.00/0.01/0.01, RBF SVC 0.09/2.7/5.6 — superlinear growth, the practical limit of kernel SVMs. Text (4 newsgroups): TF-IDF + LinearSVC 0.858 vs Logistic 0.844 vs MultinomialNB 0.842 — linear SVM is a strong, cheap text baseline.

docs.title: 12. Case study
docs.text: Text classification: TfidfVectorizer(sublinear_tf=True) + LinearSVC — default winner among classical text models for years. Digits/small images: RBF SVM until CNNs.

docs.title: 13. Comparison
docs.text: vs logistic: similar linear performance; SVM margin vs probabilities. vs k-NN: SVM compact, trained boundary. vs boosted trees: trees handle mixed types/missing values/interactions out of the box and scale better; SVM can win on small high-dimensional numeric data.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• What are support vectors? Training points with α>0 — on/inside the margin; they alone define the boundary.
  • What does C do? Trades margin width against training errors.
  • Kernel trick? Compute inner products in feature space via K(x,x') without mapping.
  • Why scale? Margin and RBF distance depend on feature units.
  • Why not for huge data? O(n²–n³) training.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Derive the dual; implement Pegasos; visualize how γ changes the RBF boundary; compare SVR with Ridge on a nonlinear regression.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Cortes & Vapnik (1995) Machine Learning; Boser, Guyon, Vapnik (1992); Platt (1998) SMO; Schölkopf & Smola, Learning with Kernels; Chang & Lin (2011) LIBSVM; sklearn SVM guide.

docs.title: Chapter 3.1 — Decision Trees (ID3 → C4.5 → CART) and Pruning
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 2.6 SVM · Next 3.2 Bagging & Random Forest · Priority 🔴 · Code: trees_scratch.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Recursive partitioning model: a flowchart of if/else questions on features, ending in leaves that predict a class or number. "Approve this loan?" — yes/no questions a human could follow.

docs.title: 2. History (a family, not a line)
docs.text:
• AID (Morgan & Sonquist 1963) and CHAID (Kass 1980): statistical-test-based splitting for survey data.
  • ID3 (Quinlan 1986; earlier CLS 1966/1979): categorical features, information gain, no pruning, no missing values.
  • C4.5 (Quinlan 1993): gain ratio (corrects ID3's bias toward many-valued features), continuous thresholds, missing-value handling, error-based pruning. C5.0 is the proprietary successor.
  • CART (Breiman, Friedman, Olshen & Stone 1984): binary splits, Gini (classification) / variance (regression), cost-complexity pruning, surrogate splits. scikit-learn implements an optimized CART.
  • Later: conditional inference trees (Hothorn et al. 2006; unbiased split selection), oblique trees. The real step-change came by combining trees (Ch 3.2–3.4).

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text:
Ask the question that best separates the classes; repeat on each side. Stop when groups are pure or small. 

              Income > 50k?
              /          \
           yes            no
    Age > 30?          Default risk: HIGH (leaf)
     /     \
  LOW      MEDIUM

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: Impurity of a node with class proportions p_k: Gini G = 1 − Σp_k²; entropy H = −Σp_k log₂p_k; regression: variance/MSE. Split quality = parent impurity − weighted child impurity (information gain for entropy). Gain ratio = IG / SplitInfo (C4.5). CART cost-complexity pruning: minimize R(T) + α|T| (error plus α per leaf); α chosen by CV (ccp_alpha). Worked example. Labels [0,0,0,1,1,1,1,1]: Gini = 1−(3/8)²−(5/8)² = 0.4688; entropy = 0.9544 bits. Candidate split → left [0,0,0,1], right [1,1,1,1]: Left Gini = 1−0.75²−0.25² = 0.375; right = 0 ⇒ weighted = (4·0.375+4·0)/8 = 0.1875; Gini gain = 0.4688−0.1875 = 0.2813. Entropy: left H=0.8113 ⇒ weighted 0.4056; information gain = 0.9544−0.4056 = 0.5488. The algorithm evaluates every feature/threshold this way and takes the best (greedy, no look-ahead). Assumptions: none about distributions or linearity; axis-aligned splits; features can be mixed scale; invariant to monotonic transformations.

docs.title: 5. Training & prediction
docs.text: Greedy top-down; stop at max_depth, min_samples_leaf/split, no gain, or purity. Cost: sorting makes it O(p·n log n) per level; prediction O(depth), tiny memory. Optimal tree is NP-complete, so greedy heuristics are used. Regression leaves predict the mean; classification leaves predict class frequencies (often poorly calibrated).

docs.title: 6. Evolution & trade-offs
docs.text: Step Improvement Cost ID3 → C4.5 Numeric features, missing values, pruning, gain ratio More complexity C4.5 → CART Regression, binary splits, principled pruning, surrogate splits Gini bias toward multi-valued/high-cardinality features Single tree → Random Forest / boosting Removes the high variance of one tree Interpretability, memory Tree → Optimal/oblique/soft trees Better splits / smoother Compute, complexity

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: interpretable rules, mixed feature types with no preprocessing, nonlinearity/interactions, quick baselines, as building blocks. Avoid as final model on noisy data (unstable), smooth/additive relations (staircase approximation), extrapolation (flat outside range), high-cardinality categoricals (bias), when stability matters.

docs.title: 8. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Interpretable, no scaling, handles interactions, fast prediction, minimal preprocessing. − High variance (small data change ⇒ different tree), overfits when deep, piecewise-constant output, greedy, biased toward high-cardinality features, cannot extrapolate.

docs.title: 9. Hyperparameters
docs.text: max_depth (↑ complexity), min_samples_leaf (↑ smoother, regularizes), min_samples_split, max_leaf_nodes, min_impurity_decrease, ccp_alpha (pruning), criterion (gini/entropy/log_loss; MSE/MAE for regression), max_features, class_weight, splitter.

docs.title: 10. Implementation
docs.text:
From scratch CART (Gini) in trees_scratch.py: 

def gini(y): p = np.bincount(y)/len(y); return 1 - (p**2).sum()
# for each feature j, each midpoint threshold t: score = (nL*gini(yL) + nR*gini(yR))/n ; keep the minimum, then recurse
Library: 
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, min_samples_leaf=5, ccp_alpha=0.001, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print(export_text(tree, feature_names=list(names)))

docs.title: 11. Evaluation & results (measured)
docs.text: Breast cancer test split (stratified): scratch vs sklearn accuracy — depth 1: 0.888 / 0.888; depth 3: 0.916 / 0.916; depth 5: 0.909 / 0.902 (tiny difference from tie-breaking in equal-gain splits). California housing: unpruned tree train RMSE 0.000, test 0.709; depth 6: train 0.656, test 0.705 — shallow beats memorizing, but both lose badly to ensembles (0.44–0.50). The train/test gap of the unpruned tree is the signature of variance.

docs.title: 12. Case study
docs.text: Credit-risk rules: fit a depth-3/4 tree with min_samples_leaf≥50, export rules for the compliance team, then compare its AUC with a boosted model to quantify the explainability cost. Check stability by refitting on bootstrap samples and noting how top splits change.

docs.title: 13. Comparison
docs.text: vs logistic/linear: trees capture interactions/nonlinearity automatically; linear models extrapolate and are smoother. vs ensembles: single trees explain; ensembles predict.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Gini vs entropy? Very similar in practice; entropy slightly more sensitive to balanced splits, Gini cheaper (no log).
  • Why do trees overfit? Can isolate every training point; fix with depth limits, min leaf size, pruning, ensembling.
  • Do trees need scaling? No; thresholds only use order.
  • Feature importance caveat? Impurity importance favors high-cardinality/continuous features; use permutation importance.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Hand-compute the best split for a 6-row dataset; implement regression-tree splitting by variance reduction; run cost-complexity pruning with cost_complexity_pruning_path and CV ccp_alpha.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Breiman et al. (1984) Classification and Regression Trees; Quinlan (1986) "Induction of decision trees," (1993) C4.5; Hothorn, Hornik, Zeileis (2006); ESL Ch 9.2; sklearn "Decision Trees" guide.

docs.title: Chapter 3.2 — Bagging, Random Forest, Extra Trees
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 3.1 · Next 3.3 AdaBoost & Gradient Boosting · Priority 🔴 · Code: trees_family.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Variance-reduction ensembles of decorrelated trees. A single deep tree has low bias but high variance; averaging many different trees keeps the low bias and cuts the variance.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) — Breiman 1996, built on Efron's bootstrap (1979). Random subspace (Ho 1995) and random split selection (Amit & Geman 1997) → Random Forest — Breiman 2001 (bagging + random feature subset at each split; OOB error; importance). Extremely Randomized Trees — Geurts, Ernst & Wehenkel 2006 (random thresholds, usually no bootstrap).

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Ask 200 slightly different experts (each saw a random sample and a random subset of clues) and average their answers. Individual mistakes cancel if the experts aren't all making the same mistake — hence the random feature subsets (to decorrelate).

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: Average of B predictors with variance σ², pairwise correlation ρ: Var = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B. More trees kill the second term; only lower ρ reduces the first ⇒ random feature subsampling. Bootstrap sample of size n leaves out each row with probability (1−1/n)ⁿ → 1/e ≈ 36.8% ⇒ out-of-bag (OOB) rows give a free validation estimate. Worked example. Five trees predict 4.0, 6.0, 5.0, 7.0, 3.0 for one house. Forest = mean 5.0. If each tree's error variance is 1 and trees are independent, ensemble variance = 1/5 = 0.2; with ρ=0.5: 0.5 + 0.5/5 = 0.6 — correlation limits the gain. Assumptions: none about distributions. Bagging reduces variance, not bias.

docs.title: 5. Training & prediction
docs.text: Trees are trained independently ⇒ trivially parallel. Cost O(B · p'·n log n) (p' = features tried per split); prediction O(B·depth); memory O(B·nodes) — can be GBs for deep forests on large n (I hit memory limits on a 5.8 GB laptop with 100 deep trees and n_jobs=-1; use min_samples_leaf, fewer trees, or fewer jobs). Defaults: regression max_features=1.0 in current sklearn, classification sqrt(p).

docs.title: 6. Evolution
docs.text: Step Improvement Cost Tree → Bagging Large variance reduction Less interpretable, memory Bagging → Random Forest Decorrelated trees, OOB, importances Another hyperparameter (max_features) RF → Extra Trees Even lower variance, faster training Slightly more bias; often competitive RF → Boosting Reduces bias too, often more accurate Sequential, more tuning, can overfit RF variants Quantile RF (prediction intervals), Isolation Forest (Ch 4.5), Random survival forests, causal forests Specialized

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: strong default for tabular data with little tuning, noisy data, mixed features, OOB estimates, importance screening, robust baseline. Avoid: need for extrapolation (flat), very high-dimensional sparse text (linear models win), tight memory/latency, when boosting gives clearly better accuracy and you can tune it.

docs.title: 8. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Robust, few hyperparameters, parallel, handles nonlinearity/interactions, OOB, hard to badly overfit by adding trees. − Big models, slow prediction for huge forests, piecewise-constant, biased impurity importance, probabilities not calibrated, usually behind tuned boosting.

docs.title: 9. Hyperparameters
docs.text: n_estimators (more is never worse in expectation, diminishing returns), max_features (↓ = more decorrelation, more bias), max_depth/min_samples_leaf (memory + smoothness), bootstrap, max_samples, oob_score, class_weight, n_jobs, random_state.

docs.title: 10. Implementation
docs.text:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, ExtraTreesRegressor, BaggingRegressor
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, max_features=0.6, min_samples_leaf=1, oob_score=True, n_jobs=2, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(rf.oob_score_)
# from scratch idea: for b in range(B): idx = rng.integers(0,n,n); tree_b = Tree(max_features=...).fit(X[idx], y[idx]); predict = mean over b

docs.title: 11. Evaluation & results (measured; California housing, test RMSE, lower is better)
docs.text: Model Train Test Linear regression 0.720 0.746 Single deep tree 0.000 0.709 Bagging (50 deep trees) 0.193 0.507 Random forest (200) 0.186 0.502 Extra Trees (200) 0.000 0.501 Forest max_features sweep (test RMSE / OOB R²): 0.33 → 0.495 / 0.819; 0.6 → 0.492 / 0.819; 1.0 → 0.502 / 0.810. A single tree → forest cuts RMSE 29% (0.709 → 0.502). Bagging alone already captures most of the gain; feature subsampling adds a little. OOB R² (0.819) lands in the same ballpark as test performance without any holdout. Importance (RF): impurity ranks MedInc 0.525, AveOccup 0.138, Latitude 0.089, Longitude 0.089, while permutation importance gives MedInc 0.733, Latitude 0.456, Longitude 0.341, AveOccup 0.204 — location matters much more than impurity suggests (impurity importance is biased toward features with many split points like AveOccup). Prefer permutation/SHAP.

docs.title: 12. Case study
docs.text: California housing: RF captures the nonlinear latitude/longitude geography that linear regression (Ch 1.1) could not, cutting test RMSE from 0.746 to 0.502 (≈33%). Next chapters show boosting pushes to ~0.44.

docs.title: 13. Comparison
docs.text: vs single tree: accuracy ↑, interpretability ↓. vs boosting: RF is easier and more robust to defaults; boosting is usually more accurate when tuned. vs Extra Trees: ET faster and sometimes smoother; same family.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why random feature subsets? Decorrelate trees; averaging correlated trees helps less.
  • What is OOB? Rows not in a tree's bootstrap sample (≈36.8%) give an unbiased-ish validation score.
  • Can a forest overfit by adding trees? No (it converges), but deep trees can still overfit noise.
  • Why can't RF extrapolate? Leaves hold averages of training targets.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Plot OOB error vs n_estimators; implement bagging by hand and verify variance reduction vs one tree; compare impurity vs permutation importance with a random noise feature added.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Breiman (1996) "Bagging predictors"; Breiman (2001) "Random forests," Machine Learning; Geurts et al. (2006); ESL Ch 15; sklearn "Ensemble methods".

docs.title: Chapter 3.3 — AdaBoost and Gradient Boosting
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 3.2 · Next 3.4 XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost/HistGB · Priority 🔴 · Code: trees_scratch.py, trees_family.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Boosting builds an ensemble sequentially: each new weak learner focuses on what the ensemble still gets wrong. Reduces bias (and variance) by stage-wise additive modeling.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Kearns & Valiant (1989) asked whether weak learners (barely better than chance) can be boosted into strong ones → Schapire (1990) proved yes → AdaBoost (Freund & Schapire 1995/1997; Gödel Prize 2003) → statistical view: "additive logistic regression" (Friedman, Hastie, Tibshirani 2000) showed AdaBoost minimizes exponential loss by stage-wise fitting → Gradient Boosting Machine (Friedman 1999/2001, "Greedy function approximation") generalized to any differentiable loss; Stochastic GB (Friedman 2002) added subsampling. Modern implementations: Ch 3.4.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text:
• AdaBoost: train a small tree; raise the weight of the points it got wrong; train the next tree on the reweighted data; combine with votes weighted by each tree's accuracy.
  • Gradient boosting: fit a tree to the current residuals (errors), add a fraction of it to the model, repeat — gradient descent in function space. 
     F0 = mean(y)  →  F1 = F0 + η·tree1(residuals)  →  F2 = F1 + η·tree2(residuals of F1)  → ...

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: AdaBoost (binary, labels ±1): weights w_i=1/n. For each round: fit h_t on weighted data; error ε_t = Σ w_i 1[h_t(x_i)≠y_i]; α_t = ½ ln((1−ε_t)/ε_t); update w_i ← w_i · exp(−α_t y_i h_t(x_i)), renormalize; final H(x)=sign(Σα_t h_t(x)). Worked example. 5 points, equal weights 0.2; stump misclassifies 1 ⇒ ε=0.2, α = ½ln(0.8/0.2) = ½ln4 = 0.693. Misclassified weight ×e^{0.693}=2 ⇒ 0.4; each correct ×e^{−0.693}=0.5 ⇒ 0.1 (four of them = 0.4). Normalize (sum 0.8): mistake 0.5, others 0.125 each — the one hard point now carries half the weight. Gradient boosting: minimize Σ L(y_i, F(x_i)). Stage m: pseudo-residuals r_im = −∂L/∂F(x_i); fit tree h_m to r_im; (optionally line-search leaf values); F_m = F_{m−1} + η h_m. - Squared error: r = y − F (plain residuals). Log-loss: r = y − p. Absolute/Huber/quantile: sign-based, robust, quantile. Worked example (MSE). y=[3,5,10], F₀=mean=6. Residuals [−3,−1,4]. Suppose a stump predicts [−2,−2,4] (splits {first two} vs {third}); with η=0.5: F₁ = 6+0.5·[−2,−2,4] = [5,5,8]; new residuals [−2,0,2]; squared error fell from 9+1+16=26 to 4+0+4=8. Each stage chips away at the error. Assumptions: none distributional; needs enough weak-learner capacity; sensitive to label noise (AdaBoost's exponential loss especially).

docs.title: 5. Training & prediction
docs.text: Sequential (can't parallelize across trees; parallelize inside a tree). Cost O(M · tree cost), prediction O(M·depth). Regularization levers: learning rate η (shrinkage), number of trees M, tree depth, subsampling, early stopping on a validation set.

docs.title: 6. Evolution
docs.text: Step Improvement Cost Bagging → AdaBoost Reduces bias via reweighting Sensitive to noisy labels/outliers AdaBoost → Gradient boosting Any loss (regression, ranking, quantile, count) More hyperparameters GBM → Stochastic GB Row subsampling: faster, regularizes One more knob GBM → XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost/HistGB Regularization, speed, histograms, categoricals (Ch 3.4) Library-specific tuning

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: tabular prediction where accuracy matters, nonlinear/interactions, mixed data, custom losses. Avoid: very noisy labels with AdaBoost, tiny datasets (overfit), need for extrapolation, strict training-time limits without histogram implementations, when a logistic baseline is within noise.

docs.title: 8. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Top accuracy on tabular data, flexible loss, little preprocessing. − Many hyperparameters, sequential training, overfit with large M and η, less interpretable, probabilities may need calibration.

docs.title: 9. Hyperparameters
docs.text: learning_rate η (↓ needs ↑ trees; 0.01–0.1 typical), n_estimators M (pick via early stopping), max_depth (3–8; depth = interaction order), subsample (0.5–1), max_features, min_samples_leaf, loss, AdaBoost estimator (stump) and learning_rate.

docs.title: 10. Implementation
docs.text:
From scratch (least-squares GBM; checked against sklearn): 

class GBM:
    def fit(self, X, y, n=200, lr=0.1, depth=3):
        self.f0 = y.mean(); F = np.full(len(y), self.f0); self.trees = []
        for _ in range(n):
            t = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth).fit(X, y - F)   # residuals = negative gradient of MSE
            F += lr * t.predict(X); self.trees.append(t)
        return self
    def predict(self, X): return self.f0 + lr * sum(t.predict(X) for t in self.trees)
Friedman-1 synthetic data (n=1000): scratch test RMSE 1.490 vs sklearn GradientBoostingRegressor 1.497 (single depth-3 tree: 3.39). Library: GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.1, subsample=0.8), AdaBoostClassifier.

docs.title: 11. Evaluation & results (measured)
docs.text: California housing test RMSE: AdaBoost(100, default depth-3 base) 0.950 (worse than even a single tree 0.709 — AdaBoost.R2 with default settings is a weak regressor here; use gradient boosting for regression), sklearn GBM(300, depth 3, η 0.1) 0.499. A deeper run (1500 trees, η 0.1) kept improving up to the last tree: RMSE 0.468 — no overfitting turning point within 1500 trees at this depth/η, so "more trees always overfit" isn't a rule; always check the validation curve. Breast-cancer 5-fold AUC: AdaBoost 0.993, GBM 0.991, RF 0.991 — all statistically indistinguishable on this small easy set. Always use early stopping (n_iter_no_change, validation_fraction) rather than a fixed M.

docs.title: 12. Case study
docs.text: Churn/credit scoring: logistic baseline → GBM with learning_rate=0.05, depth 4, subsample 0.8, early stopping; compare AUC/PR-AUC and calibration; explain with SHAP.

docs.title: 13. Comparison
docs.text: vs RF: boosting is usually more accurate but more sensitive to tuning/noise; RF is parallel and safer. vs deep nets: GBMs remain the default on tabular data of moderate size.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Bagging vs boosting? Bagging: parallel, reduces variance. Boosting: sequential, reduces bias (and some variance).
  • Why is the residual the "gradient"? For squared loss, −∂/∂F ½(y−F)² = y−F.
  • What does the learning rate do? Shrinks each step; smaller η + more trees generalizes better but costs compute.
  • Why is AdaBoost noise-sensitive? Exponential loss keeps upweighting mislabeled points.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Implement AdaBoost with stumps by hand; add log-loss gradients to the scratch GBM for classification; draw train/validation curves vs M for different η.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Freund & Schapire (1997) JCSS; Friedman, Hastie, Tibshirani (2000) Annals of Statistics; Friedman (2001) "Greedy function approximation: a gradient boosting machine"; ESL Ch 10.

docs.title: Chapter 3.4 — XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost and HistGradientBoosting
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 3.3 · Next 3.5 GMM/HMM/Bayes nets · Priority 🔴 · Code: trees_family.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Engineering- and algorithm-level upgrades to gradient boosting that made it fast, regularized and practical at scale. Same core idea as Ch 3.3; different engineering trade-offs.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text:
• XGBoost — Chen & Guestrin, KDD 2016 (open-sourced 2014; dominated Kaggle tabular competitions).
  • LightGBM — Ke et al., NeurIPS 2017 (Microsoft): histogram splits, leaf-wise growth, GOSS, EFB.
  • CatBoost — Prokhorenkova et al., NeurIPS 2018 (Yandex): ordered boosting, ordered target statistics, symmetric trees.
  • HistGradientBoosting — scikit-learn (0.21+; inspired by LightGBM): native histograms, NaN support, categorical support. Not a strict ranking — they are siblings with different strengths.

docs.title: 3. What each contributes
docs.text: Library Key ideas Strength Watch out XGBoost 2nd-order (Newton) objective, explicit leaf regularization (γ, λ), sparsity-aware splits (native missing values), column/row subsampling, approximate & exact split finders, out-of-core, GPU Robust, flexible objectives, mature More knobs; level-wise default is slower than leaf-wise LightGBM Histogram binning, leaf-wise (best-first) growth, GOSS (keep large-gradient samples), EFB (bundle exclusive sparse features), native categoricals Very fast on large/high-dim data Leaf-wise overfits small data; tune num_leaves, min_child_samples CatBoost Ordered boosting (reduces prediction-shift bias), ordered target statistics for categoricals (reduces target leakage), symmetric (oblivious) trees Best out-of-the-box with high-cardinality categoricals; strong defaults Slower on pure numeric data; fewer deployment targets HistGB (sklearn) Histograms, NaN-aware, early stopping built in Zero extra dependencies Fewer features/objectives

docs.title: 4. Math (XGBoost)
docs.text: Objective at stage t: L = Σ l(y_i, ŷ_i^{(t−1)} + f_t(x_i)) + Ω(f_t), Ω = γT + ½λΣ w_j². Second-order Taylor: with g_i=∂l/∂ŷ, h_i=∂²l/∂ŷ²: for a leaf with sums G=Σg, H=Σh: optimal leaf weight w* = −G/(H+λ); leaf score −½ G²/(H+λ) + γ. Split gain = ½[ G_L²/(H_L+λ) + G_R²/(H_R+λ) − (G_L+G_R)²/(H_L+H_R+λ) ] − γ. Split only if gain > 0 ⇒ γ is a built-in pruning threshold. Worked example (squared error ⇒ g = ŷ − y, h = 1). Four rows with g = [−2,−2,+2,+2]. Parent: G=0 ⇒ term 0. Split {−2,−2} | {+2,+2}: G_L=−4, H_L=2; G_R=4, H_R=2; λ=1: G_L²/(H_L+λ)=16/3=5.333 (same for right) ⇒ gain = ½(5.333+5.333−0) = 5.333 (γ=0). Leaf weights w_L = 4/3 = 1.333, w_R = −1.333 (pull predictions up for the left rows whose errors were negative). With λ=0 the weights would be ±2 (full correction); λ shrinks them — regularization in action. LightGBM leaf-wise: always split the leaf with largest gain, regardless of depth ⇒ lower loss per split but deeper, lopsided trees. Histogram: bin each feature into ≤255 buckets; split search O(#bins) rather than O(n); subtraction trick (sibling histogram = parent − child).

docs.title: 5. Training & cost
docs.text: Per tree: histogram building O(n·p) once per level/leaf, split search O(bins·p). Orders of magnitude faster than classic GBM on large n. GPU variants exist (XGBoost device="cuda", LightGBM/CatBoost GPU). Prediction cost O(M·depth); models are compact vs forests.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: any structured/tabular supervised problem (the default winner), ranking (LambdaRank/rank:ndcg), counts/quantiles/survival objectives, missing data, large n. Avoid: images/audio/text without embeddings, tiny data where simpler models match, when extrapolation is needed, strict interpretability mandates (use GAM/EBM or constrained monotonic GBMs).

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters (cheat sheet)
docs.text: Concept XGBoost LightGBM CatBoost Learning rate learning_rate learning_rate learning_rate Trees n_estimators + early_stopping_rounds n_estimators + callbacks iterations + early_stopping_rounds Complexity max_depth, min_child_weight, gamma num_leaves (< 2^depth), max_depth, min_child_samples depth Regularization reg_lambda, reg_alpha lambda_l2/l1, min_gain_to_split l2_leaf_reg Subsampling subsample, colsample_bytree bagging_fraction/freq, feature_fraction subsample, rsm Categorical one-hot / enable_categorical categorical_feature cat_features (native) Imbalance scale_pos_weight scale_pos_weight/is_unbalance auto_class_weights Tuning order that works: fix η≈0.05–0.1 and use early stopping → tune tree size (max_depth/num_leaves, min_child_*) → subsampling → regularization → lower η and add trees at the end. Use random search/Optuna rather than large grids.

docs.title: 8. Implementation
docs.text:
import xgboost as xgb, lightgbm as lgb, catboost as cb
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
xg = xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=500, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=6, subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8)
lg = lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=500, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=31, subsample=0.8, subsample_freq=1, colsample_bytree=0.8)
cbm = cb.CatBoostRegressor(iterations=500, learning_rate=0.08, depth=6, verbose=0)
hg = HistGradientBoostingRegressor()                 # early_stopping='auto' for n>10k
# early stopping:  xg.fit(Xtr, ytr, eval_set=[(Xval, yval)], verbose=False)  (set early_stopping_rounds in the constructor)

docs.title: 9. Evaluation & results (measured; California housing, test RMSE in $100k; 4-core laptop)
docs.text: Model Train Test Fit time Linear regression 0.720 0.746 0.0 s Random forest (200) 0.186 0.502 19.2 s sklearn GBM (300, d3) 0.444 0.499 15.9 s HistGradientBoosting 0.400 0.462 0.7 s CatBoost (500, d6) 0.380 0.459 3.5 s XGBoost (500, η .05, d6) 0.278 0.445 3.6 s LightGBM (500, 31 leaves) 0.323 0.437 1.0 s All parameters were set once, not tuned; differences of ~0.01–0.02 among the top four are within what tuning/seed changes can move, so treat them as a tie. The robust conclusions: (1) all modern boosters beat the forest (0.502) and linear model (0.746); (2) histogram-based ones train 5–20× faster than classic GBM/RF. Leaf-wise overfitting (LightGBM, only 300 training rows, test RMSE): num_leaves 4 → 0.649; 15 → 0.658; 63 → 0.692 — capacity beyond what the data supports hurts. Missing values: HistGB trained and tested with 20% of all entries randomly set to NaN: RMSE 0.589 (vs 0.462 with complete data) — works with no imputation, at an expected accuracy cost. Breast cancer 5-fold AUC: XGB 0.994, LGBM 0.993, RF 0.991 — saturated; the ranking is noise on this small easy set.

docs.title: 10. Case study
docs.text: Fraud/churn with categorical IDs: CatBoost with cat_features vs LightGBM with ordinal-encoded categories vs target-encoded logistic. Evaluate on a time-based split, report PR-AUC, calibrate, tune the threshold, and explain with SHAP. Check train/serve skew.

docs.title: 11. Comparison & decision guide
docs.text: Default start: LightGBM or HistGB for speed; XGBoost for maturity, custom objectives, GPU, distributed; CatBoost for many categorical features or robust defaults. Always compare to a regularized linear model and a random forest; and confirm gains hold on time-ordered validation.

docs.title: 12. Pitfalls
docs.text: Tuning on the test set · early stopping on the same validation set used to report · leaking via target statistics · ignoring monotonic constraints when business requires them (monotone_constraints) · treating feature importance (gain/split count) as causal · different library defaults making "default vs default" comparisons unfair.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• What did XGBoost add over GBM? 2nd-order optimization, explicit regularization, sparsity-aware splits, systems engineering (parallel/histogram/out-of-core).
  • Level-wise vs leaf-wise? Level-wise grows balanced trees; leaf-wise chooses the highest-gain leaf, faster loss reduction but overfits small data.
  • Why does CatBoost have "ordered" boosting? Standard target statistics and gradients use the row's own label, causing prediction shift/leakage; ordering avoids it.
  • Which hyperparameters first? learning rate + early stopping, then depth/leaves and min child weight.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Reproduce the table with random search per model; add monotone constraints and measure the cost; compare gain, split-count and SHAP importance on the same model.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Chen & Guestrin (2016) "XGBoost: A scalable tree boosting system"; Ke et al. (2017) "LightGBM"; Prokhorenkova et al. (2018) "CatBoost: unbiased boosting with categorical features"; Grinsztajn, Oyallon & Varoquaux (2022) "Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on typical tabular data?"; official XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost docs.

docs.title: Chapter 3.5 — Probabilistic Models: Gaussian Mixtures, Hidden Markov Models, Bayesian Networks
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Prev 3.4 · Next 4.1 K-Means · Priority 🟡 · Code: probabilistic_models.py

(Placed here because all three are likelihood-based models trained with MLE/EM from Ch 0.2; GMMs reappear in clustering, Ch 4.1–4.2.)

docs.title: Identity & problem
docs.text: Soft clustering and density estimation: data come from K Gaussian "sources"; learn their means, covariances and mixing weights, and the probability each point belongs to each.

docs.title: History
docs.text: Pearson (1894) fitted two-component mixtures by moments; EM (Dempster, Laird & Rubin 1977) made maximum-likelihood fitting practical. K-Means is the hard-assignment, spherical, equal-variance limit of a GMM. Extensions: Bayesian/Dirichlet-process mixtures, mixtures of experts, mixtures of factor analyzers.

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: Each point has a probability of coming from each cluster; clusters can be elliptical and different sizes.

docs.title: Math
docs.text: p(x) = Σ_k π_k 𝒩(x|μ_k, Σ_k). Log-likelihood Σ_i log Σ_k π_k 𝒩(x_i|μ_k,Σ_k) has no closed form. EM: E-step responsibilities r_ik = π_k 𝒩(x_i|μ_k,Σ_k) / Σ_j π_j 𝒩(x_i|μ_j,Σ_j); M-step N_k=Σ_i r_ik, π_k=N_k/n, μ_k = Σ r_ik x_i / N_k, Σ_k = Σ r_ik (x_i−μ_k)(x_i−μ_k)ᵀ / N_k. Likelihood never decreases; converges to a local optimum (initialize with K-Means, multiple restarts). Worked example (1-D, one E-step). Two components: 𝒩(0,1) and 𝒩(4,1), equal weights. Point x=1: densities ∝ exp(−½·1²)=0.607 and exp(−½·9)=0.011 ⇒ responsibilities 0.607/(0.618)=0.982 vs 0.018. A point at x=2 (midpoint) gets 0.5/0.5. Model selection: BIC = p·ln n − 2 lnL̂ (lower is better); covariance types: full, tied, diag, spherical. Singularities: a component collapsing onto one point gives infinite likelihood ⇒ reg_covar.

docs.title: Training, cost
docs.text: Per iteration O(n·K·d²) (full covariance, plus d³ for inversions). Prediction O(K·d²). Memory O(K·d²).

docs.title: When to use / not
docs.text: Use: overlapping/elliptical clusters, need soft probabilities, density estimation, anomaly scores (low score_samples), generative sampling, speaker/background modeling. Avoid: non-Gaussian/non-convex clusters (DBSCAN/spectral), high dimensions with full covariance (parameter explosion; use diag/tied or PCA first), huge K without BIC check.

docs.title: Hyperparameters
docs.text: n_components, covariance_type, n_init, init_params (kmeans / k-means++ / random), reg_covar, max_iter, tol.

docs.title: Implementation & results (measured)
docs.text:
Two elongated, overlapping Gaussians (correlation ~0.85), 600 points: | Method | Adjusted Rand Index vs true labels | |---|---| | K-Means | 0.236 | | GMM (scratch EM) | 0.980 | | GMM (sklearn) | 0.980 | Average log-likelihood per point: scratch −4.213 = sklearn −4.213 (the from-scratch EM matches). K-Means fails because it assumes spherical clusters of equal spread. BIC over K=1…6 for 3 true blobs: 6531, 5007, 4782 (K=3), 4808, 4838, 4875 — minimum at the truth. 

from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture
gm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, covariance_type="full", n_init=5, random_state=0).fit(X)
resp = gm.predict_proba(X); bic = gm.bic(X); anomaly_score = gm.score_samples(X)
Scratch EM: see em_gmm in the code file.

docs.title: Identity & problem
docs.text: Sequence model with a hidden discrete state evolving as a Markov chain and observations emitted from the state. Used for speech (classic), part-of-speech tagging, gene finding, regime detection, activity recognition.

docs.title: History
docs.text: Markov chains (1906); Baum–Welch/EM training (Baum et al., late 1960s–70s); Viterbi (1967); Rabiner's 1989 tutorial made HMMs the workhorse of speech recognition until neural sequence models (Ch 5.3–5.4) replaced them. Successors: CRFs (Lafferty et al. 2001), RNN/LSTM, Transformers; state-space models/Kalman filters are the continuous-state analogue.

docs.title: Math
docs.text: Parameters: initial π, transitions A_ij=P(s_{t+1}=j|s_t=i), emissions B_i(o). Markov: P(s_t|s_{1:t−1}) = P(s_t|s_{t−1}); output independence. Three problems: evaluation (forward algorithm, O(T·K²)), decoding (Viterbi: most likely state sequence), learning (Baum–Welch EM). Worked example. States {Rainy, Sunny}; π=(0.6, 0.4); transitions Rainy→(0.7 Rainy, 0.3 Sunny), Sunny→(0.4, 0.6); emissions Rainy: walk 0.1, shop 0.4, clean 0.5; Sunny: walk 0.6, shop 0.3, clean 0.1. Observations: walk, shop, clean. Forward: α₁ = (0.6·0.1, 0.4·0.6) = (0.06, 0.24); α₂ = ((0.06·0.7+0.24·0.4)·0.4, (0.06·0.3+0.24·0.6)·0.3) = (0.0552, 0.0486); α₃ = (0.02904, 0.00457) ⇒ P(observations) = 0.0336. Viterbi: most likely hidden path Sunny → Rainy → Rainy (prob 0.01344), confirmed by brute force over all 8 paths. (Both are in probabilistic_models.py.)

docs.title: Cost, when to use
docs.text: Forward/Viterbi O(T·K²). Use for modest discrete-state sequences, interpretable regime switching, small data. Avoid for long-range dependencies, rich observations (use RNN/Transformer), or continuous latent dynamics (Kalman). Library: hmmlearn (GaussianHMM, CategoricalHMM); pomegranate.

docs.title: Identity & problem
docs.text: Directed acyclic graph encoding a factorization of a joint distribution: P(X₁…X_n) = Π P(X_i | Parents(X_i)). Gives interpretable causal-ish structure, handling missing evidence and reasoning under uncertainty (diagnosis, risk).

docs.title: History
docs.text: Pearl (1980s; Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems, 1988); belief propagation, junction-tree algorithm (Lauritzen & Spiegelhalter 1988); structure learning (PC algorithm, score-based search such as BIC/BDeu; Spirtes–Glymour–Scheines). Naive Bayes (Ch 2.3) is the simplest Bayesian network; HMMs are dynamic Bayesian networks; modern causal inference (Ch 6.4) builds on Pearl's graphs.

docs.title: Math & worked example (inference by enumeration)
docs.text: Network: Rain → Sprinkler, Rain → WetGrass, Sprinkler → WetGrass. P(R)=0.2; P(S|R)=0.01, P(S|¬R)=0.4; P(W|R,S)=0.99, P(W|R,¬S)=0.8, P(W|¬R,S)=0.9, P(W|¬R,¬S)=0. P(W=1) = 0.4484. P(R|W) = 0.3577 (up from the 0.20 prior). Explaining away: adding evidence that the sprinkler ran gives P(R|W,S) = 0.0068. The big drop is partly built into this CPT (the sprinkler almost never runs when it rains); the qualitative lesson is that once one cause is known, the other becomes less probable. Inference: exact (variable elimination, junction tree; NP-hard in general), approximate (sampling, variational). Learning parameters: MLE/Bayesian counts; structure: constraint- or score-based.

docs.title: When to use / not
docs.text: Use: small–medium problems with expert knowledge, need explanations and what-if reasoning, missing data. Avoid: large raw-data prediction tasks (boosting/NNs win), automatic structure discovery claims of causality without assumptions. Tools: pgmpy, pomegranate, bnlearn (R).

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: GMM = unsupervised density/clustering; HMM = sequences; Bayes nets = structured reasoning. All are generative (Ch 6.1 contrasts with discriminative models) and trade accuracy for interpretability and principled uncertainty.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• EM intuition? Alternate guessing the hidden assignments (E) and refitting parameters given them (M).
  • GMM vs K-Means? Soft vs hard, full covariance vs spherical.
  • Forward vs Viterbi? Sum over paths (likelihood) vs max over paths (best sequence).
  • Explaining away? Observing one cause lowers belief in competing causes of a shared effect.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Fit a GMM on 2-D Old Faithful-style data and choose K by BIC; run Baum–Welch with hmmlearn on a synthetic regime-switching series; compute P(S|W) in the sprinkler net by hand.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Dempster, Laird, Rubin (1977); Rabiner (1989) "A tutorial on HMMs and selected applications in speech recognition"; Pearl (1988); Koller & Friedman, Probabilistic Graphical Models; Bishop PRML Ch 9, 13, 8.

docs.title: Chapter 4.1 — K-Means and K-Medoids
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 3.5 · Next 4.2 Other clustering · Priority 🔴 · Code: unsupervised_family.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Partition unlabeled data into K compact groups, each represented by a centroid. Customer segmentation, vector quantization, image color compression, preprocessing (cluster features).

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Steinhaus (1956); Lloyd (Bell Labs 1957; published 1982) for signal quantization; Forgy (1965); MacQueen (1967) coined "k-means". K-Medoids/PAM (Kaufman & Rousseeuw 1987; CLARA/CLARANS for scale) uses actual data points as centers and any distance. k-means++ (Arthur & Vassilvitskii 2007) fixed bad initialization; Mini-batch k-means (Sculley 2010) for web scale. GMM (Ch 3.5) is the probabilistic generalization.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Drop K pins; assign every point to its nearest pin; move each pin to the average of its points; repeat until pins stop moving.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: Minimize within-cluster sum of squares (inertia): J = Σ_k Σ_{x∈C_k} ‖x − μ_k‖². Lloyd's algorithm alternates assignment and mean update; each step cannot increase J, so it converges, but only to a local minimum (NP-hard globally). Worked example. 1-D points 1, 2, 9, 10, 11; initial centers 1 and 10. Assign: {1,2} → c₁, {9,10,11} → c₂. Update: c₁=1.5, c₂=10. Cost = (0.5²+0.5²)+(1+0+1) = 2.5. Reassigning changes nothing ⇒ converged. Assumptions implied: roughly spherical, similar-sized, similar-density clusters; Euclidean distance meaningful; K known. Sensitive to scale and outliers (mean).

docs.title: 5. Training & cost
docs.text: O(n·K·d) per iteration, few dozen iterations typical; memory O(nd+Kd). Use k-means++ init and several restarts (n_init). Mini-batch for millions of rows (small accuracy loss). Prediction: nearest centroid O(Kd).

docs.title: 6. Choosing K
docs.text: Elbow on inertia (subjective); silhouette (Rousseeuw 1987): s = (b−a)/max(a,b) ∈ [−1,1], a = mean intra-cluster distance, b = mean nearest-other-cluster distance; gap statistic; BIC with GMM; stability across resamples; and — most importantly — usefulness to the business.

docs.title: 7. Evolution
docs.text: Step Improvement Cost Lloyd → k-means++ Much better/faster starts Slightly slower seeding → Mini-batch Scale Mild quality loss → K-Medoids (PAM) Robust to outliers, arbitrary distances O(K(n−K)²) classic; slower → K-Modes / K-Prototypes Categorical / mixed data Different dissimilarity → Fuzzy c-means, GMM Soft membership, elliptical shape More parameters → Spectral / DBSCAN Non-convex shapes Different assumptions (Ch 4.2)

docs.title: 8. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: large numeric data, roughly blob-like clusters, quick segmentation, feature learning (distance-to-centroid features), compression. Avoid: non-convex shapes, very different densities/sizes, high dimensions without reduction (distances concentrate), categorical data, outlier-heavy data (use medoids/HDBSCAN).

docs.title: 9. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Simple, fast, scalable, easy to interpret. − Needs K, local optima, spherical bias, scale- and outlier-sensitive, hard assignments, no notion of noise.

docs.title: 10. Hyperparameters
docs.text: n_clusters, init (k-means++/random), n_init (restarts), max_iter, tol, algorithm (lloyd/elkan), batch_size (mini-batch).

docs.title: 11. Implementation
docs.text:
def kmeans(X, K, iters=100, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); C = X[rng.choice(len(X), K, replace=False)]
    for _ in range(iters):
        lab = ((X[:, None] - C[None])**2).sum(2).argmin(1)
        newC = np.array([X[lab == k].mean(0) if (lab == k).any() else C[k] for k in range(K)])
        if np.allclose(newC, C): break
        C = newC
    return C, lab
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, MiniBatchKMeans
km = KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X_scaled)

docs.title: 12. Evaluation & results (measured; 800 points, 4 true blobs)
docs.text: K Inertia Silhouette 2 12838 0.624 3 6106 0.602 4 1966 0.701 5 1765 0.602 6 1609 0.493 7 1458 0.410 Inertia always falls with K (the elbow is at 4); silhouette peaks at the true K=4. Initialization matters: one random init gave inertia 6531 versus 1966 for k-means++ with 10 restarts (a bad local optimum merged/split clusters). Other evaluation: with labels, ARI/NMI; without, silhouette/Davies–Bouldin/Calinski–Harabasz, stability, downstream task performance. On non-spherical shapes K-Means fails: ARI 0.48 on moons, 0.00 on circles (vs 1.0 for density-based methods, Ch 4.2).

docs.title: 13. Case study
docs.text: Customer segmentation on RFM (recency, frequency, monetary): log-transform skewed features, standardize, choose K by silhouette + business interpretability, profile each cluster, validate stability across months, and track drift.

docs.title: 14. Comparison
docs.text: K-Means for compact blobs at scale; GMM when clusters are elliptical or you need probabilities; DBSCAN/HDBSCAN for arbitrary shapes and noise; hierarchical when you want a dendrogram; spectral for graph-like structure.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Does K-Means converge? Yes, to a local minimum (objective monotonic, finite partitions).
  • How choose K? Elbow/silhouette/gap/stability + domain use.
  • Why scale features? Distance is dominated by large-range variables.
  • K-Means vs GMM? Hard/spherical vs soft/elliptical; K-Means is GMM with shared spherical covariance and zero variance limit.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Implement k-means++ seeding; compare inertia over 100 random restarts; run K-Medoids on data with outliers and compare centers.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Lloyd (1982) IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory; MacQueen (1967); Arthur & Vassilvitskii (2007) "k-means++"; Kaufman & Rousseeuw, Finding Groups in Data; sklearn Clustering guide.

docs.title: Chapter 4.2 — Hierarchical, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, OPTICS, Mean Shift, Spectral Clustering
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Prev 4.1 · Next 4.3 PCA family · Priority 🟠 · Code: unsupervised_family.py

Different clustering algorithms encode different definitions of a cluster. Not a linear progression — pick by the shape/noise structure of your data.

Algorithm A cluster is… Needs K? Handles noise Shape K-Means (4.1) compact blob around a mean Yes No Convex, similar size Hierarchical a branch in a merge tree Cut level No Depends on linkage DBSCAN dense region separated by sparse No (eps, minPts) Yes Arbitrary HDBSCAN stable dense region across density levels No (min cluster size) Yes Arbitrary, varying density OPTICS density ordering, extract clusters No Yes Arbitrary Mean Shift mode of a density estimate No (bandwidth) Partly Blob-like modes Spectral connected group in a similarity graph Yes No Non-convex, graph-like

docs.title: A. Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering
docs.text: History: numerical taxonomy (Sokal & Sneath 1963), Ward's minimum-variance method (1963), dendrograms. Idea: start with each point alone; repeatedly merge the two closest clusters. Linkages: single (min distance; chains, finds elongated shapes, noise-sensitive), complete (max; compact), average (UPGMA), Ward (minimize variance increase; compact, K-Means-like). Worked example. Points A=1, B=2, C=6, D=7, E=15 (1-D). Single linkage: merge (A,B) at distance 1, (C,D) at 1; then {A,B} with {C,D} at 4 (B–C); then E joins at 8 (D–E). Cutting the dendrogram between heights 4 and 8 gives 2 clusters: {A,B,C,D}, {E}; cutting between 1 and 4 gives {A,B},{C,D},{E}. Cost O(n²) memory, O(n² log n)–O(n³) time ⇒ up to ~10⁴ points. No re-assignment (greedy merges are final). Use for small data, taxonomies, heatmap ordering, when you want a dendrogram. AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters, linkage="ward"), scipy.cluster.hierarchy.

docs.title: B. DBSCAN
docs.text: History: Ester, Kriegel, Sander & Xu, KDD 1996. Definitions: a point is a core point if ≥ min_samples points lie within radius eps; clusters are chains of density-reachable core points; non-reachable points are noise (label −1). Strengths: arbitrary shapes, automatic noise, no K; cost O(n log n) with spatial index. Weaknesses: single global eps cannot fit varying densities, sensitive to scaling, struggles in high-d; eps selection via k-distance plot (knee). Hyperparameters: eps, min_samples (≥ d+1; often 2·d), metric.

docs.title: C. HDBSCAN and OPTICS
docs.text: OPTICS (Ankerst et al. 1999) produces a reachability ordering, avoiding fixed eps. HDBSCAN (Campello, Moulavi & Sander 2013; McInnes et al. 2017) builds a hierarchy over all density levels and extracts the most stable clusters ⇒ handles varying densities with one intuitive parameter (min_cluster_size); gives soft membership/outlier scores. In scikit-learn ≥1.3 as HDBSCAN. Improvement over DBSCAN: variable density; cost: heavier compute, still sensitive in high-d.

docs.title: D. Mean Shift
docs.text: Fukunaga & Hostetler (1975); Comaniciu & Meer (2002). Each point climbs the gradient of a kernel density estimate to a mode; points reaching the same mode share a cluster. Bandwidth controls cluster count; O(n²); good for small low-dimensional data (tracking, image segmentation).

docs.title: E. Spectral clustering
docs.text: Shi & Malik (2000), Ng–Jordan–Weiss (2001). Build a similarity graph, compute the graph Laplacian L = D − W, embed points with its smallest eigenvectors, run K-Means there. Finds non-convex clusters connected by similarity (rings, moons). Needs K and a graph; eigen-decomposition O(n³) (sparse/approximate methods scale further). Use affinity="nearest_neighbors" for shapes.

docs.title: Measured comparison (Adjusted Rand Index, 600 points, standardized; default-ish parameters, not tuned)
docs.text: Dataset KMeans Ward Single DBSCAN(eps .3) HDBSCAN Spectral 3 blobs 0.98 0.93 0.57 0.57 0.57 0.99 Moons 0.48 0.64 1.00 1.00 0.99 1.00 Circles 0.00 0.00 1.00 1.00 1.00 1.00 Reading: centroid/variance methods win on blobs and fail on non-convex shapes; density/graph methods win on shapes but at these settings fragmented or flagged blob points as noise (0.57; blob std is large, so eps=0.3 is too small — a reminder that DBSCAN needs eps tuning). No algorithm is universally best.

docs.title: When to use what
docs.text: Data Choose Large, blobs, speed K-Means / mini-batch Overlapping ellipses, probabilities GMM Arbitrary shapes + noise DBSCAN / HDBSCAN Varying densities HDBSCAN Need a hierarchy/dendrogram, small n Ward / average Non-convex, graph structure, small–medium n Spectral High-dimensional embeddings Reduce (PCA/UMAP) first, then HDBSCAN/K-Means

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Internal: silhouette (biased toward convex clusters), Davies–Bouldin, DBCV (density-based). External (with labels): ARI, NMI, homogeneity/completeness. Practical: stability under subsampling, cluster profiles, downstream impact. Never trust one internal metric across algorithm families.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, SpectralClustering, MeanShift, OPTICS
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
d = np.sort(NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=5).fit(Xs).kneighbors(Xs)[0][:, -1])   # k-distance plot -> pick eps at the knee
labels = DBSCAN(eps=0.3, min_samples=5).fit_predict(Xs)                          # -1 = noise
labels = HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=20).fit_predict(Xs)
labels = SpectralClustering(2, affinity="nearest_neighbors", random_state=0).fit_predict(Xs)

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: Not scaling; treating noise label −1 as a cluster; picking eps blindly; clustering raw high-dimensional data; interpreting clusters as truth rather than a useful partition.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• DBSCAN vs K-Means? Density/arbitrary shape/noise/no K vs compact blobs/needs K.
  • Why HDBSCAN? Varying densities; one stable parameter.
  • Single vs Ward linkage? Single chains and detects elongated clusters but is noise-sensitive; Ward gives compact spherical clusters.
  • How pick eps? k-distance plot knee.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Produce a dendrogram for 20 points and cut it at 3 heights; tune DBSCAN on the blob set until ARI > 0.95; compare HDBSCAN vs DBSCAN on two clusters of different density.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Ester et al. (1996); Campello et al. (2013); McInnes, Healy & Astels (2017) "hdbscan: Hierarchical density based clustering"; von Luxburg (2007) "A tutorial on spectral clustering"; Comaniciu & Meer (2002); sklearn Clustering guide.

docs.title: Chapter 4.3 — PCA, SVD, Kernel PCA, ICA, NMF
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 4.2 · Next 4.4 t-SNE & UMAP · Priority 🔴 · Code: unsupervised_family.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Linear (or kernelized) dimensionality reduction / representation learning: compress many correlated features into a few informative ones, for visualization, denoising, speed, de-collinearization, compression.

docs.title: 2. History (several related inventions)
docs.text: PCA: Pearson (1901, best-fit lines), Hotelling (1933, principal components). SVD: Eckart–Young theorem (1936) — truncated SVD is the best low-rank approximation. Probabilistic PCA (Tipping & Bishop 1999). Kernel PCA: Schölkopf, Smola & Müller (1998). ICA: Comon (1994), FastICA (Hyvärinen 1999) — finds statistically independent sources (cocktail-party problem). NMF: Paatero & Tapper (1994), Lee & Seung (1999, Nature) — parts-based, non-negative factors. Nonlinear successors: autoencoders (Ch 5.5), t-SNE/UMAP for visualization (Ch 4.4). These answer different questions, not "versions" of each other.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Rotate the axes to line up with the directions where the data vary most; keep the first few. Like finding the best angle to photograph a cloud of points so its shadow keeps the most spread.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: Center X. Covariance Σ = XᵀX/(n−1). PCA = eigen-decomposition Σ = VΛVᵀ; PCs are columns of V; scores Z = XV_k. Equivalent: SVD X = UΣ_sVᵀ, λ_i = σ_i²/(n−1). Explained variance ratio λ_i/Σλ. Reconstruction X̂ = Z_kV_kᵀ minimizes squared error among rank-k linear maps. Worked example. Points (1,2),(2,3),(3,4),(4,5): mean (2.5,3.5); centered (−1.5,−1.5),(−0.5,−0.5),(0.5,0.5),(1.5,1.5). Σ = [[1.667,1.667],[1.667,1.667]], eigenvalues 3.333 and 0; PC1 = (1,1)/√2 holds 100% of the variance — the 2-D data are really 1-D. Kernel PCA: eigen-decompose the (centered) kernel matrix K_ij=k(x_i,x_j) — nonlinear structure, no explicit map; O(n³). ICA: find unmixing W maximizing non-Gaussianity (kurtosis/negentropy). NMF: X ≈ WH with W,H ≥ 0, minimizing Frobenius or KL error — additive "parts" (topics in text, spectral components, recommender factors). Assumptions: PCA — linear structure, variance = information (so standardize if units differ), orthogonal components; ICA — independent non-Gaussian sources; NMF — non-negative data.

docs.title: 5. Training & cost
