docs.text: PCA via SVD O(min(n,p)²·max(n,p)); randomized SVD (Halko et al. 2011) O(npk) for large matrices; IncrementalPCA for streaming; TruncatedSVD for sparse matrices (LSA) without centering. NMF: iterative multiplicative/coordinate updates, local minima.

docs.title: 6. Choosing k
docs.text: Scree plot/elbow; cumulative explained variance (90–99%); cross-validated downstream score; Minka's MLE (n_components="mle"); parallel analysis.

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: collinear features, visualization (2–3 PCs), noise reduction, speeding up distance/linear models, compressing embeddings, whitening. Avoid: when interpretability of original features is required, nonlinear manifolds (use Kernel PCA/UMAP/autoencoders), when target-relevant signal sits in low-variance directions (variance ≠ relevance; consider PLS or supervised selection), tree models (little benefit).

docs.title: 8. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Fast, deterministic, closed form, decorrelates, reconstruction guarantees. − Linear only, scale-sensitive, components hard to interpret, unsupervised (ignores y), sensitive to outliers (consider robust PCA).

docs.title: 9. Hyperparameters
docs.text: PCA: n_components (int or variance fraction), whiten, svd_solver (full/randomized/arpack). Kernel PCA: kernel, gamma, n_components. ICA: n_components, fun. NMF: n_components, init, beta_loss, alpha_W/H (regularization).

docs.title: 10. Implementation
docs.text:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA, KernelPCA, FastICA, NMF, TruncatedSVD
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
pca = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(n_components=0.95))     # keep 95% variance
# from scratch:
Xc = X - X.mean(0); U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False); Z = Xc @ Vt[:k].T; ratio = S**2 / (S**2).sum()

docs.title: 11. Evaluation & results (measured; 8×8 digits, 64 features)
docs.text: Components needed for 90% / 95% / 99% variance: 21 / 29 / 41. SVD and sklearn PCA agree exactly (variance ratios 0.1489, 0.1362, 0.1179 for the first three). Logistic regression 5-fold CV accuracy after PCA (inside the pipeline): | Components | Accuracy | |---|---| | 5 | 0.825 | | 10 | 0.891 | | 20 | 0.921 | | 64 (all) | 0.928 | 20 components (31% of the features) retain 99% of the full-feature accuracy (0.921 vs 0.928). Reconstruction MSE with 10 components: 0.0192 (pixels scaled to [0,1]). Kernel PCA vs linear on concentric circles (logistic regression on the 2-D embedding, CV accuracy): linear PCA 0.448 (chance), RBF Kernel PCA (γ=2) 1.000 — linear projection can't unfold rings; a kernel can.

docs.title: 12. Case study
docs.text: Image/embedding compression and decorrelation: standardize → PCA(0.95) → logistic/k-NN; compare accuracy, training time and memory. For text: TF-IDF → TruncatedSVD(100–300) = LSA; for topic parts use NMF and print top words per component.

docs.title: 13. Comparison
docs.text: PCA (global linear variance) vs ICA (independence) vs NMF (parts, positivity) vs Kernel PCA (nonlinear, O(n³)) vs LDA (supervised separation, Ch 2.4) vs t-SNE/UMAP (visualization; no meaningful inverse transform) vs autoencoders (flexible nonlinear). PCA is the default first thing to try.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• PCA vs SVD? PCA on centered data = SVD; right singular vectors are PCs.
  • Why standardize? Otherwise large-unit features dominate variance.
  • Are PCs ordered by importance for prediction? By variance, not predictive power.
  • When use NMF over PCA? Non-negative data needing additive, interpretable parts.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Prove PCs are eigenvectors of the covariance; reconstruct a digit with k=2,5,20,64 components; apply NMF to a text corpus and name the topics.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Hotelling (1933); Jolliffe, Principal Component Analysis; Halko, Martinsson & Tropp (2011); Lee & Seung (1999); Hyvärinen & Oja (2000) "Independent component analysis: algorithms and applications"; sklearn "Decomposing signals" guide.

docs.title: Chapter 4.4 — t-SNE and UMAP (Nonlinear Embeddings for Visualization)
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 4.3 · Next 4.5 Anomaly detection · Priority 🟠 · Code: unsupervised_family.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Map high-dimensional data to 2-D/3-D so that neighbors stay neighbors, mainly to look at structure (clusters, batches, outliers). Not a clustering algorithm and not a general-purpose feature extractor.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Earlier manifold learning: MDS (Torgerson 1952), Isomap and LLE (2000), Laplacian eigenmaps. SNE (Hinton & Roweis 2002) → t-SNE (van der Maaten & Hinton, JMLR 2008): symmetric affinities and a heavy-tailed Student-t in the low-dimensional space fixed SNE's "crowding problem". Barnes–Hut (2014) and FFT-based approximations made it practical. UMAP (McInnes, Healy & Melville 2018): fuzzy topological graph + cross-entropy layout; faster, scales better, preserves more global structure in practice. Related: LargeVis, TriMap, PaCMAP.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Measure "who is whose neighbor" in the original space as probabilities; place points in 2-D and push/pull them until the 2-D neighbor probabilities match.

docs.title: 4. Math (t-SNE)
docs.text: High-dim affinities p_{j|i} = exp(−‖x_i−x_j‖²/2σ_i²)/Σ_k exp(−‖x_i−x_k‖²/2σ_i²), with σ_i chosen so that the perplexity 2^{H(P_i)} (≈ effective neighbor count) equals a target; symmetrize p_ij=(p_{j|i}+p_{i|j})/2n. Low-dim: q_ij ∝ (1+‖y_i−y_j‖²)⁻¹. Minimize KL(P‖Q) by gradient descent. KL penalizes placing near points far apart much more than the reverse ⇒ local structure is preserved; distances between far clusters are not meaningful. Worked example (perplexity). A point whose neighbor distribution is uniform over 30 neighbors has entropy log₂30 and perplexity 30; σ_i is tuned per point to hit that value, so dense and sparse regions get comparable neighborhoods. UMAP: build a weighted k-NN graph (n_neighbors), symmetrize with fuzzy union, optimize a low-dimensional layout with attractive/repulsive forces (min_dist controls tightness).

docs.title: 5. Cost
docs.text: t-SNE: Barnes–Hut O(n log n) (FFT-accelerated variants faster), practical to ~10⁵ points. UMAP: approximate-NN graph (NN-descent) plus SGD layout; scales to millions of points. Measured on the 1,797-sample digits set (4 cores): t-SNE 9–10 s, UMAP 29 s (the UMAP figure includes one-time numba compilation, so it is not representative of steady-state speed). Both are stochastic: fix random_state; PCA-initialization stabilizes global layout.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: exploratory visualization of embeddings, single-cell data, checking label/batch structure, sanity-checking learned representations, pre-clustering view. Avoid: as input features to downstream models without care (t-SNE has no transform for new points; UMAP does), reading cluster sizes/distances/densities as quantitative, drawing conclusions from one run/one hyperparameter, very high-dimensional raw data (reduce with PCA to ~50 first).

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters
docs.text: t-SNE: perplexity (5–50; ≲ n/3), learning_rate ("auto"), n_iter/max_iter (≥1000), early_exaggeration, init="pca". UMAP: n_neighbors (local vs global emphasis; 15 default), min_dist (tight vs spread), metric, n_components.

docs.title: 8. Implementation
docs.text:
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
Z = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, init="pca", random_state=0).fit_transform(PCA(50).fit_transform(X))
import umap                       # pip install umap-learn
U = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1, random_state=0).fit(X); emb = U.embedding_; new = U.transform(Xnew)

docs.title: 9. Evaluation (measured, with caveats)
docs.text: Digits (10 classes): a 5-NN classifier on the 2-D embedding scores 0.976 (t-SNE) vs 0.603 (PCA-2), showing how much more local class structure survives in t-SNE. Caveat: t-SNE was fit on all the data (labels were not used, but the test points were part of the embedding), so this cross-validated number is optimistic and is a visualization-quality check only, not a model accuracy. Better embedding metrics: trustworthiness / continuity, k-NN preservation, and stability across seeds and parameters.

docs.title: 10. Common misreadings (Wattenberg, Viégas & Johnson 2016, "How to use t-SNE effectively")
docs.text: Cluster sizes mean nothing · distances between clusters mean little · random noise can look like clusters at low perplexity · results change with perplexity — always show several.

docs.title: 11. Comparison
docs.text: PCA t-SNE UMAP Linear Yes No No Global structure Preserved Weak Better, not guaranteed Speed Fastest Slow Fast transform new data Yes No Yes Deterministic Yes No No Best for features, compression local cluster view large-scale view, features for HDBSCAN

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why t-distribution? Heavy tails let moderately distant points sit farther apart, relieving the crowding problem.
  • Can I cluster on t-SNE? You can, but distances/densities are distorted; prefer clustering in the original or PCA space and use t-SNE to display.
  • PCA vs t-SNE? Linear global variance vs nonlinear local neighborhoods.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Embed digits with perplexity 5/30/100 and describe changes; run UMAP with n_neighbors 5/15/50; check seed stability.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: van der Maaten & Hinton (2008); McInnes, Healy & Melville (2018) "UMAP"; Wattenberg et al. (2016) Distill; Kobak & Berens (2019) "The art of using t-SNE for single-cell transcriptomics."

docs.title: Chapter 4.5 — Anomaly Detection: Isolation Forest, LOF, One-Class SVM, Robust Covariance
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 4.4 · Next 4.6 Association rules · Priority 🟠 · Code: unsupervised_family.py

docs.title: 1. Problem & framing
docs.text: Find rare observations that differ from the norm: fraud, intrusions, sensor faults, defects. Three regimes: supervised (labeled anomalies; use classifiers, Ch 3.4), semi-supervised / novelty detection (train on normal only), unsupervised outlier detection (contaminated unlabeled data). Anomalies are rare, evolving, and often poorly defined — evaluation and threshold choice are the hard parts.

docs.title: 2. Methods and history
docs.text: Method Idea Origin Statistical (z-score, MAD, Mahalanobis) Far from center in standardized units Classic Robust covariance / Elliptic Envelope Fit a Gaussian with the Minimum Covariance Determinant, flag large Mahalanobis distance Rousseeuw 1984/1999 LOF Compare a point's local density to its neighbors' Breunig, Kriegel, Ng, Sander 2000 One-Class SVM Max-margin boundary around normal data in kernel space Schölkopf et al. 2001 Isolation Forest Anomalies are easy to isolate by random splits Liu, Ting, Zhou 2008 (ICDM) Autoencoders / deep one-class, Time-series methods High reconstruction error / forecasting residual 2010s Evolution: distance/statistical → density (LOF handles varying density) → isolation (fast, no distance computation, scales) → deep models for complex data. Again, siblings, not a strict ladder.

docs.title: 3. Math highlights
docs.text: Isolation Forest: recursively split on a random feature at a random threshold; anomalies are isolated in few splits. Average path length E[h(x)] over trees; score s(x,n) = 2^{−E[h(x)]/c(n)}, c(n) = 2H(n−1) − 2(n−1)/n (H harmonic number). s→1 anomaly, s≈0.5 ambiguous, s→0 normal. Worked example. n=256: c(256) ≈ 2(ln 255 + 0.5772) − 2·255/256 ≈ 10.24. A point isolated after on average 3 splits: s = 2^{−3/10.24} = 0.816 (anomalous). A typical point with path 10.24: s = 0.5. LOF: LOF(x) = mean over neighbors o of lrd(o)/lrd(x) where local reachability density lrd is the inverse of the mean reachability distance; ≈1 normal, ≫1 outlier. One-class SVM: min ½‖w‖² + (1/νn)Σξ_i − ρ; ν upper-bounds the outlier fraction. Mahalanobis: d² = (x−μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x−μ) (≈ χ²_p for Gaussian data).

docs.title: 4. Complexity
docs.text: IsolationForest O(t·ψ log ψ) training with subsample size ψ (default 256) — linear in n, tiny memory; LOF O(n²) brute / O(n log n) with trees; OCSVM O(n²–n³); Elliptic Envelope O(np²) + MCD cost.

docs.title: 5. When to use / not
docs.text: Situation Prefer Tabular, many features, large n, no assumptions Isolation Forest Clusters of different density; local outliers matter LOF (novelty=True for new data) Unimodal Gaussian-like normal data, interpretable distance Robust covariance Small n, smooth boundary, kernel structure One-Class SVM (scale features, tune γ, ν) Labeled anomalies exist Supervised model (PR-AUC) Images/sequences Autoencoders / forecasting residuals Avoid: assuming "unsupervised outlier = business-relevant anomaly" without feedback; using accuracy as the metric; high-dimensional distance methods without reduction.

docs.title: 6. Hyperparameters
docs.text: IF: n_estimators, max_samples, contamination (sets threshold only), max_features. LOF: n_neighbors (20 typical), contamination, novelty. OCSVM: nu, gamma, kernel. EllipticEnvelope: contamination, support_fraction.

docs.title: 7. Implementation
docs.text:
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor
from sklearn.svm import OneClassSVM
from sklearn.covariance import EllipticEnvelope
iso = IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(X);  score = -iso.score_samples(X)   # higher = more anomalous
lof = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20).fit(X);                  score = -lof.negative_outlier_factor_
oc  = OneClassSVM(nu=0.03, gamma="scale").fit(X);                 score = -oc.score_samples(X)
ee  = EllipticEnvelope(contamination=0.03).fit(X);                score = ee.mahalanobis(X)

docs.title: 8. Evaluation & results (measured)
docs.text: Setup: 1,000 normal points from two Gaussian clusters + 30 uniform random outliers (2.9%); labels used only for scoring. | Method | ROC-AUC | Average precision | |---|---|---| | Isolation Forest | 0.983 | 0.798 | | LOF (k=20) | 0.983 | 0.897 | | One-Class SVM | 0.963 | 0.772 | | Elliptic Envelope (assumes one Gaussian) | 0.960 | 0.714 | Reading: all work well on this easy 2-D problem; the single-Gaussian envelope is the worst because the normal data are bimodal (assumption violated); LOF has the best precision here. In real high-dimensional data expect larger gaps — evaluate on your data. How to evaluate in practice: with a small labeled set use PR-AUC / precision@k / recall at fixed alert budget; without labels, inspect top-ranked items with domain experts, track alert precision over time, and simulate injected anomalies.

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls
docs.text: Setting contamination arbitrarily (it just picks the threshold) · concept drift (retrain/monitor) · scale and categorical encoding · duplicate/near-duplicate normal patterns · tuning on the same anomalies you evaluate on · alert fatigue (choose the threshold from the cost of review).

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why does Isolation Forest work? Anomalies are few and different ⇒ shorter average isolation paths.
  • LOF vs Isolation Forest? LOF = local density, handles varying densities but quadratic; IF = global-ish random partitioning, fast, scalable.
  • Metric for imbalanced anomaly data? PR-AUC, precision@k.
  • Novelty vs outlier detection? Train on clean normal data vs find outliers inside contaminated data.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Add 50 irrelevant features and re-run the table; implement isolation trees in 30 lines; compare thresholds chosen by contamination vs by cost.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Liu, Ting & Zhou (2008); Breunig et al. (2000); Schölkopf et al. (2001); Chandola, Banerjee & Kumar (2009) "Anomaly detection: a survey"; sklearn "Novelty and outlier detection".

docs.title: Chapter 4.6 — Association Rules: Apriori, FP-Growth, Eclat
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 4.5 · Next 4.7 Feature selection · Priority ⚪ · Code: unsupervised_family.py

docs.title: 1. Problem
docs.text: Find items that frequently occur together in transactions ("market basket"): {diapers} → {beer}. Used for cross-sell, store layout, web-usage patterns, bundle design, log-pattern mining.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Association rules: Agrawal, Imielinski & Swami (1993). Apriori: Agrawal & Srikant (1994) — the downward-closure pruning idea. Eclat: Zaki (2000), vertical tid-list intersections. FP-Growth: Han, Pei & Yin (2000) — compresses the database into a prefix tree and avoids candidate generation. Successors: sequential pattern mining (GSP, PrefixSpan), and for recommendation, collaborative filtering/matrix factorization (Ch 6.2), which scale better and personalize.

docs.title: 3. Definitions
docs.text: For itemsets A, B over N transactions: support(A) = #(A)/N; confidence(A→B) = support(A∪B)/support(A); lift(A→B) = support(A∪B)/(support(A)·support(B)) (>1 positive association); also leverage, conviction. Apriori principle (downward closure): every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent ⇒ if {A} is infrequent, no superset can be frequent ⇒ prune the search space.

docs.title: 4. Worked example
docs.text: 5 baskets: {bread, milk}; {bread, diaper, beer, eggs}; {milk, diaper, beer, cola}; {bread, milk, diaper, beer}; {bread, milk, diaper, cola}. support(diaper) = 4/5 = 0.8; support(beer) = 0.6; support(diaper, beer) = 3/5 = 0.6. Rule diaper → beer: confidence = 0.6/0.8 = 0.75, lift = 0.6/(0.8·0.6) = 1.25. With minimum support 0.4 the frequent pairs include {beer,diaper}(0.6), {bread,diaper}(0.6), {bread,milk}(0.6), {diaper,milk}(0.6) (verified by the code). Five baskets are far too few to trust — real mining needs thousands.

docs.title: 5. Algorithms and cost
docs.text: Algorithm How Strength Weakness Apriori Level-wise candidate generation + pruning, multiple DB scans Simple, educational Many scans, candidate explosion FP-Growth FP-tree, recursive conditional mining Usually fastest, two scans Memory for tree Eclat Vertical format, intersect transaction-id sets Fast on dense small data Memory of tid-lists Worst case exponential in the number of items; cost controlled mainly by min support.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: exploratory basket analysis, rule-based recommendations, interpretable patterns, discovering co-occurrence in logs/alarms. Avoid: personalized recommendation at scale (use CF/MF), causal claims ("beer causes diapers"), very low support thresholds (explosion), sparse long-tail catalogs (most items below support), noisy time-ordered behavior (use sequence models).

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters & selection
docs.text: min_support (main control; start high), min_confidence, min_lift, max_len. Filter rules by lift and by business actionability; beware spurious rules from multiple testing and popular-item bias (high-confidence rules into a very popular consequent have lift ≈ 1).

docs.title: 8. Implementation
docs.text:
# pip install mlxtend
from mlxtend.preprocessing import TransactionEncoder
from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import fpgrowth, association_rules
te = TransactionEncoder(); df = pd.DataFrame(te.fit(tx).transform(tx), columns=te.columns_)
freq = fpgrowth(df, min_support=0.4, use_colnames=True)
rules = association_rules(freq, metric="lift", min_threshold=1.0)
From scratch: count single items, keep those ≥ min support, join frequent k-itemsets into (k+1)-candidates, prune candidates with an infrequent subset, repeat (see the toy Apriori in unsupervised_family.py).

docs.title: 9. Evaluation
docs.text: Rules are descriptive, so evaluate by business impact: A/B test cross-sell placements; hold-out time period to check rule stability (support/confidence persistence); precision of top-k rule-based recommendations vs a popularity baseline.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Support/confidence/lift? Frequency, conditional probability of consequent, and strength relative to independence.
  • Why Apriori prunes? Downward closure: a superset cannot be more frequent than any subset.
  • Why lift over confidence? Confidence is inflated when the consequent is simply popular.
  • Apriori vs FP-Growth? Candidate generation with repeated scans vs tree compression with two scans.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Compute all rules from the toy baskets with lift > 1; implement Eclat with Python sets; compare runtime of Apriori vs FP-Growth as min-support drops.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Agrawal & Srikant (1994); Han, Pei & Yin (2000); Zaki (2000); Aggarwal, Data Mining: The Textbook (frequent patterns chapters); mlxtend docs.

docs.title: Chapter 4.7 — Feature Selection: Filter, Wrapper, Embedded
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 4.6 · Next 5.1 MLP & backprop · Priority 🟠 · Code: unsupervised_family.py

docs.title: 1. Problem
docs.text: Choose a subset of features to improve generalization, speed, interpretability and cost-to-collect. Distinct from dimensionality reduction (PCA creates new features; selection keeps original ones).

docs.title: 2. Taxonomy (Guyon & Elisseeff 2003)
docs.text: Family Idea Examples Pros Cons Filter Score features independent of the model variance threshold, correlation, ANOVA F, χ², mutual information, ReliefF Fast, model-agnostic Ignores interactions & redundancy Wrapper Search subsets using model performance forward/backward selection, RFE (Guyon et al. 2002, SVM-RFE), genetic search Model-aware, captures interactions Expensive, overfits selection Embedded Selection happens during training L1/Lasso, ElasticNet, tree importances, regularized boosting, group lasso Efficient, principled Model-specific Other Boruta (Kursa & Rudnicki 2010; compares to shadow features), permutation importance, SHAP-based pruning, stability selection (Meinshausen & Bühlmann 2010) Robustness Compute

docs.title: 3. Math notes
docs.text: Mutual information I(X;Y) = Σ p(x,y) log[p(x,y)/(p(x)p(y))] captures nonlinear dependence (estimated by k-NN estimators). ANOVA F: between-group over within-group variance. Redundancy: two highly correlated informative features both score high individually (mRMR trades relevance against redundancy). Lasso embedded selection: coefficients driven to exactly 0 (Ch 1.3). Worked example. Feature X has correlation 0.5 with y, feature Z has 0.5 and corr(X,Z)=0.9. A filter ranks both top; a wrapper/embedded method keeps one because the second adds little given the first.

docs.title: 4. The cardinal rule
docs.text: Selection is part of the model. Do it inside cross-validation (Pipeline). Selecting on the full data first leaks label information — Ch 0.5 showed noise features producing 0.86 "accuracy" on random labels.

docs.title: 5. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: p ≫ n, collection costs, regulation/interpretability, noisy irrelevant features, linear/SVM/kNN models (sensitive to junk). Often unnecessary for boosted trees/forests with moderate p (they ignore junk), but can reduce latency and cost. Avoid: selecting by univariate p-values then claiming inference; keeping selection stability unexamined.

docs.title: 6. Hyperparameters
docs.text: k / threshold (choose by CV, e.g. RFECV), scoring function, estimator for RFE, step size, L1 strength C/alpha, stability-selection subsample count.

docs.title: 7. Implementation
docs.text:
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif, mutual_info_classif, RFE, RFECV, SelectFromModel
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
filt = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SelectKBest(f_classif, k=10), LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000))
wrap = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), RFE(LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000), n_features_to_select=10), LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000))
emb  = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(penalty="l1", solver="liblinear", C=0.1))

docs.title: 8. Evaluation & results (measured)
docs.text: Breast cancer (30 real features) + 100 pure-noise features (130 total); 5-fold CV accuracy, selection inside the pipeline: | Approach | Accuracy | |---|---| | All 130 features | 0.947 | | Filter: ANOVA top-10 | 0.951 | | Filter: mutual information top-10 | 0.951 | | Wrapper: RFE → 10 | 0.968 | | Embedded: L1 logistic (C=0.1) | 0.972 | All three families beat "keep everything" (0.947), with wrapper/embedded ahead of simple filters. The ANOVA filter's top-10 contained 0 noise features (so its gap to the others reflects the redundancy/interaction handling, not noise leakage). For reference, the clean 30-feature logistic model scores 0.979 (Ch 2.1): the 100 noise columns cost ~3 points that selection recovers most of. With more noise columns or fewer rows the gap widens.

docs.title: 9. Pitfalls
docs.text: Selection outside CV · unstable selections (report frequency across folds/bootstraps) · treating importance as causation · dropping features needed for fairness audits · correlated groups (Lasso picks arbitrarily; use ElasticNet/group methods) · impurity importance bias (use permutation).

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Filter vs wrapper vs embedded? Score independently vs search with the model vs selection inside training.
  • Why not select features on the entire dataset first? Information leakage inflates validation scores.
  • Do trees need feature selection? Less so; they down-weight irrelevant features, but selection can cut cost and variance.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Add more noise columns and plot accuracy vs number of noise features for each family; implement forward selection with CV; run stability selection with Lasso.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Guyon & Elisseeff (2003) JMLR; Guyon et al. (2002) SVM-RFE; Kursa & Rudnicki (2010) Boruta; Meinshausen & Bühlmann (2010); Kuhn & Johnson, Feature Engineering and Selection.

docs.title: Chapter 5.1 — Neural Networks: Perceptron → MLP → Backpropagation
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Prev 4.7 · Next 5.2 CNNs · Priority 🔴 · Code: deep_learning_numpy.py

Code note: NumPy code in this phase was executed and its numbers are quoted. PyTorch snippets are shown for practice but were not executed in the authoring environment (no PyTorch installed); treat them as templates and verify before use.

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: A multilayer perceptron (MLP) stacks linear maps with nonlinear activations to learn nonlinear functions from data. Backpropagation computes all gradients efficiently so gradient descent (Ch 0.3) can train it. Foundation of all deep learning.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: McCulloch–Pitts neuron (1943) → Rosenblatt perceptron (1958) → Minsky & Papert (1969) show single-layer limits (XOR) → reverse-mode differentiation (Linnainmaa 1970), applied to nets by Werbos (1974) → Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams (1986) popularize backprop with learned internal representations → universal approximation (Cybenko 1989; Hornik 1991) → second winter (SVMs/boosting dominate small data) → renaissance: GPUs, ReLU (Nair & Hinton 2010), better init (Glorot 2010; He 2015), dropout (2014), BatchNorm (2015), Adam (2014), big data (ImageNet) → deep learning.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Each layer re-describes the input in a more useful way; the last layer is just logistic/linear regression on those learned features. Backprop answers "how much did each weight contribute to the error?" by passing blame backwards with the chain rule.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: Layer: a⁰=x, z^l = W^l a^{l−1} + b^l, a^l = φ(z^l). Output loss L (cross-entropy for classification with softmax: p=softmax(z^L), L=−log p_y). Backprop: output error δ^L = p − y_onehot; propagate δ^{l} = (W^{l+1})ᵀ δ^{l+1} ⊙ φ'(z^l); gradients ∂L/∂W^l = δ^l (a^{l−1})ᵀ, ∂L/∂b^l = δ^l. Activations: sigmoid 1/(1+e^{−z}) (saturates; σ'≤0.25), tanh, ReLU max(0,z) (default; dead-unit risk), Leaky ReLU, GELU/SiLU (Transformers). Universal approximation says a wide enough single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function; depth makes it efficient. Worked example. x=1, h=ReLU(w₁x), ŷ=w₂h, target y=1, w₁=0.5, w₂=−1, L=(ŷ−y)². Forward: h=0.5, ŷ=−0.5, L=2.25. Backward: dL/dŷ=2(ŷ−y)=−3; dL/dw₂ = −3·h = −1.5; dL/dh = −3·w₂ = 3; ReLU' = 1 (z>0) ⇒ dL/dw₁ = 3·x = 3. Step lr=0.1: w₂=−0.85, w₁=0.2. New forward: h=0.2, ŷ=−0.17, L=1.369 (down from 2.25). Vanishing gradients: a product of many sigmoid derivatives shrinks geometrically — 0.25¹⁰ ≈ 9.5×10⁻⁷, 0.25³⁰ ≈ 8.7×10⁻¹⁹ — which is why ReLU, good initialization, normalization and residual connections matter. Initialization: He N(0, 2/fan_in) for ReLU, Glorot for tanh. Assumptions: differentiable model/loss; i.i.d. data; no convexity — local minima/saddles exist but wide nets train well in practice.

docs.title: 5. Training
docs.text: Mini-batch SGD/AdamW; epochs; learning-rate schedule; weight decay; dropout; early stopping; batch/layer norm; gradient clipping. Cost: forward+backward ≈ 3× forward FLOPs; parameters Σ(fan_in·fan_out + fan_out). Memory: activations stored for backward pass (checkpointing trades compute for memory).

docs.title: 6. Evolution & trade-offs
docs.text: Step Gain Cost Perceptron → MLP Non-linear boundaries (XOR) Non-convex training Sigmoid/tanh → ReLU/GELU Faster, no saturation Dead units; need init care + Dropout/BatchNorm/LayerNorm/Residuals Regularize and train deeper Extra hyperparameters MLP → CNN/RNN/Transformer Exploit structure (grid/sequence/set) Architecture-specific For plain tabular data, tuned gradient boosting usually matches or beats MLPs (Grinsztajn et al. 2022; Shwartz-Ziv & Armon 2022).

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: large data, unstructured inputs via embeddings, multi-output tasks, differentiable pipelines, a head on pretrained features. Avoid: small tabular data (use GBMs/linear), when interpretability/latency/simplicity dominate, no GPU budget for big models.

docs.title: 8. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Depth/width, activation, learning rate (most important), batch size, optimizer, weight decay, dropout rate, init, normalization, epochs/early stopping, LR schedule. Typical order: LR → architecture size → regularization.

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
From scratch (full MLP with softmax cross-entropy and backprop is in deep_learning_numpy.py, class MLP): 

def grads(self, X, Y):
    P = self.forward(X); n = len(X); d = P.copy(); d[np.arange(n), Y] -= 1; d /= n      # dL/dz_out = p - onehot
    for i in reversed(range(len(self.W))):
        gW.insert(0, self.as_[i].T @ d); gb.insert(0, d.sum(0))
        if i > 0: d = (d @ self.W[i].T) * self._df(self.zs[i-1])                         # chain rule through activation
PyTorch template (not executed here): 
import torch, torch.nn as nn
net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.1), nn.Linear(64, 10))
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(net.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-2); lossf = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
for xb, yb in loader: opt.zero_grad(); lossf(net(xb), yb).backward(); opt.step()
Always gradient-check a new layer: compare backprop with finite differences. Measured: max |analytic − numeric| = 2.5×10⁻¹⁰ (✓ correct).

docs.title: 10. Evaluation & results (measured)
docs.text:
• XOR: network with no hidden layer → accuracy 0.5 (cannot learn); one hidden layer (4 tanh units) → 1.0.
  • Digits (8×8, 1,347 train / 450 test): scratch NumPy MLP (64-64-10, 4,810 parameters, 60 epochs) test accuracy 0.973; scikit-learn MLP 0.973; multinomial logistic regression 0.969. On this small, nearly linear problem the net adds little over the linear baseline — a recurring lesson: always report the linear baseline. Diagnostics: training/validation loss curves, gradient norms, activation statistics, learning-rate range test, overfit a tiny batch first.

docs.title: 11. Case study
docs.text: Tabular churn with embeddings for categorical IDs: compare logistic, LightGBM and an MLP with embeddings on a time-based split; typically the GBM wins or ties on moderate data, the MLP helps with very high-cardinality IDs and multi-task learning.

docs.title: 12. Comparison
docs.text: vs logistic regression: nonlinear but needs tuning and more data. vs trees/GBMs: better for unstructured data, worse default on tabular. vs SVM: scale better with n, no convex guarantee.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why nonlinear activations? Without them any depth collapses to one linear map.
  • Explain backprop in two sentences. Cache forward activations; apply the chain rule from the loss backwards, reusing the downstream gradient at every layer.
  • Why ReLU over sigmoid? No saturation for positive inputs, cheaper, mitigates vanishing gradients.
  • What does BatchNorm do? Normalizes activations per batch, stabilizing and speeding training (the exact mechanism is debated).
  • Overfitting remedies? More data/augmentation, weight decay, dropout, early stopping, smaller model.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Re-derive the softmax cross-entropy gradient p − y; implement momentum/Adam in the scratch MLP; train with sigmoid vs ReLU at depth 10 and compare gradient norms.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams (1986) Nature; Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, Deep Learning (Ch 6–8); Karpathy "micrograd" and "The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation"; He et al. (2015) init; Glorot & Bengio (2010).

docs.title: Chapter 5.2 — Convolutional Networks: LeNet → AlexNet → VGG → Inception → ResNet → EfficientNet → Vision Transformers
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 5.1 · Next 5.3 Sequence models · Priority 🔴 · Code: deep_learning_numpy.py (conv demo; PyTorch snippets unexecuted)

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Networks for grid-structured data (images, spectrograms, some text/time series) using local, weight-shared filters. Exploit translation structure: a cat is a cat anywhere in the image.

docs.title: 2. History — the lineage with what each step changed
docs.text: Year Model Key advance Remaining limitation 1980 Neocognitron (Fukushima) Hierarchical local feature detectors Not trained by backprop 1989–98 LeNet-5 (LeCun) Conv + pooling trained end-to-end by backprop; digit recognition Small data/compute 2012 AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton) GPU training, ReLU, dropout, data augmentation; ImageNet error leap Large dense layers; hand-tuned 2014 VGG (Simonyan & Zisserman) Deep stacks of 3×3 convs ~138M params (VGG-16), slow 2014 Inception/GoogLeNet (Szegedy et al.) Multi-scale parallel branches, 1×1 bottlenecks, efficiency Complex design 2015 ResNet (He et al.) Residual connections y=F(x)+x make 50–150+ layer nets trainable Still fixed-size design 2017 DenseNet, MobileNet (depthwise-separable convs), SENet Feature reuse / efficiency / channel attention — 2019 EfficientNet (Tan & Le) Compound scaling of depth, width, resolution (NAS-found base) Training cost 2020 Vision Transformer (ViT) (Dosovitskiy et al.) Patches + Transformer; scales well with big data/pretraining Needs lots of data or pretraining; less inductive bias 2022 ConvNeXt (Liu et al.) Modernized CNN matching Transformers — Pattern: each step fixed a training or efficiency bottleneck of the previous one. CNNs did not "lose" to ViTs outright; hybrids and modern CNNs remain competitive, especially with limited data/compute.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Slide a small filter over the image; each position produces a "how much does this pattern appear here?" score. Early layers detect edges, later ones textures, parts, objects.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: 2-D convolution (cross-correlation in practice): Y[i,j] = Σ_{u,v} K[u,v]·X[i+u, j+v] + b. Output size ⌊(W − K + 2P)/S⌋ + 1. Parameters of a conv layer K·K·C_in·C_out + C_out — independent of image size. Pooling reduces resolution/adds invariance; receptive field grows with depth. Worked example. Image [[1,2,0,1],[3,1,2,0],[0,1,3,2],[1,0,2,1]], kernel [[1,0],[0,−1]] (stride 1, no padding) → 3×3 output [[0,0,0],[2,−2,0],[0,−1,2]] (top-left: 1·1 + 2·0 + 3·0 + 1·(−1) = 0). Parameter efficiency (computed): a 3×3 conv from 64→64 channels has 36,928 parameters; a fully connected layer mapping a 32×32×64 map to a same-size map would need 4.29×10⁹. Residual block: y = ReLU(F(x) + x) — gradient has an identity path ∂y/∂x = I + ∂F/∂x, so signals/gradients flow through very deep nets; if the optimal map is near identity, F just learns ≈0. Assumptions/inductive bias: locality, translation equivariance (not rotation/scale invariance), hierarchical composition.

docs.title: 5. Training & cost
docs.text: SGD+momentum or AdamW, large batches, augmentation (crop, flip, color jitter, mixup/CutMix, RandAugment), label smoothing, BatchNorm, weight decay, cosine LR. FLOPs ∝ H·W·K²·C_in·C_out. Transfer learning (pretrain on ImageNet-scale, fine-tune) is the default workflow for small datasets.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: image classification/detection/segmentation, audio spectrograms, medical imaging, 1-D CNNs for signals/text, feature extractors. Prefer pretrained models/fine-tuning over training from scratch. Avoid: tabular data, tiny datasets without transfer learning, tasks needing global/long-range reasoning without attention (consider ViT/hybrids), strict latency on CPU without efficient variants (MobileNet, EfficientNet-Lite, quantization).

docs.title: 7. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Few parameters per capability, strong priors, mature tooling, fast inference. − Not rotation/scale invariant, adversarial sensitivity, needs lots of labeled data (or pretraining), texture bias, black-box.

docs.title: 8. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Kernel size, channels, depth, stride/padding, pooling, normalization, augmentation strength, learning rate/schedule, weight decay, resolution, batch size, pretrained backbone choice, fine-tuning scope (freeze vs unfreeze, discriminative LRs).

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
From scratch: the sliding-window loop above. PyTorch fine-tuning template (not executed here): 

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torchvision
m = torchvision.models.resnet18(weights="DEFAULT")            # pretrained backbone
m.fc = nn.Linear(m.fc.in_features, num_classes)               # new head
for p in list(m.parameters())[:-2]: p.requires_grad = False   # stage 1: train head only; later unfreeze with a small LR

docs.title: 10. Evaluation
docs.text: Top-1/top-5 accuracy, per-class precision/recall (imbalance), confusion matrix, mAP/IoU for detection/segmentation, calibration, robustness tests (corruptions, distribution shift), Grad-CAM for sanity checks, latency/memory on target hardware. Hold out by source (patient/site/camera) to avoid leakage.

docs.title: 11. Case study (template)
docs.text: Defect detection with ~2k labeled images: baseline = HOG/color features + logistic regression; model = pretrained ResNet-18/EfficientNet fine-tune with augmentation; report PR-AUC, threshold at required recall, error gallery. Expect transfer learning to beat scratch training by a wide margin at this data scale (a typical, not guaranteed, result—measure).

docs.title: 12. Comparison
docs.text: CNN vs ViT: CNNs have inductive bias and win with less data; ViTs scale better with huge pretraining and unify modalities. CNN vs MLP: weight sharing and locality. Modern default: pretrained backbone (CNN or ViT) + task head.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why do convs work for images? Locality + weight sharing → few params, translation equivariance.
  • What problem do residual connections solve? Degradation/vanishing gradients in very deep nets via identity shortcuts.
  • Why 3×3 stacks (VGG)? Same receptive field as large kernels with fewer params and more nonlinearity.
  • 1×1 convolution? Per-pixel channel mixing; bottlenecks and dimension reduction.
  • Equivariance vs invariance? Conv is translation-equivariant; pooling/global pooling adds (approximate) invariance.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Compute output sizes and parameter counts for a given stack by hand; implement conv with im2col; fine-tune a small pretrained CNN on a 10-class subset and compare to training from scratch.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: LeCun et al. (1998) "Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition"; Krizhevsky et al. (2012); Simonyan & Zisserman (2014); Szegedy et al. (2014); He et al. (2015) "Deep residual learning"; Tan & Le (2019); Dosovitskiy et al. (2020); Liu et al. (2022) "A ConvNet for the 2020s"; CS231n notes.

docs.title: Chapter 5.3 — Sequence Models: RNN → LSTM/GRU → TCN → Seq2Seq
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 5.2 · Next 5.4 Attention & Transformers · Priority 🟠 · Code: deep_learning_numpy.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Model ordered data (text, audio, time series, events) where context from earlier steps matters. Predict next element, classify a sequence, or map sequence → sequence (translation).

docs.title: 2. History and what each step fixed
docs.text: Year Model Fixes Leaves 1986–90 Jordan/Elman RNN Hidden state carries memory; weight sharing across time Vanishing/exploding gradients; short memory (Hochreiter 1991; Bengio et al. 1994) 1997 LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber); forget gate (Gers et al. 2000) Additive cell state with gates preserves gradients Sequential compute, many parameters 2014 GRU (Cho et al.) Fewer gates, similar performance Same sequential bottleneck 2014 Seq2Seq (Sutskever et al.; Cho et al.) Encoder–decoder for variable-length input/output Fixed-size bottleneck vector 2014 Attention (Bahdanau et al.) Decoder looks at all encoder states Still recurrent 2016–18 WaveNet, TCN (Bai et al.) Dilated causal convolutions: parallel training, long receptive field Fixed receptive field 2017 Transformer (Vaswani et al.) Drops recurrence; fully parallel (Ch 5.4) Quadratic attention cost 2021– State-space models (S4, Mamba) Linear-time long-range modeling Newer, less mature ecosystem Siblings rather than a ladder: LSTMs/GRUs still serve small, streaming, low-latency and edge cases.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: An RNN reads left to right, updating a "memory" vector. LSTM adds valves: forget what's stale, write what's new, reveal what's relevant. Plain RNNs forget because gradients are multiplied by the same weights many times.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: Vanilla RNN: h_t = tanh(W_h h_{t−1} + W_x x_t + b); output y_t = W_y h_t. BPTT unrolls time; gradient through T steps involves Π ∂h_t/∂h_{t−1}, which vanishes/explodes depending on the largest singular value of W_h and the activation derivative (clip gradients for exploding case). LSTM: f=σ(W_f[x,h]+b_f), i=σ(W_i·), o=σ(W_o·), g=tanh(W_g·); c_t = f⊙c_{t−1} + i⊙g; h_t = o⊙tanh(c_t). The additive c_t update gives a gradient highway when f≈1. GRU: update gate z, reset gate r: h_t = (1−z)⊙h_{t−1} + z⊙h̃_t. Worked example (one LSTM step, scalars, all weights 1). x=0.5, h_{t−1}=0.1, c_{t−1}=0.2. Pre-activation 0.6 for every gate: f=i=o=σ(0.6)=0.6457, g=tanh(0.6)=0.5370. c_t = 0.6457·0.2 + 0.6457·0.5370 = 0.4759; h_t = 0.6457·tanh(0.4759) = 0.2860 (verified in code). Param counts: LSTM layer with input d, hidden h: 4·h·(d+h+1); GRU 3·h·(d+h+1). Training objectives: teacher forcing for generation; CTC for alignment-free speech; seq2seq cross-entropy.

docs.title: 5. Cost
docs.text: Compute O(T·h²), but inherently sequential in T (no parallelism across time) ⇒ slow to train on GPUs vs Transformers. Inference is cheap and constant-memory per step — good for streaming. Truncated BPTT limits memory.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: streaming/online inference, small datasets, low-latency edge devices, sensor/time-series with modest context, as a baseline. Avoid: very long dependencies, large-scale language modeling, tasks where parallel training matters — use Transformers/SSMs; for tabular lag features use boosted trees (Ch 6.1).

docs.title: 7. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Natural for sequences, variable length, constant-memory inference. − Hard to parallelize, long-range memory still limited, tricky to train (clipping, init), largely superseded for NLP.

docs.title: 8. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Hidden size, layers, bidirectional, dropout (variational/recurrent), sequence length/truncation, gradient clipping (norm 1–5), embedding dimension, teacher-forcing ratio, optimizer/LR, batch size (pad + mask).

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
NumPy: the LSTM step in deep_learning_numpy.py. PyTorch template (not executed here): 

import torch.nn as nn
class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(s, d, h, k): super().__init__(); s.rnn = nn.LSTM(d, h, num_layers=2, batch_first=True, dropout=0.2); s.out = nn.Linear(h, k)
    def forward(s, x): o, _ = s.rnn(x); return s.out(o[:, -1])        # last hidden state -> prediction
# clip: torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)

docs.title: 10. Evaluation
docs.text: Task metrics (accuracy/F1, perplexity for language models, BLEU/ROUGE/chrF for generation, WER for speech, RMSE/MASE for forecasting). Use chronological splits for time series; compare with a naive baseline (last value/seasonal naive) and a lag-feature gradient-boosting model before trusting a deep model.

docs.title: 11. Case study (template)
docs.text: Predictive maintenance on sensor streams: windowed features + LightGBM baseline vs 1-D CNN/LSTM on raw windows; measure recall at fixed false-alarm rate; examine latency on the edge device.

docs.title: 12. Comparison
docs.text: RNN < LSTM/GRU on long context; GRU ≈ LSTM with fewer parameters; TCN is parallel and stable; Transformers dominate large-scale NLP; SSMs target linear-time long contexts.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why do RNNs have vanishing gradients? Repeated multiplication by Jacobians with norm < 1 across time.
  • How does LSTM help? Additive cell state and forget gate near 1 pass gradient unchanged.
  • LSTM vs GRU? GRU merges gates/states — fewer params, often similar accuracy.
  • Why attention for seq2seq? The fixed-size context vector bottlenecks long inputs; attention lets the decoder look back at all encoder states.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Compute an LSTM parameter count for d=128,h=256; implement a vanilla RNN forward/backward in NumPy and observe gradient norms vs sequence length; compare an LSTM with seasonal-naive on a periodic series.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Hochreiter & Schmidhuber (1997); Cho et al. (2014); Sutskever, Vinyals & Le (2014); Bahdanau, Cho & Bengio (2014); Bai, Kolter & Koltun (2018); Gu et al. (2021) S4; Olah, "Understanding LSTM Networks".

docs.title: Chapter 5.4 — Attention and Transformers (BERT, GPT-style decoders, Encoder–Decoder)
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 5.3 · Next 5.5 Generative models · Priority 🔴 · Code: deep_learning_numpy.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Architecture that models relations among all positions of a sequence (or set) in parallel via attention, replacing recurrence. Foundation of modern NLP, vision (ViT), speech, protein models and all LLMs (Ch 6.2).

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Bahdanau et al. (2014) additive attention in seq2seq; Luong et al. (2015) multiplicative attention → "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017): Transformer encoder–decoder, parallel training, state-of-the-art translation → GPT (Radford et al. 2018, decoder-only, generative pretraining), BERT (Devlin et al. 2018, encoder-only, masked-LM), GPT-2/3 (2019/2020), T5 (Raffel et al. 2019, text-to-text enc–dec), ViT (2020), scaling laws (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022 "Chinchilla"), RoPE (Su et al. 2021), FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022), GQA/MQA, Mixture-of-Experts. Limitation motivating later work: attention cost O(n²) in sequence length.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Every token asks a question (query), every token advertises what it holds (key) and carries content (value). Each token's output is a weighted mix of all values, with weights given by query–key match. Stacks of this plus feed-forward layers build contextual meaning.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: Scaled dot-product attention: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)·V. Scaling prevents large dot products from saturating softmax. Multi-head: run h attention heads in subspaces of size d_k=d/h, concatenate, project (W_O). Self-attention: Q,K,V are linear projections of the same input X. Worked example (computed in code). Q=[[1,0],[0,1]], K=[[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]], V=[[1,0],[0,2],[3,3]], d_k=2. Query 1 scores [1,0,1]/√2 → softmax weights [0.401, 0.198, 0.401] → output 0.401[1,0]+0.198[0,2]+0.401[3,3] = [1.604, 1.599]. Query 2 weights [0.198,0.401,0.401] → output [1.401, 2.006]. Block (pre-norm): x ← x + MHA(LN(x)); x ← x + FFN(LN(x)), FFN = W₂·GELU(W₁x) with hidden ≈ 4d. Positional information is injected (sinusoidal, learned, relative, RoPE, ALiBi) since attention is permutation-equivariant. Masks: causal mask (upper triangle −∞) for autoregressive decoders — verified in code: with the mask, token 0 attends only to itself and the upper triangle weights are exactly 0. Variants: encoder-only (BERT, bidirectional; classification, embeddings, retrieval), decoder-only (GPT; next-token generation; the LLM default), encoder–decoder (T5, original Transformer; translation/summarization). Parameters per layer ≈ 12d² (4d² attention + 8d² FFN). Costs: training/inference attention O(n²·d) time, O(n²) memory per head — at n=4,096 one head's attention matrix has 16.8M entries (≈33.5 MB in fp16) per layer-head, which is why FlashAttention (IO-aware exact attention), sparse/linear attention, sliding windows, GQA and KV caching matter. Generation: KV cache makes each new token O(n·d) instead of recomputing.

docs.title: 5. Training
docs.text: Next-token or masked-token objective on massive corpora; AdamW with warmup + decay; mixed precision (bf16); gradient clipping; large batches; data/model/pipeline parallelism. Fine-tuning and adaptation: Ch 6.5.

docs.title: 6. Evolution & trade-offs
docs.text: Step Gain Cost RNN → attention-augmented RNN Long-range access Still sequential → Transformer Parallel training, scales with data/compute Quadratic attention, data hungry Encoder-only (BERT) Strong understanding/embeddings Not generative Decoder-only (GPT) Unified generation, in-context learning Unidirectional context + MoE / GQA / FlashAttention / long-context tricks Capacity/efficiency Engineering complexity, routing instability

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: text, code, speech, multi-modal, large pretraining + fine-tuning, anything with long-range dependencies and enough data/compute (or a pretrained checkpoint). Avoid: small tabular data, tiny datasets with no pretrained model, hard real-time on tiny devices, very long sequences without efficient attention.

docs.title: 8. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Layers L, model dim d, heads h, FFN ratio, context length, vocab/tokenizer, dropout, LR/warmup/schedule, weight decay, batch tokens, positional scheme, norm placement (pre vs post), initialization.

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
NumPy (verified): scaled dot-product attention and a causal multi-head attention in deep_learning_numpy.py: 

S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(dk); S += np.triu(np.full((n, n), -1e9), 1)       # causal mask
A = np.exp(S - S.max(-1, keepdims=True)); A /= A.sum(-1, keepdims=True); out = A @ V
Hugging Face template (not executed here): 
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased"); m = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased", num_labels=2)
Evaluation (shape check, measured): multi-head output (5,16) for 5 tokens, 4 heads of size 4, attention tensor (4,5,5).

docs.title: 10. Evaluation
docs.text: Perplexity (LM), task metrics (accuracy/F1, ROUGE/BLEU/BERTScore, exact match), human/LLM-judged quality (Ch 6.11), calibration, robustness, latency (time-to-first-token, tokens/s), memory (KV cache size), cost per request. Hold-out must exclude contamination from pretraining data when benchmarking.

docs.title: 11. Case study (template)
docs.text: Support-ticket classification: TF-IDF+logistic baseline vs fine-tuned small encoder vs prompted LLM; compare macro-F1, cost and latency; the linear baseline is often within a few points for easy label sets, transformers win on nuance and low-data multilingual settings (check on your data).

docs.title: 12. Comparison
docs.text: Transformers vs RNN/TCN: parallelism + long-range. Transformers vs CNN for vision: less bias, more data. Transformers vs SSMs: quality/ecosystem vs linear-time long context.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why divide by √d_k? Dot products grow with dimension, pushing softmax into saturation with tiny gradients.
  • Why multiple heads? Different subspaces/relations attended in parallel.
  • Why positional encodings? Attention alone ignores order.
  • BERT vs GPT? Bidirectional masked-LM encoder vs causal next-token decoder.
  • Why is long context expensive? O(n²) attention and O(n) KV cache per token.
  • What does the causal mask do? Prevents positions from attending to the future during training/generation.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Implement a full pre-norm Transformer block in NumPy; count parameters for d=768, L=12 (compare with ~85M in non-embedding weights: 12·12·768² ≈ 85M); measure attention memory growth with n.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Vaswani et al. (2017); Devlin et al. (2018); Radford et al. (2018/2019); Brown et al. (2020); Raffel et al. (2019); Kaplan et al. (2020); Hoffmann et al. (2022); Dao et al. (2022); Jay Alammar "The Illustrated Transformer"; Karpathy "Let's build GPT".

docs.title: Chapter 5.5 — Generative Models: Autoencoders, VAE, GAN (and a pointer to Diffusion)
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 5.4 · Next 5.6 Graph neural networks · Priority 🟠 · Code: deep_learning_numpy.py · Diffusion: Ch 6.7

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Learn a model of the data distribution p(x) (or compressed representations) to generate new samples, denoise, compress, or detect anomalies.

docs.title: 2. History & relationships
docs.text: Autoencoder (Rumelhart et al. 1986; deep AEs Hinton & Salakhutdinov 2006) → denoising/sparse/contractive AEs (Vincent et al. 2008) → VAE (Kingma & Welling 2013): probabilistic latent variable, trainable by backprop → GAN (Goodfellow et al. 2014): adversarial training for sharp samples → DCGAN, WGAN (Arjovsky 2017), StyleGAN (Karras 2018) → normalizing flows (Rezende & Mohamed 2015) → autoregressive models (PixelCNN; Transformers/LLMs) → diffusion (Sohl-Dickstein 2015; Ho et al. 2020), now dominant for images/audio/video. Not a single line: AE/VAE are likelihood-based, GAN is implicit, diffusion is score-based, AR models factorize the likelihood exactly.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text:
• Autoencoder: squeeze through a narrow code, reconstruct; the code is a learned compression.
  • VAE: same, but the code is a distribution; a penalty keeps codes organized so you can sample from the prior and decode new data.
  • GAN: a forger (generator) and a detective (discriminator) improve each other.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: AE: minimize ‖x − g(f(x))‖²; with linear maps it recovers PCA subspace (Ch 4.3). VAE: encoder q_φ(z|x)=𝒩(μ,σ²), decoder p_θ(x|z), prior p(z)=𝒩(0,I). Maximize the ELBO: log p(x) ≥ E_q[log p(x|z)] − KL(q(z|x)‖p(z)). Reparameterization z = μ + σ⊙ε, ε~𝒩(0,I) makes sampling differentiable. KL for Gaussians: ½Σ(σ² + μ² − 1 − log σ²). Worked example (KL). μ=[1,0], σ²=[1,4]: dim1 ½(1+1−1−0)=0.5; dim2 ½(4+0−1−ln4)=0.8069; total KL 1.3069 (verified). GAN: min_G max_D E_x[log D(x)] + E_z[log(1−D(G(z)))]. For fixed G the optimal discriminator is D*(x)=p_data/(p_data+p_g); at the optimum p_g=p_data, D*=1/2, value −log 4 ≈ −1.386. In practice: non-saturating generator loss, spectral norm, WGAN-GP. Failure modes: mode collapse, unstable training, no likelihood to evaluate. Assumptions: data lie near a low-dimensional manifold; sufficient capacity and data.

docs.title: 5. Training & cost
docs.text: AE/VAE train stably with Adam; VAE balances reconstruction vs KL (β-VAE; KL annealing; posterior collapse risk). GANs need careful balance of G and D updates, normalization, tuned LRs. Sampling: VAE/GAN single forward pass (fast); diffusion needs many steps (slow, higher quality); autoregressive token by token.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Need Use Compression, denoising, anomaly detection (reconstruction error) (Denoising) autoencoder Smooth latent space, semi-supervised, structured generation VAE Fast sharp samples, image-to-image translation (historically) GAN State-of-the-art image/audio/video generation Diffusion (Ch 6.7) Text/code generation Autoregressive Transformers (Ch 6.2) Avoid: generative models when a discriminative model answers the question (Ch 6.1); GANs without capacity to tune/monitor; trusting generated data as real for evaluation leakage.

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Latent dimension, architecture, β (KL weight), reconstruction loss (MSE/BCE/perceptual), LR, noise level (denoising), D/G update ratio, regularization (R1, spectral norm), batch size.

docs.title: 8. Implementation
docs.text:
Measured NumPy/sklearn comparison on digits (8-dimensional code, held-out test MSE, pixels in [0,1]): PCA(8): 0.0246 vs sklearn MLP autoencoder (32-8-32, tanh): 0.0303. The small nonlinear AE did not beat PCA with ~1.3k training images — nonlinear AEs need more data/tuning to pay off, and PCA is a strong baseline. VAE template (PyTorch, not executed here): 

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
class VAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(s, d=784, h=256, z=16): super().__init__(); s.e = nn.Linear(d, h); s.mu = nn.Linear(h, z); s.lv = nn.Linear(h, z); s.d1 = nn.Linear(z, h); s.d2 = nn.Linear(h, d)
    def forward(s, x):
        h = F.relu(s.e(x)); mu, lv = s.mu(h), s.lv(h); z = mu + torch.randn_like(mu) * torch.exp(0.5 * lv)
        return torch.sigmoid(s.d2(F.relu(s.d1(z)))), mu, lv
def loss(xr, x, mu, lv): return F.binary_cross_entropy(xr, x, reduction="sum") - 0.5 * torch.sum(1 + lv - mu.pow(2) - lv.exp())

docs.title: 9. Evaluation
docs.text: Reconstruction error/ELBO; for samples: FID and Inception Score (images), precision/recall of distributions, human preference studies; diversity vs fidelity; privacy/memorization checks. For anomaly detection: AUROC/PR-AUC on held-out anomalies.

docs.title: 10. Case study (template)
docs.text: Industrial anomaly detection: train an autoencoder on normal images only; score by reconstruction error; compare with Isolation Forest on embeddings (Ch 4.5); calibrate the threshold on a validation set with some labeled defects.

docs.title: 11. Comparison
docs.text: AE VAE GAN Diffusion Autoregressive Likelihood No Bound (ELBO) No Bound/score Exact Sample quality Not generative Blurry Sharp Very high High Training Easy Easy Hard Moderate Easy Sampling speed — Fast Fast Slow Slow (sequential)

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why the reparameterization trick? Moves randomness to ε so gradients flow through μ,σ.
  • Why do VAE samples look blurry? Pixelwise Gaussian likelihood averages plausible outputs; the KL regularization limits detail.
  • Mode collapse? Generator produces limited variety because it can fool D with a few modes.
  • GAN vs VAE? GAN: implicit, sharp, unstable; VAE: explicit bound, stable, blurrier.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Derive the Gaussian KL; show a linear AE recovers the PCA subspace numerically; train a tiny GAN on a 1-D mixture in NumPy.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Kingma & Welling (2013); Goodfellow et al. (2014); Arjovsky et al. (2017); Karras et al. (2019); Doersch (2016) "Tutorial on VAEs"; Lilian Weng "From autoencoder to Beta-VAE" and "What are diffusion models?".

docs.title: Chapter 5.6 — Graph Neural Networks: GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT, Message Passing
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 5.5 · Next 5.7 Self-supervised learning · Priority 🟡 · Code: deep_learning_numpy.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Learn from data shaped as graphs: molecules, social/citation networks, road networks, knowledge graphs, fraud rings, recommender interaction graphs. Tasks: node classification, link prediction, graph classification/regression.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Graph spectral theory and early GNN models (Gori 2005; Scarselli et al. 2009) → spectral CNNs (Bruna et al. 2013), ChebNet (Defferrard 2016) → GCN (Kipf & Welling 2016) simplification → GraphSAGE (Hamilton et al. 2017; inductive, sampling) → GAT (Veličković et al. 2017; attention over neighbors) → unifying message-passing NN framework (Gilmer et al. 2017) → GIN (Xu et al. 2018; expressive power ~ Weisfeiler–Leman test) → graph transformers, equivariant GNNs for 3-D molecules. Problems that motivated each step: scalability (sampling), inductiveness, anisotropic weighting, expressiveness, over-smoothing.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Each node repeatedly collects its neighbors' feature vectors, mixes them, and updates itself. After k rounds a node "knows" its k-hop neighborhood.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: Message passing: h_v^{(l+1)} = UPDATE(h_v^{(l)}, AGG({h_u^{(l)} : u ∈ N(v)})). GCN layer: H' = σ(Â H W), Â = D̃^{-1/2}(A+I)D̃^{-1/2} (self-loops + symmetric normalization). GraphSAGE: h_v' = σ(W·[h_v ‖ mean(h_u)]) with neighbor sampling. GAT: attention coefficients α_vu = softmax_u(LeakyReLU(aᵀ[Wh_v‖Wh_u])). Worked example (computed). Path graph 1–2–3, A=[[0,1,0],[1,0,1],[0,1,0]]; A+I degrees (2,3,2). Â=[[0.5,0.408,0],[0.408,0.333,0.408],[0,0.408,0.5]]. Features H=[[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]], W=I: ÂH = [[0.5,0.408],[0.816,0.742],[0.5,0.908]] — node 2 now mixes all three nodes (verified in code). Over-smoothing: many layers average features until nodes are indistinguishable; over-squashing: long-range info compressed through bottlenecks. Remedies: residual/jumping connections, normalization, graph rewiring, transformers with positional/structural encodings.

docs.title: 5. Training & cost
docs.text: Full-batch for small graphs (O(|E|·d) per layer); mini-batch with neighbor sampling (GraphSAGE), cluster-GCN, or subgraph sampling for large graphs. Semi-supervised node classification trains on few labeled nodes using the whole graph structure.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: relational/structured data where relationships carry signal—molecular property prediction, fraud rings, recommendations, traffic, knowledge graph completion. Avoid: when features alone suffice (compare to GBM on tabular + graph features such as degree/PageRank/node2vec embeddings), when the graph is noisy/arbitrary, or when simple label propagation already works.

docs.title: 7. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Uses structure explicitly, inductive variants generalize to new nodes. − Over-smoothing, scalability complexity, heterophily (neighbors differ) hurts basic GCNs, evaluation pitfalls (leakage across splits via edges), limited expressiveness beyond 1-WL.

docs.title: 8. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Layers (2–3 typical), hidden size, aggregator (mean/sum/max/attention), sampling fanout, dropout, residuals, normalization, learning rate, readout for graph tasks (sum/mean/attention pooling).

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
NumPy GCN layer verified above. PyTorch Geometric template (not executed here): 

import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from torch_geometric.nn import GCNConv
class GCN(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, h, c):
        super().__init__(); self.c1 = GCNConv(d, h); self.c2 = GCNConv(h, c)
    def forward(self, x, edge_index):
        x = F.dropout(F.relu(self.c1(x, edge_index)), p=0.5, training=self.training)
        return self.c2(x, edge_index)
Libraries: PyTorch Geometric, DGL.

docs.title: 10. Evaluation
docs.text: Node tasks: accuracy/F1 on public splits (Planetoid: Cora/Citeseer/Pubmed) but also random/ time-based splits; link prediction: AUC/AP/Hits@k with proper negative sampling and no edge leakage; graph tasks: scaffold splits for molecules (random splits overstate performance). Baselines: MLP on features, label propagation, node2vec+GBM.

docs.title: 11. Case study (template)
docs.text: Transaction fraud: baseline LightGBM on tabular features; add graph features (degree, shared device/IP neighbors, PageRank); then GraphSAGE embeddings; evaluate on a forward-in-time split, measuring PR-AUC and investigator workload.

docs.title: 12. Comparison
docs.text: GCN: simple, transductive-leaning. GraphSAGE: inductive, scalable. GAT: learned neighbor weights. GIN: expressive for graph classification. Graph Transformers: global attention, costlier.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why add self-loops and normalize? Keep a node's own features and prevent high-degree nodes from dominating scale.
  • Over-smoothing? Repeated averaging makes node embeddings converge.
  • Transductive vs inductive? Test nodes seen at training time vs generalizing to unseen nodes/graphs.
  • Can GNNs beat feature-only models? Only if neighbors add information—test against strong tabular baselines.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Compute two GCN layers by hand on a 4-node graph; implement mean aggregation in NumPy; compare Cora accuracy of MLP vs GCN.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Kipf & Welling (2016); Hamilton, Ying & Leskovec (2017); Veličković et al. (2017); Gilmer et al. (2017); Xu et al. (2018); Bronstein et al. (2021) "Geometric Deep Learning"; Hamilton, Graph Representation Learning (free).

docs.title: Chapter 5.7 — Self-Supervised and Representation Learning
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 5.6 · Next 6.1 Time series · Priority 🔴 · Code: deep_learning_numpy.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Learn useful representations from unlabeled data by inventing a prediction task from the data itself. Labels are expensive; raw data is abundant. The learned encoder is then reused (transfer learning, Ch 6.5) with few labels.

docs.title: 2. History and families
docs.text: Family Pretext task Landmarks Predict context Predict neighbors/words word2vec (Mikolov et al. 2013), GloVe, skip-gram with negative sampling Autoregressive Predict the next token GPT (2018→), PixelCNN, wav2vec-style Masked prediction Reconstruct masked parts BERT (2018), MAE (He et al. 2021), BEiT, data2vec Contrastive Pull augmented views of the same item together, push others apart CPC / InfoNCE (van den Oord 2018), MoCo (He 2019), SimCLR (Chen 2020), CLIP (Radford 2021; image–text pairs) Non-contrastive / self-distillation Match representations without negatives BYOL (Grill 2020), SimSiam, DINO (Caron 2021), VICReg Generative Reconstruct/denoise autoencoders, VAEs, diffusion (Ch 5.5, 6.7) Earlier ideas Pseudo-tasks (rotation prediction, jigsaw), restricted Boltzmann machines/deep belief nets pretraining (Hinton 2006), semi-supervised "pseudo-labeling" (Ch 6.6) — The progression is driven by removing costs: manual labels → negative pairs (BYOL) → hand-crafted augmentations (masking/AR objectives that scale cleanly).

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Hide part of the data and make the model fill it in, or show two versions of the same thing and ask the model to recognize they match. To succeed, the model must learn structure—grammar, objects, physics-like regularities.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: InfoNCE / NT-Xent: for anchor i, positive i⁺, set of negatives N: L_i = −log [ exp(sim(z_i,z_{i⁺})/τ) / ( exp(sim(z_i,z_{i⁺})/τ) + Σ_{j∈N} exp(sim(z_i,z_j)/τ) ) ], sim = cosine similarity, temperature τ. It lower-bounds mutual information between views. Worked example (computed). Unit vectors: anchor (1,0), positive (0.994,0.110), negatives (0,1) and (−1,0); τ=0.5. Similarities/τ: positive 1.988, negatives 0 and −2. Numerator e^{1.988}=7.30; denominator 7.30+1+0.135=8.435; loss =−ln(7.30/8.435)= 0.1446. Make the negative (−1,0) become (1,0) (identical to the anchor): the denominator grows and the loss rises — the objective penalizes confusing others with the anchor. Masked LM: minimize −Σ_{masked} log p(x_i | x_{\setminus masked}) (≈15% masked in BERT). Next-token: −Σ log p(x_t|x_{<t}). Collapse (all outputs equal) is avoided by negatives (contrastive), momentum/stop-gradient (BYOL/SimSiam), or variance/covariance regularization (VICReg). Assumptions: augmentations preserve the semantics you care about; the pretext task requires the features you need.

docs.title: 5. Training & cost
docs.text: Pretraining is expensive (large batches for SimCLR, big corpora for LLMs); downstream use is cheap: linear probe, fine-tune, or k-NN on frozen embeddings. Typical large-scale recipe: huge unlabeled data → pretrain → small labeled set.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: abundant unlabeled data, scarce labels, need general embeddings (search, clustering, recommendation, anomaly detection), domain adaptation (continued pretraining). Often best to start from a public pretrained model rather than pretraining yourself. Avoid: when you have plenty of labels and a small domain-specific task (supervised training may suffice), or lack compute for meaningful pretraining.

docs.title: 7. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Exploits unlabeled data, produces transferable features, foundation of modern AI. − Compute-hungry, augmentation/pretext design sensitive, possible bias/privacy issues from web-scale data, representation quality hard to evaluate.

docs.title: 8. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Temperature τ, batch size/number of negatives, augmentation strength/composition, mask ratio, projection head size, momentum coefficient (MoCo/BYOL), learning rate and schedule, embedding dimension.

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
NumPy InfoNCE (verified): 

z = z / np.linalg.norm(z, axis=1, keepdims=True); sim = z @ z.T / tau
loss = -np.log(np.exp(sim[a, p]) / (np.exp(sim[a, p]) + sum(np.exp(sim[a, j]) for j in negs)))
Practical: use a pretrained encoder (e.g. sentence-transformers, CLIP, DINOv2) and train a light head. sentence-transformers template (not executed here): 
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
emb = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2").encode(["text one", "text two"], normalize_embeddings=True)

docs.title: 10. Evaluation
docs.text: Linear-probe accuracy, k-NN accuracy on frozen features, few-shot fine-tuning curves, retrieval recall@k, clustering quality, robustness/shift tests, and downstream task metrics. Always compare to a supervised baseline trained on the same labeled subset and to a random-init encoder.

docs.title: 11. Case study (template)
docs.text: Product search with 10k labeled queries: baseline BM25; add a pretrained sentence encoder for dense retrieval (hybrid), fine-tune with contrastive loss on click pairs; evaluate recall@k and NDCG; see Ch 6.4 for the RAG context.

docs.title: 12. Comparison
docs.text: Contrastive: strong but needs negatives/large batches. Masked: simple, scalable (BERT/MAE). Autoregressive: supports generation (LLMs). Non-contrastive: avoids negatives but needs anti-collapse tricks.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why is it "self"-supervised? Labels come from the data itself.
  • Role of temperature in InfoNCE? Controls how sharply hard negatives are penalized.
  • How does BYOL avoid collapse without negatives? Predictor + momentum (EMA) target network with stop-gradient (the exact reason is still analyzed).
  • Linear probing vs fine-tuning? Measure representation quality vs maximize task performance.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Compute the InfoNCE loss for a batch of 4 pairs by hand; implement skip-gram negative sampling on a toy corpus; compare linear-probe accuracy of random vs pretrained embeddings.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Mikolov et al. (2013); Devlin et al. (2018); van den Oord et al. (2018); Chen et al. (2020) SimCLR; Grill et al. (2020) BYOL; He et al. (2021) MAE; Radford et al. (2021) CLIP; Balestriero et al. (2023) "A Cookbook of Self-Supervised Learning".

docs.title: Chapter 6.1 — Time-Series Forecasting: Baselines, ETS, ARIMA/SARIMA, State Space, Boosting, Deep Models
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 5.7 · Next 6.2 Recommenders · Priority 🟠 · Code: timeseries_demo.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Predict future values of a series ordered in time (demand, load, prices, traffic, sensor values). Data are autocorrelated, non-i.i.d., and often have trend, seasonality, holidays and regime changes. The evaluation protocol matters as much as the model.

docs.title: 2. History (several lineages, not one)
docs.text:
• Smoothing: simple/Holt/Holt–Winters exponential smoothing (Brown 1956; Holt 1957; Winters 1960) → ETS state-space formulation (Hyndman et al. 2002).
  • Stochastic-process models: AR (Yule 1927), MA (Slutsky/Wold), ARMA; Box & Jenkins (1970) ARIMA/SARIMA methodology (identify–estimate–check).
  • State space & filtering: Kalman filter (1960), structural time series, Prophet (Taylor & Letham 2018, decomposable trend + seasonality + holidays).
  • ML: lag-feature gradient boosting (LightGBM-based solutions were prominent among top M5 entries), deep learning: DeepAR (Salinas et al. 2017), N-BEATS (Oreshkin 2019), Temporal Fusion Transformer (Lim et al. 2019), PatchTST (Nie 2022), and recent pretrained "foundation" forecasters (e.g. Chronos, TimesFM) — evaluate them cautiously against strong baselines. The M-competitions repeatedly showed simple, well-tuned methods are hard to beat.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: A forecast = pattern in the past carried forward: level + trend + repeating seasonal shape + short-term momentum (autocorrelation) + noise.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text:
• Stationarity: constant mean/variance/autocovariance; achieved by differencing (∇y_t=y_t−y_{t−1}, seasonal y_t−y_{t−s}) or transforms (log). Test with ADF/KPSS.
  • AR(p): y_t = c + φ₁y_{t−1}+…+φ_p y_{t−p} + ε_t. MA(q): y_t = μ + ε_t + θ₁ε_{t−1}+…. ARIMA(p,d,q) = ARMA on d-times differenced data; SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_s adds seasonal terms. Identification via ACF/PACF (AR: PACF cuts off; MA: ACF cuts off), then compare by AIC/BIC and residual whiteness (Ljung–Box).
  • Simple exponential smoothing: ℓ_t = αy_t + (1−α)ℓ_{t−1}; forecast = ℓ_t. Holt adds trend; Holt–Winters adds seasonality (additive/multiplicative). Worked examples. AR(1) with φ=0.8, c=0, last value 10: forecasts 8, 6.4, 5.12,… decaying to the mean 0 (mean reversion). SES with α=0.5: observations 10, 12 → ℓ₁=10, ℓ₂=0.5·12+0.5·10=11 (forecast for all horizons).
  • Metrics: MAE, RMSE, MAPE/sMAPE (fail near 0), MASE = MAE / MAE_in-sample seasonal-naive (scale-free; <1 beats naive), pinball loss and coverage for probabilistic forecasts (Ch 1.4). Assumptions: ARIMA — linear dynamics, stationarity after differencing, constant variance; ETS — error/trend/season structure; ML — features carry the information (needs careful lag/leakage handling).

docs.title: 5. Training & cost
docs.text: ARIMA/ETS: per-series fits in milliseconds–seconds (good for many series, "local" models). ML/deep models are usually "global" (one model across many series; shares strength, handles cross-learning, needs more engineering). Multi-step strategies: recursive (feed predictions back), direct (a model per horizon), multi-output.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Situation Prefer Few series, clear trend/seasonality ETS, SARIMA, Prophet-like decomposition Many related series, covariates, promotions, intermittent demand Global GBM/NN with lag, calendar and price features Need probabilistic forecasts Quantile GBM, DeepAR, conformal intervals Very short history Seasonal naive, ETS; borrow strength via hierarchies/global models Regime shifts / structural breaks Robust baselines, monitoring, re-fitting, scenario models Avoid: shuffled k-fold CV (leaks the future), reporting a single train/test split, forecasting without a naive baseline, using future-known covariates that aren't known at forecast time, deep models on a handful of points.

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters
docs.text: ARIMA orders (p,d,q)(P,D,Q,s) via auto_arima/AIC; ETS error/trend/season type and damping; GBM: lags, rolling stats, calendar features, tree complexity; NN: context length, horizon, patch size, loss; global: normalization per series.

docs.title: 8. Implementation
docs.text:
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing
sarima = SARIMAX(y, order=(1,1,1), seasonal_order=(0,1,1,12)).fit(disp=False); fc = sarima.forecast(12)
ets = ExponentialSmoothing(y, trend="add", seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=12).fit(); fc2 = ets.forecast(12)
# Boosted lags: build lag/rolling/calendar features, model the *seasonal difference* (see results), forecast recursively

docs.title: 9. Evaluation & results (measured)
docs.text: Data: monthly atmospheric CO₂ (526 months, 1958–2001; statsmodels bundled), clear trend + strong annual seasonality. ADF p-value raw 0.999 (non-stationary) vs 0.0 after first + seasonal differencing. Rolling-origin evaluation: 12-month-ahead forecasts from successive origins in the last 20% of data. MASE uses the in-sample seasonal-naive scale (values > 1 mean worse than the in-sample seasonal-naive error; the test period has trend so even seasonal naive scores 1.27): | Method | MAE (ppm) | MASE | |---|---|---| | Naive (last value) | 1.739 | 1.34 | | Seasonal naive | 1.647 | 1.27 | | Holt–Winters ETS | 0.472 | 0.36 | | SARIMA (1,1,1)(0,1,1,12) | 0.442 | 0.34 | | LightGBM on lags, raw target | 1.610 | 1.24 | | LightGBM on lags, seasonal-difference target | 0.822 | 0.63 | Lessons: (1) classical models win on a single clean series with trend and seasonality; (2) trees cannot extrapolate a trend — LightGBM with a raw target ≈ seasonal naive, but modeling the seasonal difference nearly halved the error (1.610 → 0.822); (3) still behind ETS/SARIMA here (one series, 400 training rows) — global ML wins mainly with many series/covariates. ACF of the differenced series at lag 1 and 12: 0.70 and 0.92, confirming remaining seasonality in single-differenced data.

docs.title: 10. Case study (template)
docs.text: Retail demand for thousands of SKUs: baselines (seasonal naive, ETS) → global LightGBM with price/promo/calendar features and per-series scaling → quantile outputs for inventory service levels. Evaluate with rolling-origin CV by week, MASE/WRMSSE, bias, and inventory/business simulation.

docs.title: 11. Comparison
docs.text: ETS ARIMA Prophet-style GBM (global) Deep global Few series Strong Strong Good Weak Weak Many series + covariates Weak Weak OK Strong Strong Interpretability High Medium High Medium Low Extrapolates trend Yes Yes Yes No (needs differencing/detrending) Depends

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why can't you use random k-fold? It lets future data train the model for past points; use rolling-origin/expanding-window.
  • What does d in ARIMA do? Number of differences to make the series stationary.
  • ACF vs PACF? ACF = correlation at lag k including indirect effects; PACF removes intermediate lags — AR order from PACF, MA order from ACF.
  • Why do trees struggle with trends? They predict averages of seen targets; they can't output values beyond the training range.
  • What is MASE? MAE scaled by the naive in-sample error.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Fit AR(1) to simulated data and recover φ; build a rolling-origin evaluation with 3 horizons; add Fourier terms and holiday dummies to the boosted model; produce 80% prediction intervals by quantile regression and check coverage.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (free, fpp3); Box, Jenkins, Reinsel & Ljung, Time Series Analysis; Taylor & Letham (2018); Makridakis et al. M4/M5 papers; Salinas et al. (2020) DeepAR; Oreshkin et al. (2020) N-BEATS; statsmodels/sktime/darts/statsforecast docs.
