docs.title: Chapter 6.2 — Recommender Systems: Popularity → CF → Matrix Factorization → Two-Tower → Ranking
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 6.1 · Next 6.3 Reinforcement learning · Priority 🟠 · Code: recsys_demo.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Rank items (movies, products, videos, jobs) for each user from interaction history and side information. Interactions are usually implicit (clicks, views, purchases) rather than ratings, sparse, biased by exposure, and non-stationary.

docs.title: 2. History and what each stage fixed
docs.text: Era Approach Contribution Limitation Baseline Popularity / recency Strong, cheap No personalization 1990s Content-based filtering; user-based CF (GroupLens, Resnick et al. 1994) Personalization from similar users O(users²), sparse overlap 2003 Item-based CF (Sarwar 2001; Amazon, Linden et al. 2003) Stable item similarities, scalable Weak on sparse/long-tail 2006–09 Matrix factorization from the Netflix Prize (Koren, Bell & Volinsky 2009), implicit ALS (Hu, Koren & Volinsky 2008), BPR (Rendle 2009), Factorization Machines (Rendle 2010) Latent taste vectors, handles sparsity, add biases/side features Cold start, linear interaction 2015– Deep & neural: Neural CF (He 2017), YouTube two-stage deep retrieval/ranking (Covington 2016), two-tower retrieval, sequential models (GRU4Rec 2015, SASRec 2018), graph (LightGCN 2020), Transformer-based and generative recommenders Rich features, sequences, scalable ANN retrieval Data/infra heavy, offline-online gap Industrial architecture: candidate generation (retrieval) → ranking → re-ranking (diversity, business rules).

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: People who liked what you liked will like what you haven't seen; or: each user and item is a point in a taste space and affinity = dot product.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text:
• Explicit MF: r̂_ui = μ + b_u + b_i + p_u·q_i; minimize Σ(r_ui − r̂_ui)² + λ(‖p_u‖²+‖q_i‖²+b²) by SGD or ALS.
  • Implicit ALS: preference p_ui = 1[r_ui>0], confidence c_ui = 1+α r_ui; minimize Σ c_ui (p_ui − x_uᵀy_i)² + λ(‖x_u‖²+‖y_i‖²); alternate closed-form ridge solves for users/items.
  • BPR: maximize Σ log σ(x_uᵀy_i − x_uᵀy_j) for observed i vs sampled unobserved j (pairwise ranking).
  • Two-tower: s(u,i) = ⟨f(u), g(i)⟩ with in-batch sampled-softmax; item embeddings indexed with ANN for sub-linear retrieval (Ch 2.5). Worked SGD step. True rating 4; p=[1,0.5], q=[2,1] ⇒ r̂=1·2+0.5·1=2.5, error e=1.5. With lr 0.1 (λ=0): p ← p + lr·e·q = [1.3, 0.65], q ← q + lr·e·p_old = [2.15, 1.075] ⇒ new r̂=1.3·2.15+0.65·1.075=3.494, much closer to 4. Ranking metrics: Recall/HitRate@K, Precision@K, MRR, NDCG@K = DCG/IDCG, DCG=Σ rel_i/log₂(i+1); also coverage, diversity, novelty, calibration.

docs.title: 5. Training & cost
docs.text: ALS O((n_u+n_i)f²·nnz/…) per sweep, parallelizable; SGD O(nnz·f) per epoch; kNN CF needs O(n²) similarities (use sparse/ANN). Serving: precompute embeddings, ANN retrieval (HNSW/IVF) in milliseconds, then a heavier ranker on a few hundred candidates.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: catalogs too big to browse, personalization drives value. Choose by data: little data → popularity/content; moderate interactions → item-kNN/MF; large-scale with rich features → two-tower + ranker; sessions → sequence models. Avoid: optimizing offline accuracy alone (feedback loops, popularity bias, filter bubbles), ignoring cold start (new users/items → content features, onboarding, bandits), leaking the future in splits.

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Factors f, regularization λ, confidence α, negative sampling ratio, learning rate, neighbors k, embedding dims, temperature (softmax), candidate pool size, re-rank diversity weight.

docs.title: 8. Implementation
docs.text:
Scratch implicit ALS in recsys_demo.py: 

for u in range(n_users):    # fix item factors Y, solve each user's ridge problem
    Cu = C[u]; X[u] = np.linalg.solve((Y.T * Cu) @ Y + lam*np.eye(f), (Y.T * Cu) @ R[u])
Libraries: implicit (ALS/BPR), surprise (explicit CF), LightFM, TensorFlow Recommenders, RecBole, torchrec.

docs.title: 9. Evaluation & results (measured; synthetic data)
docs.text: Synthetic world: 400 users × 300 items, rank-5 taste structure + global popularity, 16% density; one positive held out per user; metrics on 400 test users (standard error of HitRate ≈ ±0.02): | Method | HitRate@10 | NDCG@10 | |---|---|---| | Random | 0.030 | 0.013 | | Popularity | 0.147 | 0.076 | | Item-kNN | 0.170 | 0.095 | | ALS MF, f=2 | 0.172 | 0.083 | | ALS MF, f=5 (true rank) | 0.217 | 0.113 | | ALS MF, f=10 | 0.152 | 0.068 | | User-kNN (k=30) | 0.230 | 0.116 | Reading: personalization beats popularity by 50–60% in hit rate; MF peaks at the true latent rank (f=5) and overfits at f=10 (no tuning of λ/α here); user-kNN vs MF(f=5) is within noise (0.230 vs 0.217) — don't conclude one is better from a single small synthetic run. Real-data results differ; use temporal splits and report on your own logs. Offline vs online: offline metrics can mislead (exposure bias); validate with A/B tests (CTR, conversion, retention), counterfactual/off-policy evaluation, and guardrail metrics.

docs.title: 10. Case study (template)
docs.text: E-commerce "recommended for you": popularity baseline → ALS embeddings → two-tower retrieval with item text/image features → GBM ranker with price/recency/context → diversity re-rank. Cold start: content-based fallback; exploration via bandits (Ch 6.3).

docs.title: 11. Comparison
docs.text: Popularity: strong baseline. CF: needs overlap. MF: compact and strong on interaction matrices. Two-tower: scalable with features. Ranker: precision on a short list, uses cross-features. Sequence/Transformer models: capture order and intent.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Explicit vs implicit feedback? Ratings are scarce; clicks are plentiful but ambiguous (absence ≠ dislike), so treat as confidence-weighted preference.
  • Cold start? Content/metadata features, popularity within segment, onboarding questions, exploration.
  • Why two stages? Cheap retrieval over millions of items, then expensive ranking over hundreds.
  • Popularity bias? Models over-recommend popular items; mitigate with re-ranking, debiasing, exposure-aware training.
  • Evaluate offline? Time-based split, leave-last-out, HitRate/NDCG@K against popularity; then A/B test.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Derive the ALS user update; implement BPR with sampled negatives; add item popularity bias terms; study how HitRate changes with density.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Koren, Bell & Volinsky (2009) "Matrix factorization techniques for recommender systems"; Hu, Koren & Volinsky (2008); Rendle et al. (2009) BPR; Covington, Adams & Sargin (2016); Ricci et al., Recommender Systems Handbook; Aggarwal, Recommender Systems: The Textbook.

docs.title: Chapter 6.3 — Reinforcement Learning: Bandits → DP → MC/TD → Q-Learning/SARSA → DQN → Policy Gradients → PPO/SAC
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 6.2 · Next 6.4 Causal inference · Priority 🟠 · Code: rl_demo.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: An agent interacts with an environment, takes actions, observes states and rewards, and learns a policy that maximizes cumulative (discounted) reward. Games, robotics, control, recommendation/ads (bandits), resource allocation, and alignment of LLMs (RLHF, Ch 6.6). No labeled "correct action"; credit assignment over time is the core difficulty.

docs.title: 2. History — a tree of ideas
docs.text: Branch Milestones Bandits Thompson sampling (1933); Robbins (1952); UCB (Auer et al. 2002); contextual bandits (LinUCB, Li et al. 2010) Dynamic programming Bellman (1957) equations; policy/value iteration (Howard 1960) — need a known model Monte Carlo Learn from full episodes, no model Temporal difference TD(λ) (Sutton 1988), Q-learning (Watkins 1989), SARSA (Rummery & Niranjan 1994) Function approximation TD-Gammon (Tesauro 1992) → DQN (Mnih et al. 2013/2015: replay buffer + target network), Double DQN, Dueling, Rainbow Policy gradient REINFORCE (Williams 1992), actor–critic, A2C/A3C, TRPO (Schulman 2015), PPO (Schulman 2017), DDPG, TD3, SAC (Haarnoja 2018) Model-based & search Dyna, AlphaGo/AlphaZero (MCTS + nets), MuZero, Dreamer Value-based methods learn "how good is each action"; policy-based methods directly optimize the policy; actor–critic combines both. Not a strict succession: PPO and SAC coexist, chosen by action-space and sample-efficiency needs.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Trial and error with memory: try things, notice which led to reward, shift probability toward them—while still exploring enough to discover better options.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: MDP (S,A,P,R,γ); return G_t=Σγ^k r_{t+k+1}. Value V^π(s)=E[G_t|s], Q^π(s,a). Bellman optimality: Q*(s,a) = E[r + γ max_{a'} Q*(s',a')]. - Q-learning (off-policy): Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ max_{a'}Q(s',a') − Q(s,a)]. SARSA (on-policy): uses the action actually taken, Q(s',a'). - Policy gradient: ∇J(θ)=E[∇log π_θ(a|s)·(G_t − b(s))]; advantage A=Q−V reduces variance. PPO maximizes the clipped objective E[min(ρ_t A_t, clip(ρ_t,1−ε,1+ε)A_t)], ρ_t=π_θ/π_old, keeping updates small and stable. Worked example (one Q-learning update). Q(s,a)=0, reward −1, max Q(s',·)=2, α=0.5, γ=0.9: target =−1+0.9·2=0.8; Q ← 0+0.5(0.8−0)=0.4. Value iteration (verified): corridor of 5 states, reward 1 on reaching the right end, γ=0.9 ⇒ V* = [0.729, 0.81, 0.9, 1.0, 0] = γ^{steps−1}. Assumptions: Markov property, stationary dynamics, adequate exploration, well-specified reward (reward hacking is a real failure). Key issues: exploration–exploitation, credit assignment, sample inefficiency, instability of off-policy + function approximation + bootstrapping ("deadly triad"), reward design, sim-to-real gap.

docs.title: 5. Cost
docs.text: Tabular: O(|S||A|) memory, cheap updates. Deep RL: millions–billions of environment steps, GPUs and simulators; PPO is relatively robust and widely used; SAC is sample-efficient for continuous control; offline RL learns from logged data without interaction (distribution-shift challenges).

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: sequential decisions with delayed reward and a simulator/safe exploration; bandits for one-step choices (ads, UI variants, recsys exploration). Avoid: when supervised learning on logged expert data suffices, when mistakes are costly and no simulator exists, when the reward can't be specified, or when a simple heuristic/optimizer (OR methods) works. Consider imitation learning, offline RL, or contextual bandits first.

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters
docs.text: γ, learning rates, exploration schedule (ε, entropy bonus, noise), replay size/batch, target-update rate (τ), clip range ε (PPO), GAE λ, number of parallel envs, network size, reward scaling/normalization.

docs.title: 8. Implementation
docs.text:
All from scratch in NumPy (rl_demo.py). Core Q-learning/SARSA loop: 

target = r + (0 if done else gamma * (Q[s2][a2] if alg == "sarsa" else Q[s2].max()))
Q[s][a] += alpha * (target - Q[s][a])
Libraries: Gymnasium (environments), Stable-Baselines3 (PPO/SAC/DQN), CleanRL, RLlib. PyTorch/SB3 templates were not executed here.

docs.title: 9. Evaluation & results (measured)
docs.text: 10-armed Gaussian bandit (300 runs × 1000 steps; last 500 steps): % pulls of the optimal arm — greedy 70.0%, ε-greedy (0.1) 80.1%, UCB (c=2) 84.1%, Thompson sampling 90.9%; mean true value of the chosen arm: 1.450 / 1.383 / 1.493 / 1.539. Greedy gets stuck early on a suboptimal arm in many runs; ε-greedy keeps wasting 10% on random pulls; UCB and Thompson explore in a directed way. (Single seeds per run set; absolute numbers depend on settings.) Cliff walking (4×12, ε=0.1, 30 seeds, 500 episodes): | Algorithm | Mean online return (last 100 episodes) | Greedy policy reaches goal | Median greedy path length | |---|---|---|---| | Q-learning | −48.8 | 30/30 | 13 (optimal, hugs the cliff) | | SARSA | −26.6 | 25/30 | 17 (safer route) | The textbook result reproduced: Q-learning learns the optimal path but, because it keeps exploring with ε-greedy next to the cliff, falls off more often during training (lower online return); SARSA accounts for its own exploration and learns a safer path. (SARSA's greedy policy failed to reach the goal in 5/30 seeds within 100 steps at 500 episodes: not yet converged.) REINFORCE on a 3-arm bandit (means 0.2, 0.5, 1.0): final policy [0.001, 0.002, 0.996] — concentrates on the best arm. Real evaluation: average return with confidence intervals over many seeds, learning curves, sample efficiency, robustness to environment perturbations; report seeds (RL results are high-variance).

docs.title: 10. Case study (template)
docs.text: Dynamic pricing/ads: start with a contextual bandit (LinUCB/Thompson) with off-policy evaluation on logs; only move to full RL if actions change future states (e.g. long-term retention). Always include a safe fallback policy and constraints.

docs.title: 11. Comparison
docs.text: Q-learning/DQN SARSA Policy gradient/PPO SAC/DDPG Bandits Actions Discrete Discrete Discrete/continuous Continuous Discrete Policy type Off-policy value On-policy value On-policy policy Off-policy actor-critic One-step Sample efficiency Medium Low Low–medium High Very high Stability Tricky Better Good (PPO) Good (with tuning) Excellent

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Q-learning vs SARSA? Off-policy (max over next actions) vs on-policy (action actually taken); cliff example.
  • Why a replay buffer and target network in DQN? Break correlation of samples and stabilize bootstrapped targets.
  • Why does PPO clip? Prevents destructively large policy updates.
  • Exploration–exploitation? ε-greedy, UCB, Thompson sampling, entropy bonuses, curiosity.
  • When use a bandit instead of RL? Actions don't affect future states.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Implement Double Q-learning and compare overestimation; add a baseline to REINFORCE and plot variance; implement LinUCB on synthetic contextual data; run PPO on CartPole with SB3.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed., free); Mnih et al. (2015) Nature; Schulman et al. (2017); Haarnoja et al. (2018); Spinning Up in Deep RL (OpenAI); Lattimore & Szepesvári, Bandit Algorithms (free).

docs.title: Chapter 6.4 — Causal Inference: Potential Outcomes, Propensity Scores, IPW, Matching, DiD, Causal Forests
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 6.3 · Next 6.5 Survival analysis · Priority 🟡 · Code: causal_survival_semisup.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Predictive ML answers "what will happen?"; causal inference answers "what would happen if we intervened?" — does the discount increase retention, does the drug work, which customers are persuadable? Observational data are confounded: people who received treatment differ from those who did not.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Neyman (1923) potential outcomes for experiments; Fisher's randomization; Rubin (1974) potential-outcomes framework; Wright (1920s path analysis) and Pearl (graphical models, do-calculus, 1995; Causality 2000); Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983) propensity score; Horvitz–Thompson IPW (1952); instrumental variables (Wright 1928; Angrist, Imbens & Rubin 1996 LATE); regression discontinuity (Thistlethwaite & Campbell 1960); difference-in-differences (Ashenfelter & Card 1985; Card & Krueger 1994); doubly robust estimators (Robins et al. 1994); Double/Debiased ML (Chernozhukov et al. 2018); meta-learners (Künzel et al. 2019); causal forests (Wager & Athey 2018); uplift modeling in marketing. Two main schools (Rubin potential outcomes, Pearl graphs) are complementary.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: For each person there are two potential outcomes, Y(1) treated and Y(0) untreated, but only one is observed — the fundamental problem of causal inference. Randomization (or a convincing substitute) makes the untreated group a valid stand-in for what the treated group would have experienced.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: Estimands: ATE E[Y(1)−Y(0)], ATT, CATE τ(x)=E[Y(1)−Y(0)|X=x]. Identification assumptions: unconfoundedness (Y(0),Y(1)) ⫫ T | X; overlap 0<e(x)<1 where e(x)=P(T=1|X=x); SUTVA (no interference, consistent treatment). Randomized experiments satisfy the first two by design. Estimators: regression adjustment; IPW τ̂ = mean(TY/e) − mean((1−T)Y/(1−e)); matching; stratification; doubly robust (AIPW); meta-learners — S, T (separate models per arm), X, R, DR; double ML; causal forests. DiD: τ̂ = (Ȳ_T,post − Ȳ_T,pre) − (Ȳ_C,post − Ȳ_C,pre), valid under parallel trends. Worked example (measured). Simulated confounded data: x → treatment and outcome; true ATE 2.0. | Estimator | Estimate | |---|---| | Naive difference in means | 5.18 (heavily biased by confounding) | | Regression adjustment (T + x) | 2.034 | | IPW (estimated propensity) | 2.068 | | Matching on x (1-NN, ATT) | 2.033 | | Unobserved confounder, regress on T only | 5.15 (no method using only observed variables can fix this) | Propensity scores ranged 0.002–0.997 — near-violations of overlap make IPW weights huge and unstable (clip/trim in practice). DiD (simulated, true effect 5, common trend +3, baseline gap 4): post-only comparison = 9.06 (wrong), DiD = 5.04. Heterogeneous effects (T-learner with boosted trees; true τ(x)=1+2x): at x=−0.8: true −0.60, est −0.56; x=0: 1.00 vs 1.06; x=+0.8: 2.60 vs 2.70.

docs.title: 5. Training & cost
docs.text: Standard supervised models inside estimators (logistic/GBM for propensity, outcome models), cross-fitting to avoid overfitting bias. Cost is modest; the real cost is design, data collection, and assumption checking.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: decisions about interventions; policy evaluation; A/B tests with heterogeneity analysis; observational studies with good covariates, natural experiments (DiD, RDD, IV). Avoid: causal claims from predictive feature importance; adjusting for colliders/mediators; conditioning on post-treatment variables; poor overlap; strong unobserved confounding. Always prefer randomized experiments when feasible.

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters & design choices
docs.text: Covariate set (guided by a DAG, not by predictive power), propensity model/trimming thresholds, matching caliper, learner types, cross-fitting folds, number of trees (causal forest), clustering of standard errors, placebo/falsification tests.

docs.title: 8. Implementation
docs.text:
e = LogisticRegression().fit(X, t).predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
ate_ipw = np.mean(t*y/e) - np.mean((1-t)*y/(1-e))
m1 = GradientBoostingRegressor().fit(X[t==1], y[t==1]); m0 = GradientBoostingRegressor().fit(X[t==0], y[t==0])
cate = m1.predict(X) - m0.predict(X)                      # T-learner
Libraries: DoWhy, EconML, CausalML, statsmodels, grf (R) for causal forests. (Full simulation code in causal_survival_semisup.py.)

docs.title: 9. Evaluation
docs.text: No ground truth in real data: use randomized experiments as the gold standard, covariate balance checks (standardized mean differences), overlap plots, placebo tests, sensitivity analysis to unobserved confounding (E-values, Rosenbaum bounds), uplift/Qini curves for CATE ranking, and agreement across estimators. Simulations (like above) validate method behavior.

docs.title: 10. Case study (template)
docs.text: Marketing coupon: run an A/B test; estimate ATE with covariate adjustment (CUPED); fit uplift models on the experiment to target persuadable customers; evaluate with Qini curve on a held-out randomized sample; deploy with a holdout group to monitor lift.

docs.title: 11. Comparison
docs.text: Method Needs Handles unobserved confounding? RCT Randomization Yes (by design) Adjustment/IPW/matching Unconfoundedness + overlap No DiD Panel/repeated data, parallel trends Time-invariant ones IV Valid instrument Yes (if valid) RDD Assignment cutoff Locally

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Correlation vs causation? Confounders create associations without causal effect (naive estimate 5.18 vs true 2.0).
  • What is a propensity score? P(treatment | covariates); balancing score.
  • Why DiD? Removes time-invariant group differences and common shocks; needs parallel trends.
  • Pitfall of "controlling for everything"? Conditioning on colliders/mediators introduces bias.
  • ATE vs CATE? Average vs covariate-specific effect (uplift).

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Draw a DAG with a collider and show bias from adjusting for it by simulation; implement doubly robust estimation; run a placebo-outcome test on the simulated data.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Hernán & Robins, Causal Inference: What If (free); Pearl, Glymour & Jewell, Causal Inference in Statistics: A Primer; Imbens & Rubin, Causal Inference; Chernozhukov et al. (2018); Wager & Athey (2018); Facure, Causal Inference for the Brave and True (free); Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments.

docs.title: Chapter 6.5 — Survival Analysis: Kaplan–Meier, Cox Proportional Hazards, Parametric & ML Models
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 6.4 · Next 6.6 Semi-supervised & weak supervision · Priority 🟡 · Code: causal_survival_semisup.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Model time until an event (churn, failure, death, default, relapse) when some subjects are censored (the event hasn't happened by the end of observation, or they dropped out). Ordinary regression/classification on "did it happen" or on observed times is biased because it ignores censoring.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Life tables (Graunt 1662; Halley); Kaplan & Meier (1958) product-limit estimator; log-rank test (Mantel 1966); Cox (1972) proportional hazards (semi-parametric); parametric models (Weibull, exponential, log-normal; accelerated failure time); competing risks (Fine & Gray 1999); frailty models; random survival forests (Ishwaran et al. 2008); gradient-boosted survival (XGBoost survival:cox/AFT); neural: DeepSurv (Katzman 2018), DeepHit (Lee 2018); discrete-time classification formulations. Concordance index (Harrell 1982) for evaluation.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: At each time an event occurs, look at who is still "at risk" and ask what fraction experienced the event; multiply the survival fractions. Censored subjects contribute information up to the time they leave.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: Survival S(t)=P(T>t); hazard h(t)=lim P(t≤T<t+dt | T≥t)/dt; cumulative hazard H(t)=∫h, S(t)=exp(−H(t)). Kaplan–Meier: Ŝ(t)=Π_{t_i≤t} (1 − d_i/n_i) (d_i events, n_i at risk at time t_i). Worked example (computed). Times [2,3,3,5,6,8], event indicator [1,1,0,1,0,1] (0 = censored): - t=2: at risk 6, 1 event ⇒ S = 5/6 = 0.8333 - t=3: at risk 5, 1 event (one subject censored at 3 stays in the risk set until 3) ⇒ S = 0.8333·4/5 = 0.6667 - t=5: at risk 3, 1 event ⇒ S = 0.6667·2/3 = 0.4444 - t=8: at risk 1, 1 event ⇒ S = 0. lifelines gives the same S(5)=0.4444. Cox model: h(t|x)=h₀(t)·exp(βᵀx); β estimated by the partial likelihood Π_{events} exp(βᵀx_i)/Σ_{j∈R(t_i)} exp(βᵀx_j) without specifying h₀. exp(β_j) = hazard ratio per unit of feature j. Assumption: proportional hazards (ratios constant over time) — check Schoenfeld residuals; fix with stratification, time-varying covariates, or other models. Other assumptions: non-informative censoring, independent subjects, log-linear covariate effects. Parametric/AFT: log T = βᵀx + σε (Weibull etc.) — gives full survival curves and extrapolation beyond observed time.

docs.title: 5. Training & cost
docs.text: KM is O(n log n). Cox fits by Newton–Raphson on the partial likelihood (O(n·p²)-ish with ties handling). Random survival forests and GBMs cost like their non-survival analogues. Prediction: risk score / survival curve per subject.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: churn timing, predictive maintenance, clinical trials, credit default timing, time-to-conversion, any censored duration data. Avoid: plain regression on durations with censored rows dropped or treated as events; classification at a fixed horizon if censoring is heavy (or use IPCW); proportional-hazards model when hazards clearly cross (use AFT, stratified, or ML models).

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Cox: penalizer (ridge/lasso), tie method (Efron), strata, time-varying covariates; AFT: distribution family; forests: trees, min node size, max_features; GBM: usual boosting knobs with survival objective; discretization of time for classification-style approaches.

docs.title: 8. Implementation
docs.text:
from lifelines import KaplanMeierFitter, CoxPHFitter
from lifelines.datasets import load_rossi
km = KaplanMeierFitter().fit(durations, event_observed)
cph = CoxPHFitter(penalizer=0.01).fit(df, duration_col="week", event_col="arrest"); cph.print_summary(); cph.check_assumptions(df)
# scikit-survival: RandomSurvivalForest, GradientBoostingSurvivalAnalysis, concordance_index_censored

docs.title: 9. Evaluation & results (measured)
docs.text: Rossi recidivism data (432 released prisoners, time to rearrest, censored at 52 weeks) — Cox model: fin (financial aid) coef −0.379 ⇒ hazard ratio 0.684 (≈32% lower hazard, p=0.047); age coef −0.057 ⇒ HR 0.944 per year (≈5.6% lower hazard per year older, p=0.009); race (HR 1.369, p=0.308) and wexp (HR 0.861, p=0.480) not significant at conventional levels. Concordance index 0.64 (0.5 = random, 1 = perfect) — modest discrimination, typical for behavioral outcomes. (Treat hazard ratios as associations, not causal effects, unless the design supports it—Ch 6.4.) Metrics: concordance index (ranking), time-dependent AUC, integrated Brier score (calibration + discrimination over time, with IPCW for censoring), calibration plots at chosen horizons, log-rank test for group comparison. Validate on out-of-time/held-out patients.

docs.title: 10. Case study (template)
docs.text: Subscription churn: KM curves by plan; Cox with features and time-varying usage; compare with random survival forest and a monthly discrete-time LightGBM; evaluate C-index and calibration at 3/6/12 months; use predicted survival curves to target retention offers (and causal designs to test them).

docs.title: 11. Comparison
docs.text: Model Pros Cons Kaplan–Meier Nonparametric, easy No covariates (except by strata) Cox PH Interpretable HRs, no baseline assumption Proportional hazards, linear AFT/Weibull Full curves, extrapolation Distribution assumption Random survival forest / GBM Nonlinear, interactions Less interpretable Deep survival Complex inputs Data hungry, tuning

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• What is censoring? Event not observed within follow-up; right-censoring is most common. Dropping or treating censored as events biases estimates.
  • Hazard vs survival function? Instantaneous risk given survival so far vs probability of surviving past t.
  • Proportional hazards assumption? Ratio of hazards between subjects is constant over time.
  • Interpret HR=0.68? 32% lower instantaneous event rate at any time, holding others fixed.
  • What does the C-index measure? Probability that, for a comparable pair, the one with higher predicted risk fails first.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Hand-compute KM for a new dataset; fit Cox and test proportional hazards; compare Weibull AFT vs Cox predicted median survival; build a discrete-time hazard model with logistic regression.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Kaplan & Meier (1958); Cox (1972) JRSS B; Klein & Moeschberger, Survival Analysis; Harrell, Regression Modeling Strategies; lifelines and scikit-survival documentation; Kvamme, Borgan & Scheel (2019) on Cox-based neural nets.

docs.title: Chapter 6.6 — Semi-Supervised Learning and Weak Supervision
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Prev 6.5 · Next 7 Comparisons · Priority 🟡 · Code: causal_survival_semisup.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Labels are expensive. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) uses a small labeled set plus abundant unlabeled data. Weak supervision replaces hand labels with noisy, programmatic or partial labels (heuristics, knowledge bases, crowd, other models). Related: self-supervised pretraining (Ch 5.7), active learning, transfer learning.

docs.title: 2. History and methods
docs.text: Approach Idea Landmarks Self-training / pseudo-labeling Train → predict unlabeled → add confident predictions → retrain Scudder (1965); Yarowsky (1995); Lee (2013) for deep nets Co-training Two views teach each other Blum & Mitchell (1998) Graph / label propagation Labels diffuse over a similarity graph Zhu & Ghahramani (2002); Label Spreading (Zhou et al. 2004) Generative / EM Model p(x,y) with unlabeled x via EM Nigam et al. (2000) Consistency regularization Predictions invariant to perturbation Π-model / Temporal ensembling (Laine & Aila 2016), Mean Teacher (Tarvainen 2017), UDA (Xie 2019) Hybrid Pseudo-labels + consistency + strong augmentation MixMatch (2019), FixMatch (Sohn et al. 2020) Weak supervision Label functions combined by a generative label model Distant supervision (Mintz 2009), Snorkel/data programming (Ratner et al. 2016/2017) Noisy-label learning Find/handle label errors Confident learning (Northcutt et al. 2021), co-teaching, robust losses Active learning Choose which points to label Uncertainty / query-by-committee sampling (Settles) Modern practice: pretrain self-supervised/foundation model → fine-tune on few labels, which often dominates classic SSL; zero/few-shot LLM labeling is now a common weak-supervision source (with verification).

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Unlabeled data reveal the shape of the data (clusters, manifolds). If decision boundaries should lie in low-density gaps (cluster/smoothness assumption), unlabeled points tell you where the gaps are.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: Assumptions (without them SSL can hurt): smoothness (nearby points share labels), cluster/low-density separation, manifold (data lie on low-dim manifold). Pseudo-labeling: L = L_sup + λ(t)·Σ_{u: max p(y|u) ≥ τ} CE(p(y|u), argmax p(y|u)). Consistency: L_u = ‖f(Aug₁(u)) − f(Aug₂(u))‖². FixMatch: pseudo-label from a weak augmentation (if confidence ≥ τ) supervises prediction on a strong augmentation. Label propagation: build affinity W, normalized S=D^{-1/2}WD^{-1/2}, iterate F ← αSF + (1−α)Y to a fixed point F* = (1−α)(I−αS)^{-1}Y. Worked mini-example (label propagation intuition). Chain A—B—C with A labeled +, C labeled −, B unlabeled equidistant: B receives equal pulls from both ⇒ ≈0 (uncertain). Add D connected only to A: D inherits + through A. Structure carries the labels. Weak supervision label model: each labeling function (LF) votes/abstains; a generative model estimates LF accuracies and correlations without ground truth and outputs probabilistic labels to train a discriminative model.

docs.title: 5. Training & cost
docs.text: Typically 1–3× the supervised training cost (extra forward passes, graph construction O(n²) or kNN O(n log n)). Label spreading needs a graph over all points (memory!). Weak supervision shifts cost from labeling to writing/debugging labeling functions.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: many unlabeled, few labeled; labels expensive/delayed; class structure is cluster-like; domain knowledge easily encoded as rules. Avoid: when unlabeled data come from a different distribution; when classes overlap heavily (assumptions fail); when labels are cheap (just label more); when pseudo-label errors would reinforce confirmation bias; without a clean labeled validation set.

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Confidence threshold τ, unlabeled/labeled ratio, loss weight ramp-up, augmentations, number of neighbors/kernel width (graph), α (propagation), iterations, label-model settings, LF coverage/accuracy thresholds.

docs.title: 8. Implementation
docs.text:
from sklearn.semi_supervised import SelfTrainingClassifier, LabelSpreading
y_partial = np.full(len(y), -1); y_partial[labeled_idx] = y[labeled_idx]           # -1 means unlabeled
st = SelfTrainingClassifier(SVC(probability=True), threshold=0.8).fit(X, y_partial)
ls = LabelSpreading(kernel="knn", n_neighbors=10).fit(X, y_partial)
Weak supervision: snorkel library (labeling functions + LabelModel); cleanlab for label-error detection.

docs.title: 9. Evaluation & results (measured)
docs.text: Digits (1,300 training images, 30 labels = 3 per class, 497 test images): | Method | Test accuracy | |---|---| | Supervised SVC, 30 labels only | 0.785 | | Self-training SVC (threshold 0.8) | 0.785 (no gain) | | Label Spreading (kNN graph, k=10) | 0.899 | | Upper bound: SVC with all 1,300 labels | 0.986 | Label propagation recovers ~57% of the gap between 30 labels and full supervision using only the data's geometry (digits form tight clusters—assumption holds). Self-training gave no improvement here: with few, possibly mislabeled confident predictions it mostly reinforces the initial classifier — the classic confirmation-bias failure; it needs a reasonably accurate base model and careful thresholds. Always evaluate on a held-out labeled set and compare with the supervised-only baseline.

docs.title: 10. Case study (template)
docs.text: Document classification with 200 labeled and 50k unlabeled texts: baseline TF-IDF+logistic on labeled; add embeddings from a pretrained sentence encoder (Ch 5.7) → logistic (often the largest jump); then pseudo-label with high confidence, add weak labeling functions (keywords, metadata), review disagreement with cleanlab, track accuracy on a small gold set, and watch per-class drift.

docs.title: 11. Comparison
docs.text: Self-supervised pretraining + fine-tuning (most scalable) > classic SSL (consistency/pseudo-label) > label propagation (small data, strong cluster structure) > pure weak supervision (fast, noisy). Active learning complements all: spend the labeling budget where the model is uncertain.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why can SSL hurt? If the cluster/smoothness assumption is false or unlabeled data are off-distribution, pseudo-labels inject errors.
  • What is confirmation bias in pseudo-labeling? The model reinforces its own mistakes; mitigate with thresholds, ramp-up, ensembling, strong augmentation.
  • Weak vs semi-supervised? Weak: noisy/programmatic labels for many points; semi: few true labels plus unlabeled data.
  • How do you validate? A small trusted labeled validation set; never trust the pseudo-labels themselves.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Vary the number of labels (10, 30, 100, 300) and plot self-training vs label spreading vs supervised; implement FixMatch's weak/strong augmentation idea on digits; write 5 labeling functions for a text task and measure coverage and conflict.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Chapelle, Schölkopf & Zien, Semi-Supervised Learning; Zhu & Goldberg, Introduction to Semi-Supervised Learning; Lee (2013); Sohn et al. (2020) FixMatch; Ratner et al. (2017) Snorkel; Northcutt, Jiang & Chuang (2021) "Confident learning"; Settles, Active Learning.

docs.title: Section 7 — Comparisons, Decision Matrices and Benchmarks
docs.text: ← Roadmap · Code: tabular_benchmark.py

docs.title: 1. A fair benchmark protocol
docs.text: Same data, same folds, preprocessing inside the pipeline, metrics chosen before looking, a baseline, repeated/stratified CV, report spread, and cost (time/memory/latency). Differences smaller than the fold-to-fold standard deviation are ties.

docs.title: 2. Measured benchmark: OpenML "adult" (census income, mixed types)
docs.text:
10,000-row random subsample, 14 features (6 numeric, 8 categorical), 24.2% positive; 5-fold stratified CV; default-ish hyperparameters (not tuned); 2 CPU threads. Linear models/k-NN/SVM/MLP use imputation + scaling + one-hot; tree models use imputation + ordinal encoding.

Model ROC-AUC (±sd) PR-AUC Log loss Fit s/fold Majority baseline 0.500 0.242 — 0.05 Logistic regression 0.903 ± 0.010 0.764 0.324 0.16 k-NN (k=25) 0.889 ± 0.011 0.712 0.422 0.05 RBF SVM 0.899 ± 0.010 0.764 n/a (no probabilities) 2.02 MLP (64,32) 0.909 ± 0.007 0.775 0.316 1.65 Random forest (200) 0.911 ± 0.009 0.792 0.312 1.19 HistGradientBoosting 0.919 ± 0.009 0.812 0.295 0.48 XGBoost 0.923 ± 0.008 0.819 0.287 0.27 LightGBM 0.921 ± 0.007 0.816 0.290 0.30

How to read it - The three boosted models are statistically tied (differences ≤ 0.004 AUC vs sd ≈ 0.008); they beat the random forest by ~0.01 AUC and logistic regression by ~0.02 AUC. - A well-regularized logistic regression is already strong (0.903) and 10× cheaper than an SVM; most of the "easy" lift is available from a linear baseline. - k-NN is cheapest to fit but worst here (mixed categorical features and one-hot distance are a poor fit). - This is one dataset. Rankings change with size, noise, feature types, and tuning (Grinsztajn et al. 2022 benchmark over many tabular datasets: tree ensembles tend to lead on medium-sized tabular data).

docs.title: 3. Master comparison table (rules of thumb)
docs.text: Algorithm Task Data size sweet spot Nonlinear Interpretability Train cost Predict cost Key weakness Chapter Linear/Ridge/Lasso Reg Any No High Very low Very low Linear only 1.1–1.3 Logistic Clf Any No High Low Very low Linear boundary 2.1 Naive Bayes Clf Small / text Limited High Very low Very low Independence, calibration 2.3 LDA/QDA Clf Small Quadratic Medium Low Low Gaussian assumption 2.4 k-NN Both Small–medium Yes High (cases) None High Curse of dimensionality 2.5 SVM (kernel) Both ≤ ~50k rows Yes Low High Medium Scales poorly 2.6 Decision tree Both Any Yes High (small) Low Low High variance 3.1 Random forest Both Medium–large Yes Medium Medium Medium Memory, no extrapolation 3.2 Gradient boosting (XGB/LGBM/Cat) Both Medium–large Yes Medium Medium Low Tuning, no extrapolation 3.3–3.4 GMM Cluster/density Small–medium Gaussian mix Medium Medium Low Gaussian assumption 3.5 K-Means Cluster Any No High Low Low Spherical clusters 4.1 DBSCAN/HDBSCAN Cluster Small–medium Yes Medium Medium — Parameter/density sensitivity 4.2 PCA Reduction Any No Medium Low Low Linear 4.3 t-SNE/UMAP Visualization ≤ 10⁶ Yes Low High — Distortion 4.4 Isolation Forest/LOF Anomaly Any Yes Medium Low Low Thresholding 4.5 MLP Both Large Yes Low High Medium Tuning, data hunger 5.1 CNN Images/signals Large / pretrained Yes Low High Medium Data, compute 5.2 RNN/LSTM Sequences Medium Yes Low High Low (streaming) Long range, sequential 5.3 Transformer Sequences/multimodal Very large / pretrained Yes Low Very high High O(n²) attention, cost 5.4

docs.title: 4. Decision flow (tabular supervised)
docs.text:
Start → define metric, baseline, split strategy
  │
  ├─ Is the data tabular?  ─ yes → Logistic/Ridge baseline → LightGBM/XGBoost/HistGB → compare, tune lightly
  │                         no  → images/audio/text/graphs → pretrained deep model + fine-tune (Ch 5, 6.x)
  │
  ├─ Need explanations/regulation? → linear/GAM/shallow tree/monotone GBM; add SHAP/permutation for the rest
  ├─ Very few rows (<500)? → regularized linear, NB, SVM, k-NN; avoid big nets
  ├─ Temporal? → time-based CV, seasonal baseline, differenced/lag features
  ├─ Rare target? → PR-AUC, class weights, threshold from cost
  └─ Latency/memory tight? → linear, small GBM, quantized model

docs.title: 5. Model-selection pitfalls
docs.text: Comparing default settings of one model vs tuned another · different preprocessing · leaking via encoders · comparing on a split reused for tuning · ignoring variance across folds/seeds · optimizing the wrong metric · neglecting calibration/latency/maintainability.

docs.title: 6. Evolution chains recap (what changed, what it cost)
docs.text: Chain Improvement Cost OLS → Ridge → Lasso → ElasticNet Stability → sparsity → grouping Bias, tuning Tree → RF → GBM → XGB/LGBM/Cat Variance ↓ → bias ↓ → speed/regularization/categoricals Interpretability, tuning Perceptron → SVM → kernel SVM Max-margin → nonlinear Quadratic scaling MLP → CNN → ResNet → ViT Structure → depth → global attention Data/compute RNN → LSTM → Attention → Transformer Memory → long range → parallelism O(n²) VAE/GAN → Diffusion Fidelity & stability Sampling cost Prompt → RAG → LoRA → Agents Behavior → knowledge → specialization → autonomy Complexity, evaluation burden

docs.title: Project 1 — End-to-End Tabular ML: Income Classification (OpenML "adult")
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Code: project_adult_income.py · Uses: Ch 0.5, 0.6, 2.1, 3.4

A realistic pipeline you can reuse: baseline → pipeline → tuning → calibration → threshold → single final test → error analysis → model card. Data: 20,000-row random sample of OpenML adult (fetched with fetch_openml), 14 mixed features, 23.9% positives. Split: 12,000 train / 4,000 validation / 4,000 test (stratified; test touched once).

docs.title: 1. Problem framing
docs.text: Predict whether annual income exceeds $50K from census attributes. (A standard benchmark; do not use such a model to make real decisions about people. The data are from 1994 and encode historical inequities.) Define upfront: primary metric PR-AUC (positive class is the minority), secondary ROC-AUC, log loss/Brier for probability quality; baseline = regularized logistic regression.

docs.title: 2. Steps and results (all measured)
docs.text:
Step Validation result Baseline: standardized numerics + one-hot categoricals + logistic AUC 0.905, PR-AUC 0.767, logloss 0.319, Brier 0.1028 LightGBM, near-default (300 trees, lr 0.05, 15 leaves) AUC 0.924, PR-AUC 0.821, logloss 0.283, Brier 0.0901 + Randomized search (20 trials × 4-fold CV on train, scoring PR-AUC) best CV PR-AUC 0.822; validation AUC 0.925, PR-AUC 0.823 + Isotonic calibration (4-fold) AUC 0.926, PR-AUC 0.825, logloss 0.280, Brier 0.0893 Best parameters found: num_leaves 15, lr 0.05, n_estimators 400, min_child_samples 10, subsample 1.0, colsample 0.8, reg_lambda 1.

Lessons: (1) the model family (+0.054 PR-AUC from logistic → boosted trees) mattered far more than tuning (+0.002); (2) calibration helped probabilities slightly (Brier 0.0894 → 0.0893 — a tiny gain because LightGBM was already well calibrated; check, don't assume); (3) without a baseline you couldn't say the gain is real.

docs.title: 3. Threshold selection
docs.text: On validation predictions: F1-optimal threshold 0.36 (F1 0.730). With an example cost ratio (missed positive costs 5× a false alarm), the cost-optimal threshold is 0.16. The "right" threshold is a business decision, not 0.5.

docs.title: 4. Final evaluation (test set, once)
docs.text: Model AUC PR-AUC logloss Brier Baseline logistic (refit on train+val) 0.906 0.774 0.319 0.1014 Final: tuned LightGBM + isotonic (refit on train+val) 0.926 0.827 0.287 0.0883 Threshold Precision Recall F1 --- --- --- --- 0.50 0.774 0.650 0.707 0.36 (F1-opt) 0.690 0.780 0.732 0.16 (cost-opt) 0.532 0.924 0.675 Test results match validation closely (no sign of overfitting to validation).

docs.title: 5. Error and subgroup analysis (test)
docs.text: Slice n AUC Actual positive rate Mean predicted Male 2,647 0.906 0.308 0.302 Female 1,353 0.946 0.106 0.111 Age < 30 1,214 0.948 0.046 0.051 Age 30–50 1,904 0.904 0.311 0.316 Age ≥ 50 882 0.887 0.350 0.324 Calibration is good within slices (mean prediction ≈ actual rate), but base rates differ greatly across groups (e.g. selection rate at 0.5: 26.3% for males vs 8.1% for females), so any use of this model for decisions requires fairness analysis, legal review and a clear definition of acceptable disparity—not a purely technical fix. Discrimination is weakest for ages ≥ 50 (AUC 0.887).

docs.title: 6. Explainability
docs.text: Permutation importance (drop in validation PR-AUC): capital-gain 0.247, education-num 0.062, age 0.047, marital-status 0.043, capital-loss 0.039, relationship 0.025. Capital-gain dominates because it is highly informative (and zero for most people). Permutation importance on correlated features can understate shared signal (e.g. marital-status/relationship); use SHAP/partial dependence for deeper analysis.

docs.title: 7. Deliverables checklist (a real project)
docs.text:
• [ ] Problem statement, metric, cost matrix, success threshold agreed with stakeholders
  • [ ] Data audit: leakage, duplicates, drift, missingness, label quality
  • [ ] Baseline + single pipeline object (preprocessing + model) saved with versioned config
  • [ ] Time/group-aware split documented
  • [ ] Tuning with a budget; report tuned vs default honestly
  • [ ] Calibration + threshold policy; fairness and slice analysis
  • [ ] Model card (intended use, data, metrics, limits), monitoring plan (input drift, performance by slice, calibration), rollback plan
  • [ ] Serving test: latency, memory, train/serve parity

docs.title: 8. Minimal serving sketch
docs.text:
import joblib, pandas as pd
joblib.dump(final, "model.joblib")                    # pipeline includes preprocessing
model = joblib.load("model.joblib")
proba = model.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame([row]))[0, 1]
decision = proba >= 0.36                              # threshold from the business cost analysis

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Re-run with a time-based split if you add a date; replace LightGBM with logistic + interactions and see how much gap remains; add monotone constraints on education-num; run a drift simulation by shifting age.

docs.title: Section 9 — Natural Language Processing (NLP)
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Next section: 10 — GenAI & LLMs

A dedicated, detailed NLP track that sits before GenAI/LLMs: it teaches how text becomes numbers, how classical and neural NLP models work, and how the field moved from counting words to pretrained transformers — the foundation that LLM chapters build on.

How the evidence is organized - ✅ Executed locally (numbers quoted in chapters): code/nlp_text_basics.py, nlp_topics_lm.py, nlp_embeddings.py, nlp_sequence_labeling.py (scikit-learn 1.9.1, NLTK 3.10, sklearn-crfsuite, seqeval). - 📓 Notebooks for Google Colab: notebooks/nlp_1_classical.ipynb (CPU; re-runs everything above) and notebooks/nlp_2_transformers.ipynb (GPU; BERT/DistilBERT/T5/MiniLM/NER/QA/BLEU). The transformer notebook was not run by the author — chapters N.8–N.10 mark which numbers are measured and which are for you to fill in. Run the notebook and paste your results into the "Your results" tables.

docs.title: The NLP timeline (what each era fixed)
docs.text:
1950s-80s  rules, grammars, WordNet-style lexicons ......... brittle, labor intensive
1990s      statistical NLP: n-grams, HMMs, naive Bayes ..... needs counts, sparse
2000s      feature engineering + linear models, CRFs, LDA .. engineered features
2013-2016  word2vec/GloVe, RNN/LSTM, seq2seq + attention ... dense semantics, end-to-end
2017-2019  Transformer, ELMo/BERT pretraining ............... contextual transfer learning
2020-now   LLMs: prompting, RAG, tools, agents .............. see Section 10

docs.title: Chapter N.1 — Text Preprocessing and Tokenization
docs.text: ← NLP index · Next N.2 Text representation · Priority 🔴 · Code: nlp_text_basics.py (executed) · Notebook: nlp_1_classical.ipynb

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Text is a variable-length string; models need discrete units. Preprocessing cleans and normalizes text; tokenization splits it into units (words, subwords, characters, bytes). Choices here silently determine vocabulary size, out-of-vocabulary (OOV) rate, sparsity and downstream accuracy.

docs.title: 2. Historical background
docs.text: Rule-based tokenizers and sentence splitters (Penn Treebank conventions) → statistical segmenters (Punkt, Kiss & Strunk 2006) → stemmers (Lovins 1968; Porter 1980) and lexicon-based lemmatization (WordNet) → subword units to kill OOV: BPE (Gage 1994; applied to NMT by Sennrich et al. 2016), WordPiece (Schuster & Nakajima 2012; BERT), Unigram LM / SentencePiece (Kudo 2018) → byte-level BPE (GPT-2) — no unknown characters. Modern LLM pipelines mostly skip stemming/stopword removal and rely on subwords.

docs.title: 3. Pipeline stages and decisions
docs.text: Stage Options Notes Cleaning Unicode normalization (NFC/NFKC), strip HTML/markup, fix encodings, remove boilerplate Do not over-clean: punctuation, case and emoji often carry sentiment/entity signal Case Lowercase vs keep Lowercasing merges "Apple/apple" (entity loss); keep case for NER/cased models Sentence splitting Rules / Punkt / learned Abbreviations break naive splitting (see below) Tokenization Whitespace, regex, rule-based (Treebank), subword (BPE/WordPiece/Unigram), char, byte Language-dependent: Chinese/Japanese/Thai have no spaces; German compounds; Arabic clitics Normalization Stemming (crude suffix stripping), lemmatization (dictionary form with POS) Stemming faster; lemmatization linguistically cleaner Stopwords Remove very frequent function words Helps bag-of-words noise; hurts negation/phrases and is unnecessary for neural models Filtering min_df/max_df, length limits, numbers/URLs → placeholders Control vocabulary size

docs.title: 4. Executed examples
docs.text: Tokenizer contrast on Dr. Smith didn't pay $3.50 for U.S. e-mail; it's well-known... #NLP @user https://x.co: - whitespace: ['Dr.', 'Smith', "didn't", 'pay', '$3.50', 'for', 'U.S.', 'e-mail;', "it's", 'well-known...', '#NLP', '@user', 'https://x.co'] — punctuation glued to words - regex \w+: ['Dr','Smith','didn','t','pay','3','50',…,'e','mail',…,'https','x','co'] — splits didn't, 3.50, URL (destroys structure) - NLTK word_tokenize: ['Dr.','Smith','did',"n't",'pay','$','3.50','for','U.S.','e-mail',';','it',"'s",'well-known','...','#','NLP','@','user','https',':','//x.co'] — handles clitics and abbreviations but still splits the URL/hashtag. No tokenizer is "correct": social-media text needs a tweet-aware tokenizer; URLs may be normalized to a placeholder. Sentence splitting: "Dr. Smith arrived at 5 p.m. He left. Mr. Lee stayed." → Punkt gives ['Dr. Smith arrived at 5 p.m.', 'He left.', 'Mr. Lee stayed.'] — handled abbreviations correctly here; splitting on ". " would have produced 5 fragments. Stemming vs lemmatization: | word | Porter stem | lemma (verb) | lemma (noun) | |---|---|---|---| | running | run | run | running | | studies | studi | study | study | | better | better | better | better | | happily | happili | happily | happily | | universities | univers | universities | university | | was | wa | be | wa | Stems need not be words (studi, happili, wa); lemmatization depends on POS (was → be only as a verb); neither converts better → good (needs the adjective POS tag and WordNet exceptions).

docs.title: 5. Statistics of text: Zipf's and Heaps' laws (executed on the Brown corpus)
docs.text: Brown corpus: 981,716 alphabetic tokens, 40,234 types. - Zipf's law: frequency ∝ 1/rank, i.e. rank × frequency ≈ constant. | Rank | Word | Frequency | rank × freq | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | the | 69,971 | 69,971 | | 10 | he | 9,548 | 95,480 | | 100 | well | 897 | 89,700 | | 1,000 | built | 103 | 103,000 | | 10,000 | generalizations | 7 | 70,000 | - Hapax legomena (words seen once): 15,367 = 38.2% of all types — a huge long tail, the reason OOV words are unavoidable with word-level vocabularies. - Heaps' law: vocabulary grows sublinearly with corpus size: first 10,000 tokens → 2,470 types; 100,000 → 12,235; 500,000 → 30,049; all 981,716 → 40,234. Vocabulary never saturates. Consequences: (1) a few hundred words cover most tokens, (2) most types are rare, (3) count-based estimates for rare events are unreliable → smoothing (N.4), subwords, embeddings (N.5).

docs.title: 6. Subword tokenization
docs.text: BPE: start from characters, repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair until reaching the target vocabulary size (worked example with merges in Section 10, Ch G.2). WordPiece chooses merges maximizing corpus likelihood; Unigram LM starts with a large vocabulary and prunes by likelihood loss and can sample multiple segmentations (regularization). Executed with bert-base-uncased: - unbelievably tokenization is fun → un ##bel ##ie ##va ##bly token ##ization is fun - COVID-19 vaccines → co ##vid - 19 vaccines - ChatGPT hallucinates pseudoscience → chat ##gp ##t hall ##uc ##inates pseudo ##sc ##ience - hello world → ids [101, 7592, 2088, 102] = [CLS] hello world [SEP] Observations: new words split into pieces (no OOV), but pieces need not be morphemes; vocabulary of a model trained before 2020 splits "COVID" awkwardly. Always use the tokenizer that matches the pretrained model.

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Situation Recommendation Classical bag-of-words Light cleaning, lowercase, keep negations; stopword removal optional (test it) Neural/pretrained models Use the model's own tokenizer; minimal cleaning Morphologically rich or low-resource languages Subwords / character models; lemmatizers with language-specific tools Social media Tweet-aware tokenizer, normalize URLs/@mentions, keep emoji/hashtags Languages without spaces Segmenters (jieba, MeCab) or character n-grams/subwords Avoid: aggressive stemming for tasks needing precision (search for names), lowercasing for NER, removing stopwords for tasks where function words matter (authorship, negation).

docs.title: 8. Pitfalls
docs.text: Train/serve tokenizer mismatch · fitting vocabulary on test data · dropping negation ("not good" → "good") through stopword removal · unicode confusables · truncating long texts silently (transformer max length 512 tokens) · leaking PII into vocabularies.

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
import nltk, re
from nltk.stem import PorterStemmer, WordNetLemmatizer
nltk.word_tokenize(text); nltk.sent_tokenize(text)
PorterStemmer().stem("studies")              # 'studi'
WordNetLemmatizer().lemmatize("was", "v")    # 'be'
from transformers import AutoTokenizer       # subword (see notebook nlp_2)
AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased").tokenize("tokenization")
spaCy (spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")) provides a fast rule-based tokenizer, lemmatizer, POS tagger and NER pipeline.

docs.title: 10. Evaluation of preprocessing
docs.text: Treat each choice as a hyperparameter: ablate with cross-validation on the downstream task (N.3 shows stopword removal and stemming did not help sentiment accuracy with TF-IDF+LR: 0.859 → 0.855 / 0.854). Track vocabulary size, OOV rate on validation, average sequence length (cost), and error examples.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Stemming vs lemmatization? Rule-based suffix chopping (fast, may give non-words) vs dictionary/POS-aware base forms (slower, cleaner).
  • Why subword tokenization? Fixed-size vocabulary with no OOV; shares statistics across related words.
  • State Zipf's law and its implication. Frequency ∝ 1/rank; heavy tail means most types are rare → sparsity.
  • Should you remove stopwords for BERT? No.
  • Why can sentence splitting fail? Abbreviations, decimals, quotations.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Train BPE on your own corpus and inspect merges; plot the Zipf log-log curve for Brown vs a tweet corpus; measure OOV rate vs vocabulary size cutoffs; compare lowercasing vs cased features for NER (N.7).

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Jurafsky & Martin, Speech and Language Processing, Ch 2 (Regular expressions, text normalization); Sennrich et al. (2016); Kudo & Richardson (2018) SentencePiece; Porter (1980); Manning, Raghavan & Schütze, Introduction to Information Retrieval Ch 2.

docs.title: Chapter N.2 — Text Representation: Bag-of-Words, TF-IDF, n-grams, Hashing, LSA
docs.text: ← NLP index · Prev N.1 · Next N.3 Classification · Priority 🔴 · Code: nlp_text_basics.py (executed)

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Turn a document into a fixed-length numeric vector so ML models (Ch 1–3) can use it. The classical answer ignores word order and counts words; modern answers learn dense contextual vectors (N.5, N.8).

docs.title: 2. Lineage
docs.text: Boolean/vector-space model for retrieval (Salton, 1960s–70s) → TF-IDF (Spärck Jones 1972: IDF; Salton & Buckley 1988 weighting) → probabilistic retrieval/BM25 (Robertson et al., 1990s) → n-grams to capture local order → hashing trick (Weinberger et al. 2009) for memory-bounded vocabularies → LSA/LSI (Deerwester et al. 1990; SVD of the term–document matrix) to capture synonymy → probabilistic topic models (N.6) → dense neural embeddings (N.5, N.8). Each step addresses a sparsity/semantics limitation of the previous; none dominates everywhere (TF-IDF remains a very strong baseline).

docs.title: 3. Representations
docs.text: Representation Definition Pros Cons One-hot / BoW counts x_j = count(word j in doc) Simple, interpretable High-dim, sparse, no order/semantics Binary BoW presence/absence Robust for short docs (sentiment) Loses frequency TF-IDF tf × idf, idf = log(N/df) (+ smoothing) Down-weights common words, strong baseline Still no semantics n-grams counts of word sequences (n=2,3) or char n-grams Captures negation/phrases ("not good"), robust to typos (char) Explodes vocabulary Hashing index = hash(token) mod 2^b Fixed memory, streaming, no vocabulary Collisions, not invertible LSA truncated SVD of TF-IDF → k dims Dense, synonym-aware Linear, hard to interpret Embedding averages / contextual N.5/N.8 Semantic Need pretrained models

docs.title: 4. Mathematics
docs.text:
Term frequency tf(t,d) (raw count, or sublinear 1+log tf); inverse document frequency idf(t) = log((1+N)/(1+df(t))) + 1 (scikit-learn smooth variant); tfidf = tf·idf, then L2-normalize rows so cosine(d₁,d₂) = d₁·d₂. Worked example (executed). Documents: the cat sat on the mat, the dog sat on the log, cats and dogs (N=3). Vocabulary (alphabetical): and, cat, cats, dog, dogs, log, mat, on, sat, the. Count matrix: 

         and cat cats dog dogs log mat on sat the
doc1      0   1   0    0   0    0   1   1   1   2
doc2      0   0   0    1   0    1   0   1   1   2
doc3      1   0   1    0   1    0   0   0   0   0
Document frequencies: cat=1, the=2, on=2, sat=2, … So idf(cat) = ln((1+3)/(1+1)) + 1 = ln 2 + 1 = 1.693; idf(the) = ln(4/3) + 1 = 1.288 (matches scikit-learn's idf_). Notice "cat" and "cats", "dog" and "dogs" are unrelated columns — the lexical-gap problem that stemming/lemmatization (N.1) or embeddings address. BM25 (retrieval variant) adds term-frequency saturation and length normalization (details in RAG, Ch G.4). LSA: X ≈ U_k Σ_k V_kᵀ; document coordinates U_kΣ_k; query folding q_k = q V_k Σ_k⁻¹. Cosine in the latent space can match documents sharing no words but sharing co-occurring words.

docs.title: 5. Costs
docs.text: BoW/TF-IDF matrices are sparse (store only non-zeros): memory ∝ total tokens, not N×V. Typical vocabulary 10⁴–10⁶; linear models train in seconds on sparse data. LSA: randomized SVD O(nnz·k); dense output N×k. Hashing: constant memory.

docs.title: 6. Executed comparison (sentiment, 2,000 movie reviews, 5-fold CV accuracy)
docs.text: Representation / classifier Accuracy Majority baseline 0.500 Binary BoW + Naive Bayes 0.822 Count BoW + Naive Bayes 0.816 Count BoW + LR 0.836 TF-IDF (sublinear) + LR 0.859 TF-IDF + bigrams (min_df=2) + LR 0.855 TF-IDF + bigrams + LinearSVC 0.879 TF-IDF, stopwords removed + LR 0.855 TF-IDF, Porter stemming + LR 0.854 Hashing 2¹⁶, bigrams, L2-normalized counts, no idf + LR (C=1) 0.752 Hashing 2¹⁶ + TF-IDF weighting + LR 0.856 Reading: (1) TF-IDF > raw counts (+2.3 points for LR); (2) bigrams helped the SVM but not LR here — gains depend on the classifier and regularization; (3) stopword removal and stemming did not help (differences of 0.4–0.5 points are within the ~±1.5-point noise of a 2,000-document CV, so treat as "no benefit"); (4) hashing works once weights are reasonable — the 0.752 result is an under-fit caused by tiny L2-normalized count features with default C, not a flaw of hashing itself (adding TF-IDF weighting recovered 0.856). LSA on the 6-newsgroup corpus (executed): the first 6 components explain only 0.3–0.9% of variance each — text variance is spread across thousands of directions, so LSA needs 100–300 dims in practice, and tuning k matters.

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use TF-IDF+linear for: baselines, small/medium labeled sets, interpretability (coefficients = words), speed, high-dimensional sparse regimes. Use hashing for: streaming, huge/unbounded vocabularies. Use n-grams when negation/phrases matter. Use LSA for quick semantic smoothing/visualization. Avoid bag-of-words for: tasks needing word order/syntax/coreference, paraphrase matching, or long-range context — use contextual models (N.8).

docs.title: 8. Hyperparameters
docs.text: ngram_range, min_df/max_df (prune rare/ubiquitous), max_features, sublinear_tf, norm, binary, stop_words, lowercase, analyzer (word/char/char_wb), hashing n_features, LSA n_components. Tune with CV on the training folds only (pipeline) to avoid vocabulary leakage.

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer, CountVectorizer, HashingVectorizer, TfidfTransformer
from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
vec = TfidfVectorizer(sublinear_tf=True, ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=2)
lsa = make_pipeline(vec, TruncatedSVD(200, random_state=0))
hv = make_pipeline(HashingVectorizer(n_features=2**18, alternate_sign=False, norm=None), TfidfTransformer(sublinear_tf=True))
From scratch: build a vocabulary dict, a scipy.sparse CSR matrix of counts, multiply columns by idf, row-normalize.

docs.title: 10. Evaluation
docs.text: Judge representations by the downstream metric under cross-validation with a fixed classifier; for similarity, use retrieval metrics (precision@k) on labeled pairs. On topic retrieval (8 newsgroups, 300 queries, precision@10; executed in the RAG chapter): BM25 0.432, TF-IDF cosine 0.400, LSA-150 0.383, random 0.122.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why IDF? Words appearing in many documents are less discriminative; IDF down-weights them.
  • Why L2-normalize TF-IDF? So document length doesn't dominate cosine/dot products.
  • Hashing trick trade-off? Fixed memory and no vocabulary vs collisions and no feature names.
  • What does LSA capture? Co-occurrence-based latent dimensions: synonyms land close.
  • When does BoW fail? Negation scope, word sense, long-range dependencies, paraphrase.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Implement TF-IDF from scratch and verify against scikit-learn; plot accuracy vs min_df; compare word and character n-grams on typo-heavy text; inspect LR coefficients for top positive/negative n-grams.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Spärck Jones (1972); Salton & Buckley (1988); Deerwester et al. (1990); Weinberger et al. (2009) "Feature hashing for large scale multitask learning"; Manning et al., IR Ch 6; scikit-learn "Working with text data".

docs.title: Chapter N.3 — Text Classification and Sentiment Analysis
docs.text: ← NLP index · Prev N.2 · Next N.4 Language models · Priority 🔴 · Code: nlp_text_basics.py (executed), classification_family.py · Notebook: nlp_2_transformers.ipynb §6

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Assign one or more labels to a document: spam vs ham, topic, intent, language, toxicity, sentiment (positive/negative/neutral or aspect-level). The most common production NLP task, and the one where a simple baseline is usually surprisingly strong.

docs.title: 2. Historical progression (and trade-offs)
docs.text: Era Approach Strength Limit 1960s–90s Hand rules, keyword lists, sentiment lexicons (General Inquirer, SentiWordNet) Interpretable, no data Brittle, domain-specific 1990s Naive Bayes (Ch 2.3), Rocchio, decision trees Fast, small data Independence, weak features 2002 Pang, Lee & Vaithyanathan: movie-review sentiment with NB/ME/SVM; unigrams+SVM strong; binary features helped Established ML baseline Ignores order 2000s TF-IDF + linear SVM/LR (Joachims 1998) — long-time champion; NB-SVM (Wang & Manning 2012) Excellent small/medium data No semantics 2013–16 Averaged embeddings, CNNs (Kim 2014), LSTMs, fastText (Joulin 2016) Dense semantics, speed Need data/tuning 2018+ Fine-tuned BERT-family encoders State of the art on most benchmarks Compute, latency 2020+ Prompted/zero-shot LLMs, embeddings + LR No/low labeled data Cost, consistency, calibration

docs.title: 3. Choosing a method
docs.text:
labels available?
 ├ few (<100) ......... zero/few-shot LLM prompt or sentence-embedding + LR; NB as baseline
 ├ moderate (1e2-1e4) . TF-IDF + LR/SVM baseline  → embeddings + LR → fine-tune small encoder
 └ many (>1e4) ........ fine-tuned transformer usually best; distill to small model for latency
latency/cost tight? → TF-IDF linear or small distilled encoder
need explanations? ..→ linear model coefficients, LIME/SHAP, rationale extraction

docs.title: 4. Mathematics (recap)
docs.text: Linear classifier on TF-IDF: p(y=1|x)=σ(wᵀx+b) (Ch 2.1); Naive Bayes: argmax_c log P(c)+Σ_j x_j log θ_cj with Laplace smoothing (Ch 2.3); SVM maximizes margin (Ch 2.6). Multi-label: one-vs-rest sigmoid outputs; multi-class: softmax. Fine-tuned encoders: p(y|x)=softmax(W h_[CLS] + b) trained with cross-entropy, all weights updated with a small learning rate (N.8). Worked example (NB log-odds). Word "great" appears in 8% of positive and 2% of negative reviews: log-likelihood ratio ln(0.08/0.02)=1.386; "awful": 1% vs 6% → ln(1/6)=−1.792. A review containing both has evidence 1.386−1.792=−0.406 (+ prior log-odds) → leans negative; each word contributes additively, which is why NB coefficients are interpretable but over-confident when words are correlated.

docs.title: 5. Executed results — sentiment on 2,000 movie reviews (5-fold CV, accuracy)
docs.text:
Full table in N.2. Key rows: majority 0.500 · NB (binary) 0.822 · LR on counts 0.836 · TF-IDF + LR 0.859 · TF-IDF + bigrams + LinearSVC 0.879. Preprocessing ablations (stopwords, stemming) did not help (0.855, 0.854). A 4-class topic task (20 newsgroups; Ch 2.3/2.6): MultinomialNB 0.842, TF-IDF+LR 0.844, TF-IDF+LinearSVC 0.858. Takeaway: the classical stack reaches ~0.86–0.88 on this long-review task (document-level sentiment is easier than sentence-level; published numbers for fine-tuned transformers on full IMDB reach the low 90s, which you can reproduce in the notebook with truncation limits in mind). Always compare against it before building something heavy. Notebook (not executed by the author): SST-2 sentence-level sentiment — TF-IDF(1,2)+LR vs frozen MiniLM embeddings + LR vs fine-tuned DistilBERT. Record your validation accuracies here:

Model (SST-2 validation, 872 sentences) Your accuracy TF-IDF(1,2) + LR run notebook §6 MiniLM embeddings (frozen) + LR run notebook §6 DistilBERT fine-tuned (2 epochs, 20k train) run notebook §6

docs.title: 6. Hyperparameters and design
docs.text: Representation (N.2), regularization C (tune on log grid), class weights for imbalance, thresholds per class (multi-label), calibration (Ch 0.5), text length truncation (transformers: typically ≤512 tokens; long documents → chunk and aggregate), learning rate 2e-5–5e-5 / epochs 2–4 / batch 16–32 for fine-tuning.

docs.title: 7. Sentiment-specific issues
docs.text: Negation scope ("not good", "not bad at all"), sarcasm, domain shift (a "predictable" plot is bad in a movie review, good in a utility's reliability report), aspect-based sentiment ("great food, slow service" → per-aspect labels), neutral class ambiguity, label noise (inter-annotator agreement often 70–85%), emoji and slang. Lexicon tools (VADER, TextBlob) are quick zero-training baselines for social media but domain-limited.

docs.title: 8. Evaluation
docs.text: Accuracy only for balanced data; otherwise macro-F1, per-class precision/recall, PR-AUC, confusion matrix; stratified CV; hold out by source/time/author to avoid leakage (same-author reviews inflate scores); measure calibration; error analysis by slice (length, domain, negation). Report confidence intervals: with 2,000 examples and accuracy 0.86, standard error ≈ 0.8 points, so differences under ~2 points need paired tests.

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold
clf = make_pipeline(TfidfVectorizer(sublinear_tf=True, ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=2), LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000, C=10))
scores = cross_val_score(clf, texts, y, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0))
top = sorted(zip(clf[-1].coef_[0], clf[0].get_feature_names_out()))[-15:]      # most positive n-grams
Fine-tuning with Hugging Face: see the notebook (plain PyTorch loop, version-robust).

docs.title: 10. Case study (template)
docs.text: Support-ticket routing, 12 intents, 6k labeled: TF-IDF+LR baseline → add char n-grams → sentence embeddings + LR → fine-tune a small encoder. Compare macro-F1, p95 latency, cost; examine confusions between near-synonymous intents; set a reject threshold so low-confidence tickets go to humans.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Best baseline for text classification? TF-IDF (word+char n-grams) with logistic regression or linear SVM.
  • Why does NB work for text? Needs correct ranking of class scores, not calibrated probabilities; high-dimensional sparse data suit its low variance.
  • When fine-tune vs prompt an LLM? Enough labels, stable label set, volume/latency/cost constraints → fine-tune a small model; few labels or fast-changing label definitions → prompting.
  • How handle long documents? Chunk + aggregate, hierarchical models, long-context models, or summarize first.
  • Class imbalance? Class weights, resampling, PR-AUC, threshold tuning.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Build the TF-IDF baseline on a dataset of your choice and report top n-grams; add a negation-aware feature (prefix tokens after "not" until punctuation) and measure its effect; fine-tune DistilBERT (notebook) and compare errors with the linear model; calibrate and choose a rejection threshold.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Pang & Lee (2008) Opinion Mining and Sentiment Analysis; Joachims (1998); Wang & Manning (2012) NBSVM; Kim (2014) CNN for sentences; Joulin et al. (2016) fastText; Devlin et al. (2018) BERT; Liu (2012) Sentiment Analysis and Opinion Mining.

docs.title: Chapter N.4 — Statistical Language Models: n-grams, Smoothing, Perplexity
docs.text: ← NLP index · Prev N.3 · Next N.5 Word embeddings · Priority 🟠 · Code: nlp_topics_lm.py (executed)

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Assign probabilities to word sequences: P(w₁…w_n). Used for speech recognition, machine translation (fluency), spelling/autocomplete, OCR, and as the conceptual ancestor of neural LMs and LLMs (Section 10).

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Shannon (1948, 1951: entropy of English via n-gram approximations) → Markov assumption; Jelinek & IBM speech group (1970s–80s) → smoothing: Good–Turing (1953), Katz back-off (1987), Jelinek–Mercer interpolation, Kneser–Ney (1995; Chen & Goodman 1998 showed modified KN is best) → large-scale n-gram models (Brants et al. 2007, "stupid backoff") → neural LM (Bengio et al. 2003) → RNN LMs (Mikolov 2010) → Transformers (2017) → LLMs. Why neural models won: n-grams cannot share statistical strength between similar words/contexts and the table of contexts grows exponentially with n.

docs.title: 3. Mathematics
docs.text: Chain rule: P(w₁…w_n) = Π P(w_i | w_{<i}). Markov assumption of order n−1: P(w_i|w_{<i}) ≈ P(w_i | w_{i−n+1…i−1}). MLE for a bigram: P(w_i|w_{i−1}) = c(w_{i−1}w_i)/c(w_{i−1}). Worked example. Corpus: <s> I am Sam </s>, <s> Sam I am </s>, <s> I do not like green eggs </s>. c(I)=3, c(<s> I)=2, c(I am)=2 ⇒ P(I|<s>)=2/3, P(am|I)=2/3, P(Sam|am)=1/2. So P(<s> I am Sam </s>) = P(I|<s>)P(am|I)P(Sam|am)P(</s>|Sam) = 2/3·2/3·1/2·1/2 = 0.111. Any unseen bigram (e.g. "I like") gets probability 0, so a single novel pair zeroes a whole sentence's probability → smoothing is mandatory. Smoothing methods - Add-k (Laplace): (c(w₁w₂)+k)/(c(w₁)+kV) — simple but gives too much mass to unseen events. - Interpolation: P = λP_bigram + (1−λ)P_unigram (λ tuned on held-out data). - Absolute discounting + Kneser–Ney: P_KN(w|v) = max(c(vw)−D,0)/c(v) + D·N₁₊(v•)/c(v) · P_cont(w), where P_cont(w) = N₁₊(•w)/N₁₊(••) counts how many distinct contexts w follows. Intuition: "Francisco" is frequent but only after "San" — its continuation probability is low, so it shouldn't fill probability mass in other contexts. - Back-off (Katz), stupid backoff (web scale). Perplexity: PP = exp(−(1/N) Σ log P(w_i|context)) — the weighted average branching factor; lower is better; compare only on identical tokenization/vocabulary and test data. Uniform over V gives PP = V.

docs.title: 4. Executed results (Brown "news", 90/10 sentence split, vocabulary = words with count ≥2 plus <unk>: 5,843 types; 10,496 test tokens)
docs.text: Model Test perplexity Unigram, add-1 303 Bigram, MLE ∞ (3,396 of 10,496 = 32.4% of test bigrams never seen in training) Bigram, add-1 747 Bigram, interpolated with unigram (λ=0.7) 184 Bigram, Kneser–Ney-style (D=0.75) 150 Trigram, interpolated (0.5/0.3/0.2, untuned) 246 Lessons: (1) a third of test bigrams are unseen even in a 100k-sentence-scale corpus — sparsity is the central problem; (2) add-1 smoothing badly hurts bigrams (747, worse than a unigram model at 303) because it moves too much probability mass to the 34M possible unseen pairs; (3) good smoothing (interpolation, KN) cuts perplexity 4–5× vs add-1; (4) the trigram did not beat the bigram here because the interpolation weights were fixed rather than tuned and the corpus is small (~1M tokens) — trigrams need far more data and proper KN/back-off. (Brown is small; numbers are for illustration of relative behavior, not benchmark-comparable.)

docs.title: 5. Using n-gram LMs
docs.text: Sentence scoring/ranking (spell correction, ASR rescoring), autocomplete (argmax next word), language identification (character n-grams), text generation (sampling; produces locally fluent, globally incoherent text), feature extraction (perplexity as a fluency/domain-shift signal), data filtering (KenLM is widely used to filter web corpora). Tools: KenLM, NLTK nltk.lm, SRILM.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: fast, tiny, interpretable LM for rescoring, low-resource/embedded settings, language ID, data filtering, baselines and teaching. Avoid: long-range dependencies, semantics, generation quality — use neural LMs (Section 10).

docs.title: 7. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Trivial to train (counting), fast, no GPU, exact probabilities, well understood. − Sparse, exponential growth with n, no generalization across similar words/contexts, fixed short context, memory-heavy at scale.

docs.title: 8. Hyperparameters
docs.text: n (order), vocabulary cutoff / <unk> policy, smoothing method and discount D, interpolation weights (fit by EM on held-out data), pruning thresholds.

docs.title: 9. Implementation (core of the executed code)
docs.text:
import math, collections
u = collections.Counter(w for s in train for w in s); b = collections.Counter((s[i], s[i+1]) for s in train for i in range(len(s)-1))
bc = collections.Counter(s[i] for s in train for i in range(len(s)-1))
cont = collections.Counter(w2 for (w1, w2) in b); n_types = len(b); fol = collections.Counter(w1 for (w1, w2) in b)
def p_kn(w1, w2, D=0.75):
    pc = cont[w2] / n_types
    return pc if bc[w1] == 0 else max(b[(w1, w2)] - D, 0) / bc[w1] + D * fol[w1] / bc[w1] * pc
ppl = math.exp(-sum(math.log(p_kn(s[i-1], s[i])) for s in test for i in range(1, len(s))) / n_test_tokens)

docs.title: 10. Evaluation
docs.text: Intrinsic: perplexity (held-out, same vocabulary). Extrinsic: downstream WER (speech), BLEU (MT), accuracy of spelling correction. Beware: perplexity is not comparable across different tokenizations; <unk> handling changes values dramatically.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• What is perplexity? Exponentiated average negative log-likelihood per token; effective number of equally likely choices.
  • Why smoothing? Unseen n-grams otherwise get probability 0.
  • Why Kneser–Ney works better than add-1? It redistributes mass according to how many contexts a word can follow, not its raw frequency.
  • Limitations vs neural LMs? No generalization across similar words, short context, sparse counts.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Implement stupid backoff and compare with interpolation; tune λ on a validation set; compute character-level n-gram perplexity for two languages and use it for language ID; generate text from bigram vs trigram and compare coherence.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Jurafsky & Martin Ch 3 (N-gram language models); Chen & Goodman (1998) "An empirical study of smoothing techniques for language modeling"; Kneser & Ney (1995); Heafield (2011) KenLM; Bengio et al. (2003).

docs.title: Chapter N.5 — Word Embeddings: Co-occurrence, word2vec, GloVe, fastText
docs.text: ← NLP index · Prev N.4 · Next N.6 Topic modeling · Priority 🔴 · Code: nlp_embeddings.py (executed)

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Represent each word as a dense vector (50–300 dims) so that similar words have similar vectors and arithmetic/similarity captures meaning. Replaces sparse one-hot/BoW features (where "cat" and "dog" are orthogonal) with a learned geometry; pretrained vectors provide transfer learning from unlabeled text.

docs.title: 2. Lineage — distributional semantics
docs.text: "You shall know a word by the company it keeps" (Firth 1957; Harris 1954) → count-based vectors: co-occurrence matrices + PPMI + SVD (LSA 1990; HAL; Bullinaria & Levy 2007) → neural LMs learn embeddings as parameters (Bengio et al. 2003; Collobert & Weston 2008) → word2vec (Mikolov et al. 2013: CBOW and skip-gram with negative sampling, fast and scalable) → GloVe (Pennington et al. 2014: weighted least squares on log co-occurrences) → fastText (Bojanowski et al. 2017: word = sum of character n-gram vectors; handles OOV and morphology) → theory linking SGNS to factorizing a shifted PMI matrix (Levy & Goldberg 2014) → contextual embeddings (ELMo 2018, BERT 2018; N.8) because a single vector per word cannot represent polysemy ("bank").

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Words occurring in similar contexts get similar vectors. Skip-gram: given a center word, predict its neighbors; the vectors are the by-product that makes predictions work.

docs.title: 4. Mathematics
docs.text: Skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS): for each (center w, context c) pair from a window, maximize log σ(v_w·u_c) + Σ_{k=1..K} E_{n~P_n}[log σ(−v_w·u_n)], with noise distribution P_n ∝ f^{3/4} and frequent-word subsampling P(keep) ≈ √(t/f). Gradients for one pair: with g_pos = σ(v·u_c) − 1, g_neg,k = σ(v·u_nk): ∂/∂v = g_pos u_c + Σ g_neg,k u_nk. Worked example. v·u_c = 0.5: positive term log σ(0.5) = −0.474; negative samples with v·u_n = 0.3, −0.2: log σ(−0.3)=−0.854, log σ(0.2)=−0.598. Objective contribution −0.474−0.854−0.598 = −1.926; gradients push v toward u_c (weight σ(0.5)−1 = −0.378) and away from negatives (weights 0.574 and 0.450). PPMI + SVD: PMI(w,c) = log [P(w,c) / (P(w)P(c))], PPMI = max(PMI,0); context distribution smoothing P(c)^{0.75}; truncated SVD P ≈ UΣVᵀ; embeddings U Σ^{1/2}. GloVe: minimize Σ f(X_ij)(w_iᵀw̃_j + b_i + b̃_j − log X_ij)². Similarity: cosine. Analogies: king − man + woman ≈ queen works when the corpus is large (billions of tokens) and is partly an artifact of evaluation conventions (the query words are excluded from the answers). Properties and caveats: embeddings encode biases of the training text (gender/occupation stereotypes; Bolukbasi et al. 2016); frequency effects distort cosine; word vectors from different training runs are not aligned (rotation ambiguity).

docs.title: 5. Executed experiment (Brown corpus, ~0.88M tokens kept, vocabulary = 6,056 words with count ≥15)
