docs.text: Two embedding methods built from scratch: PPMI+SVD (window 4, 100 dims) and skip-gram negative sampling (60 dims, 3 epochs, 5 negatives, batch gradient updates in NumPy; ~142 s on CPU). Nearest neighbors by cosine: | Query | PPMI+SVD | SGNS | |---|---|---| | president | kennedy, vice, richard, chairman, former, nixon | kennedy, vice, nixon, eisenhower, senator, elected | | car | parked, truck, cars, driver, up, shayne | driver, cars, parked, drive, garage, truck | | church | fellowship, catholic, congregation, churches, christian, roman | fellowship, congregation, churches, worship, christian, catholic | | money | pay, farming, taxes, amount, bills, income | chances, worries, checks, giffen, bills, trouble | | war | world, communism, wars, russia, civil, communist | russian, lao, katanga, communists, civil, battle | | university | harvard, college, graduate, portland, dartmouth, school | harvard, graduate, carleton, attended, college, dartmouth | Neighbors are sensible and reflect the 1960s news corpus (Kennedy, Nixon, Katanga). Neighbors mix similarity and relatedness (car–driver, church–worship). Proxy quantitative check: Spearman correlation between cosine similarity and WordNet path similarity over 3,997 random noun pairs: random vectors 0.013, SGNS 0.073, PPMI+SVD 0.127. Both beat random, but absolute values are low — WordNet path similarity is a crude proxy, and a 1M-token corpus is tiny (published embeddings use billions of tokens). The count-based PPMI+SVD beat my short SGNS run here, consistent with Levy & Goldberg's finding that well-configured count methods are competitive on small corpora; I did not tune SGNS (epochs, dimensions, learning rate).

docs.title: 6. Using pretrained embeddings
docs.text: Load GloVe/fastText/word2vec vectors, average (optionally TF-IDF-weighted) for document features, or initialize embedding layers. Typical gains over TF-IDF are modest for large labeled sets and larger for small ones; contextual encoders (N.8) usually dominate. fastText is a good default for morphologically rich languages and noisy text (OOV via subwords). Evaluate with word-similarity benchmarks (WordSim-353, SimLex-999), analogy sets, and — most importantly — the downstream task.

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: small labeled data with unlabeled domain text, features for classical models, fast lightweight semantic search, initializing models, domain-specific embeddings trained on your corpus (legal, medical). Avoid: polysemy-heavy tasks (use contextual models), when a pretrained sentence encoder is available and compute is fine, or when bias would cause harm without auditing.

docs.title: 8. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Dimension (50–300), window (small ⇒ syntactic similarity, large ⇒ topical), negative samples (5–20 small data), subsampling threshold (1e-5–1e-3), min count, epochs, learning rate schedule, P_n exponent 0.75; fastText: n-gram range 3–6. For PPMI+SVD: window weighting, context smoothing α=0.75, eigenvalue weighting exponent (0.5 here).

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
# From scratch core of one SGNS minibatch (see code/nlp_embeddings.py)
gp = 1/(1+np.exp(-(vc*uo).sum(1))) - 1; gn = 1/(1+np.exp(-np.einsum('bd,bkd->bk', vc, un)))
dvc = gp[:,None]*uo + np.einsum('bk,bkd->bd', gn, un)
np.add.at(Win, c, -lr*dvc); np.add.at(Wout, o, -lr*gp[:,None]*vc); np.add.at(Wout, n, -lr*gn[:,:,None]*vc[:,None,:])
# Library (gensim, on a machine where it installs):
# from gensim.models import Word2Vec, FastText
# w2v = Word2Vec(sentences, vector_size=100, window=5, min_count=5, sg=1, negative=10, epochs=5)

docs.title: 10. Comparison
docs.text: PPMI+SVD word2vec GloVe fastText Contextual (BERT) Training SVD of counts SGD, streaming Weighted LS on counts SGD + subwords Pretraining, expensive OOV No No No Yes Yes (subwords) Polysemy No No No No Yes Cost Cheap Cheap Cheap Cheap High

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why negative sampling? Replaces an expensive softmax over the vocabulary with a few binary classifications.
  • word2vec vs GloVe? Predictive online vs count-based regression on log co-occurrences; similar quality in practice.
  • How does fastText handle OOV? Sums character n-gram vectors.
  • Limitations? One vector per word (no polysemy), embeds corpus bias, no sentence composition.
  • Relation to SVD/LSA? SGNS implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Train both embeddings on a domain corpus and compare neighbors; replace Brown with a larger corpus and recompute the WordNet-proxy correlation; implement analogy evaluation with exclusion of query words; measure gender-bias directions.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Mikolov et al. (2013a,b); Pennington, Socher & Manning (2014); Bojanowski et al. (2017); Levy & Goldberg (2014) "Neural word embedding as implicit matrix factorization"; Levy, Goldberg & Dagan (2015) "Improving distributional similarity with lessons learned from word embeddings"; Bolukbasi et al. (2016); Jurafsky & Martin Ch 6.

docs.title: Chapter N.6 — Topic Modeling: LSA, NMF, LDA
docs.text: ← NLP index · Prev N.5 · Next N.7 Sequence labeling · Priority 🟡 · Code: nlp_topics_lm.py (executed)

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Discover latent themes in an unlabeled collection and represent each document as a mixture of topics. Used for corpus exploration, search/browse, trend tracking, feature generation, and summarizing large archives (news, support tickets, papers, reviews).

docs.title: 2. Lineage
docs.text: LSA/LSI (Deerwester et al. 1990; SVD) → pLSA (Hofmann 1999; probabilistic, but overfits, no generative model for new docs) → LDA (Blei, Ng & Jordan 2003; Dirichlet priors give a proper generative model) → NMF for topics (Lee & Seung 1999; Arora et al. 2012 theory), hierarchical/dynamic/correlated topic models (HDP 2006; Dynamic TM 2006; CTM 2007) → neural/embedding-based topic modeling (ETM 2019; BERTopic 2022 — embed documents, reduce dimension, cluster with HDBSCAN, label with class-based TF-IDF). Not a strict ladder: LDA's probabilistic semantics vs NMF's speed/stability vs embedding-clustering's semantic quality.

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: A document is a mixture of topics; a topic is a distribution over words. LDA generative story: for each document draw topic proportions θ ~ Dirichlet(α); for each word draw a topic z ~ θ then a word w ~ φ_z (φ_k ~ Dirichlet(β)). Inference runs this backwards.

docs.title: 4. Mathematics
docs.text:
• LSA: X ≈ U_kΣ_kV_kᵀ — dimensions are signed, hard to read as topics.
  • NMF: X ≈ WH, W,H ≥ 0 (docs × topics, topics × words) — additive parts, readable topics; minimize Frobenius or KL divergence.
  • LDA: joint p(θ,z,w|α,β) = p(θ|α) Π_n p(z_n|θ) p(w_n|z_n,β). Inference: variational Bayes (batch/online, Hoffman et al. 2010) or collapsed Gibbs sampling. α small ⇒ sparse topic mixtures per document; β small ⇒ sparse word distributions per topic. Worked example. Two topics: A = {game 0.5, team 0.4, car 0.1}, B = {car 0.6, engine 0.3, game 0.1}. A document with θ = (0.7 A, 0.3 B) has word probabilities P(game) = 0.7·0.5+0.3·0.1 = 0.38, P(car)=0.7·0.1+0.3·0.6 = 0.25, P(team)=0.28, P(engine)=0.09. Given observed counts the posterior over θ shifts toward A if "game/team" dominate. Model selection: choose K by held-out perplexity or likelihood, coherence (NPMI/UMass/C_v correlate better with human judgments than perplexity — Chang et al. 2009 "Reading tea leaves"), stability across seeds, and interpretability for the use case.

docs.title: 5. Executed results (6 newsgroups: space, autos, politics, graphics, hockey, medicine; ~3.4k posts)
docs.text: NMF topics (TF-IDF): (0) people don just think like know make time — generic chatter; (1) geb dsl cadre shameful n3jxp chastity skepticism intellect — a single prolific poster's signature quotes (garbage topic); (2) game team hockey players play games season nhl ✔ hockey; (3) thanks graphics files does know image mail file ✔ graphics; (4) space nasa shuttle launch orbit earth lunar station ✔ space; (5) car cars dealer engine new price good like ✔ autos. LDA topics (counts): (0) president think people government time mr work going ✔ politics; (1) image use graphics edu software file like does ✔ graphics; (2) 10 25 11 55 12 16 14 18 — numbers/stats tables (junk); (3) space nasa data launch center 1993 information university ✔ space; (4) don just people think like know game did — mixed chatter/hockey; (5) car edu com like just cars don new ✔ autos. Assigning each document to its top LDA topic and comparing with the true category: purity 0.541 (chance ≈ 0.17) — much better than random, far from clean. Held-in perplexity for K = 2/6/12: 3,320 / 2,799 / 2,646 (always decreases with K on training data, so it cannot choose K; use held-out data). LSA's first components each explain <1% variance. Honest reading: 3–4 of 6 topics per model align with real categories; others are boilerplate or chatter topics, typical when preprocessing is minimal (no thread/header cleaning, no bigram phrases, limited tuning). Improving results = better stopword/min_df/max_df filters, bigrams, more iterations, tuned α/β, K sweep with coherence, removing signatures/quotes.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: exploring unfamiliar corpora, generating candidate categories to label, dimensionality reduction for interpretable features, monitoring theme prevalence over time. Avoid: short texts (tweets) with classical LDA (sparse; use biterm/embedding methods), expecting topics to equal human categories, final classification (supervised models win), tasks needing precise semantics.

docs.title: 7. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Unsupervised, interpretable, scalable (online LDA), probabilistic (LDA). − Choosing K, instability across runs, junk topics, bag-of-words (no order), sensitive to preprocessing, evaluation is subjective.

docs.title: 8. Hyperparameters
docs.text: K, α (doc-topic prior), β/η (topic-word prior), learning method/iterations, vocabulary filters (min_df, max_df, stopwords, n-grams), random seed; NMF: init (nndsvd), regularization, loss.

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer, TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.decomposition import LatentDirichletAllocation, NMF
cv = CountVectorizer(stop_words='english', max_df=.5, min_df=5); C = cv.fit_transform(docs)
lda = LatentDirichletAllocation(n_components=6, learning_method='batch', max_iter=25, random_state=0).fit(C)
def top_words(model, names, n=8): return [' '.join(names[i] for i in comp.argsort()[::-1][:n]) for comp in model.components_]
nmf = NMF(6, init='nndsvd', random_state=0, max_iter=400).fit(TfidfVectorizer(stop_words='english', max_df=.5, min_df=5).fit_transform(docs))
Libraries: gensim (LDA + coherence), BERTopic, Top2Vec, tomotopy.

docs.title: 10. Evaluation
docs.text: Held-out likelihood/perplexity, topic coherence (NPMI), topic diversity, human evaluation (word intrusion, topic intrusion tasks), downstream usefulness (does topic-augmented retrieval/classification improve?), stability (Jaccard overlap of top words across seeds). With labels: purity/NMI/ARI as a sanity check only.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• LDA vs LSA? Probabilistic, non-negative, Dirichlet-regularized mixtures vs linear algebra decomposition with signed factors.
  • How choose K? Coherence and held-out likelihood sweeps plus human inspection; no single right answer.
  • What do α and β control? Sparsity of document–topic and topic–word distributions.
  • Why do junk topics appear? Boilerplate/frequent patterns form coherent but uninteresting clusters; preprocess or add as stopwords.
  • Modern alternative? Embed documents, cluster (HDBSCAN), extract topic words with class-based TF-IDF (BERTopic).

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Re-run with bigrams and a custom stopword list and re-measure purity; sweep K with coherence; compare NMF vs LDA stability across 5 seeds; try the embedding-clustering approach using the notebook's MiniLM model.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Blei, Ng & Jordan (2003) JMLR; Blei (2012) "Probabilistic topic models" CACM; Chang et al. (2009); Hoffman, Blei & Bach (2010) online LDA; Röder et al. (2015) coherence measures; Grootendorst (2022) BERTopic.

docs.title: Chapter N.7 — Sequence Labeling: POS Tagging, NER, Chunking (HMM → CRF → Neural), plus Parsing & Information Extraction
docs.text: ← NLP index · Prev N.6 · Next N.8 Pretrained transformers · Priority 🟠 · Code: nlp_sequence_labeling.py (executed), probabilistic_models.py (HMM forward/Viterbi)

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Assign a label to every token in a sequence, where neighboring labels depend on each other. Tasks: POS tagging (NOUN, VERB…), named-entity recognition (PER/ORG/LOC), chunking (NP/VP), slot filling in dialogue, keyphrase extraction, medical/legal entity extraction, token-level toxicity/PII detection.

docs.title: 2. Lineage (and what each step fixed)
docs.text: Era Model Fixes Limit 1960s–90s Rule/lexicon taggers (Brill 1992 transformation-based) Interpretable Manual rules 1990s HMM (Church 1988; Brants TnT 2000) Probabilistic, Viterbi decoding Generative, local features only, poor OOV 1996–2000 Maximum-entropy / MEMM (Ratnaparkhi 1996) Rich overlapping features Label bias 2001 CRF (Lafferty, McCallum & Pereira) Globally normalized, no label bias, arbitrary features Feature engineering 2008–2015 Neural taggers: Collobert & Weston (2011), BiLSTM-CRF (Huang et al. 2015; Lample et al. 2016) with char-CNN/LSTM Learn features, OOV via characters Needs data; slow vs linear 2018+ Pretrained transformers with token-classification heads (BERT, RoBERTa, XLM-R) Context, transfer, multilingual Compute; subword↔word alignment 2020+ LLM prompting/few-shot extraction, span/generative IE (UIE-style) No labels, flexible schemas Cost, consistency

docs.title: 3. Mathematics
docs.text: HMM tagger: argmax_t Π P(t_i|t_{i−1}) P(w_i|t_i), decoded by Viterbi DP in O(nT²); parameters by counting with smoothing; OOV words need a suffix/shape model. CRF (linear-chain): P(y|x) = (1/Z(x)) exp Σ_i [Σ_k λ_k f_k(y_{i−1},y_i,x,i)], Z(x) computed by the forward algorithm; trained by maximizing regularized conditional log-likelihood (L-BFGS); features: word identity, suffixes/prefixes, capitalization, neighbors, gazetteers, POS tags. Global normalization lets the model learn that I-PER cannot follow B-ORG. BIO tagging: B-X begin, I-X inside, O outside: Angela(B-PER) Merkel(I-PER) visited(O) Berlin(B-LOC). Entity-level evaluation counts an entity correct only if its span and type match exactly. Worked Viterbi example (weather HMM from Ch 3.5): observations walk, shop, clean → best hidden path Sunny → Rainy → Rainy, probability 0.01344 (executed and verified by brute force over all 8 paths). POS tagging is the same algorithm with tags as hidden states and words as observations. Neural taggers: contextual encoder → per-token softmax (or CRF layer over BiLSTM/transformer outputs). With wordpiece tokenization, label the first subword of each word and ignore the rest in the loss.

docs.title: POS tagging — NLTK Penn Treebank sample, universal tagset (12 tags); 3,131 training / 783 test sentences, 20,039 test tokens; 8.5% of test tokens are unseen in training
docs.text: Model Overall accuracy Accuracy on OOV tokens (1,706) Most-frequent-tag baseline (unknown → most common tag) 0.9297 0.564 HMM (bigram tag transitions) + Viterbi + suffix model for unknowns 0.9434 0.725 CRF (word/suffix/prefix/capitalization/digit/neighbor features) 0.9705 0.883 Reading: the simple baseline is already 93% (ambiguity is limited with a coarse 12-tag set) — so always report it. Gains concentrate on OOV words (0.56 → 0.88) where features such as suffixes and capitalization matter; the CRF removes ~57% of the baseline's errors. A pretrained transformer reaches ~97–98% on the full Penn Treebank with the fine tagset; I did not run one here. ### NER — CoNLL-2002 Spanish (8,323 train / 1,517 test sentences), CRF with word, suffix, shape, POS and neighbor features Entity-level micro precision 0.793 · recall 0.781 · F1 0.787; token accuracy 0.9709 — misleading, because 88.0% of tokens are O (always predicting O gets 0.880 accuracy and entity F1 = 0). Entity Precision Recall --- --- --- PER 0.842 0.878 ORG 0.780 0.806 LOC 0.805 0.772 MISC 0.664 0.494 Reading: MISC (heterogeneous category) is hardest; PER easiest (capitalized names). A BiLSTM-CRF or fine-tuned multilingual transformer typically improves these numbers substantially — run notebook nlp_2_transformers.ipynb §4 for a pretrained English NER demo; add your measured numbers below. Your results (notebook) Value Pretrained dslim/bert-base-NER qualitative output on your sentences run notebook §4

docs.title: 5. Beyond tagging: parsing and information extraction (overview)
docs.text:
• Dependency parsing: head-dependent arcs (transition-based: Nivre 2003; graph-based: McDonald et al. 2005; neural biaffine: Dozat & Manning 2017). Evaluation: UAS/LAS. Used in relation extraction, grammar tools, linguistics; much less necessary for end-to-end neural pipelines.
  • Constituency parsing: CKY/PCFG → neural span parsers. Coreference resolution: link mentions to entities ("Marie … she"); neural end-to-end models (Lee et al. 2017).
  • Relation extraction & event extraction: classify relations between entity pairs ("Curie — born_in — Warsaw"), distant supervision (Mintz 2009), pretrained encoders with entity markers; entity linking maps mentions to knowledge-base IDs.
  • Open IE extracts (subject, relation, object) triples without a fixed schema. Pipeline: tokenization → NER → entity linking → relation extraction → knowledge graph.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: CRF with good features: small labeled sets, fast CPU inference, interpretable, strong baseline — still used in production for well-defined entities. Transformers: when you have moderate labeled data or a pretrained domain model (BioBERT, LegalBERT). LLM prompting: few labels or evolving schemas, with validation. Regex/gazetteers/rules: high-precision patterns (IDs, emails, dates). Hybrid is common: rules for structured entities + model for the rest.

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters
docs.text: CRF: c1 (L1), c2 (L2), features, max_iterations, algorithm. Neural: encoder size, char features, CRF layer, dropout, LR (2e-5–5e-5 for transformers), max length, label scheme (BIO vs BIOES), subword-label alignment policy.

docs.title: 8. Implementation (executed code pattern)
docs.text:
import sklearn_crfsuite
def feats(s, i):
    w = s[i][0]
    f = {'bias': 1, 'w.lower': w.lower(), 'suf3': w[-3:], 'suf2': w[-2:], 'istitle': w.istitle(), 'isupper': w.isupper(), 'isdigit': w.isdigit()}
    if i: f.update({'-1:w': s[i-1][0].lower(), '-1:title': s[i-1][0].istitle()})
    else: f['BOS'] = True
    if i < len(s)-1: f['+1:w'] = s[i+1][0].lower()
    else: f['EOS'] = True
    return f
crf = sklearn_crfsuite.CRF(algorithm='lbfgs', c1=0.1, c2=0.1, max_iterations=100, all_possible_transitions=True)
crf.fit([[feats(s, i) for i in range(len(s))] for s in train], train_labels)
from seqeval.metrics import classification_report; print(classification_report(gold, crf.predict(X_test)))

docs.title: 9. Evaluation
docs.text: Token accuracy (POS), entity-level precision/recall/F1 (strict span+type; also report partial-match/relaxed variants), per-type metrics, confusion between types, error taxonomy (boundary errors, type errors, missed, spurious), out-of-domain test (news-trained NER collapses on tweets/clinical text), annotation consistency (inter-annotator F1 sets a ceiling). Use seqeval.

docs.title: 10. Pitfalls
docs.text: Evaluating NER with token accuracy · leaking test sentences via document-level duplicates · inconsistent tag schemes (BIO vs IOB1) between data and evaluator · subword–word alignment mistakes · domain shift · nested/overlapping entities (flat taggers can't represent them) · annotation guideline drift.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• HMM vs CRF? Generative with local independence vs discriminative, globally normalized, arbitrary overlapping features.
  • Why Viterbi? Dynamic programming finds the best tag sequence in O(nT²) instead of T^n.
  • What is label bias? Locally normalized models (MEMM) prefer states with few outgoing transitions; CRFs avoid it with global normalization.
  • Why not token accuracy for NER? O dominates; use entity-level F1.
  • BIO vs BIOES? BIOES adds explicit end/single tags, sometimes small gains.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Add gazetteer and cluster features to the CRF and measure F1; implement Viterbi for a tagger from scratch and verify against brute force; compute strict vs relaxed entity F1; fine-tune a transformer for NER on the same data (notebook extension).

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Lafferty, McCallum & Pereira (2001); Jurafsky & Martin Ch 8 (Sequence labeling); Huang, Xu & Yu (2015); Lample et al. (2016); Devlin et al. (2018) NER results; Tjong Kim Sang (2002) CoNLL-2002; Sutton & McCallum (2012) An Introduction to Conditional Random Fields.

docs.title: Chapter N.8 — Contextual Embeddings and Pretrained Transformers for NLP (ELMo → BERT family → sentence embeddings)
docs.text: ← NLP index · Prev N.7 · Next N.9 Seq2seq tasks · Priority 🔴 · Notebook: nlp_2_transformers.ipynb (GPU; not run by the author except where noted) · Architecture details: Ch 5.4

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Replace one static vector per word (N.5) with representations that depend on the whole sentence, learned by pretraining a large network on unlabeled text, then transfer to any task by fine-tuning or by using frozen features. This "pretrain → fine-tune" paradigm (2018) replaced task-specific architectures and feature engineering across NLP.

docs.title: 2. Lineage and what each step fixed
docs.text: Year Model Idea Limitation it fixed / left 2013–14 word2vec, GloVe Static word vectors One vector per word; no polysemy 2015 Semi-supervised sequence learning (Dai & Le) Pretrain LSTM LM, fine-tune Early; small scale 2018 ELMo (Peters et al.) Contextual features from bidirectional LSTM LMs Used as frozen features; LSTM sequential 2018 ULMFiT (Howard & Ruder) Fine-tune a pretrained LM with discriminative LRs Established transfer recipe 2018 GPT (Radford et al.) Transformer decoder, fine-tune Left-to-right only 2018 BERT (Devlin et al.) Bidirectional Transformer encoder, masked LM + next-sentence prediction 512-token limit; MLM mismatch ([MASK] only in pretraining) 2019 RoBERTa (more data, no NSP, dynamic masking), ALBERT (parameter sharing), DistilBERT (distillation: ~40% smaller, ~60% faster, retains most accuracy per authors), ELECTRA (replaced-token detection, sample-efficient), XLNet Better training recipes/efficiency Still encoders with fixed windows 2019 XLM-R, mBERT Multilingual pretraining over 100 languages "Curse of multilinguality", low-resource gaps 2019 Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych) Siamese bi-encoder → fast semantic similarity Needs task-fine-tuned encoder 2019–20 T5, BART Encoder–decoder text-to-text pretraining Larger 2020–now GPT-3-style LLMs, instruction-tuned models Few-shot prompting, generation (Section 10) Cost, reliability Domain variants BioBERT, SciBERT, ClinicalBERT, LegalBERT, FinBERT, CodeBERT Continued pretraining on domain text Need domain corpus

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Pretraining forces the model to predict masked or next words, so it learns syntax, semantics and world knowledge in its weights. A static embedding gives "bank" one vector; BERT gives different vectors depending on neighbors because every layer mixes information through attention.

docs.title: 4. Mathematics and mechanics
docs.text:
• Input: WordPiece tokens + [CLS], [SEP]; embedding = token + position + segment; Transformer encoder (Ch 5.4) with bidirectional self-attention.
  • Masked LM objective: choose ~15% of tokens; of those 80% → [MASK], 10% random token, 10% unchanged; loss −Σ_{masked} log P(x_i | x_{\setminus masked}).
  • Fine-tuning heads: sequence classification softmax(W h_[CLS]); token classification softmax(W h_i) per token (NER); span extraction (QA) start/end logits; sentence-pair tasks via [CLS] A [SEP] B [SEP] (NLI, paraphrase).
  • Parameter counts: BERT-base ≈ 110M (12 layers, hidden 768, 12 heads), BERT-large ≈ 340M; DistilBERT-base ≈ 66M. Per-layer ≈ 12d² weights ⇒ 12·12·768² ≈ 85M non-embedding parameters + ≈23M embeddings (30,522 × 768).
  • Fine-tuning recipe: LR 2e-5 to 5e-5, 2–4 epochs, batch 16–32, warmup ~6–10%, linear decay, weight decay 0.01, max length 128–512. Small datasets are unstable across seeds — report mean ± std over several seeds.
  • Sentence embeddings: mean-pool token vectors, train with contrastive/triplet or NLI objectives so cosine similarity is meaningful (raw BERT [CLS] vectors are poor for similarity). Retrieval: encode corpus once, cosine/ANN search (Ch 2.5, RAG Ch G.4). Worked example (masked LM). Executed with bert-base-uncased: "The capital of France is [MASK]." → paris 0.417, lille 0.071, lyon 0.063. "She was [MASK] to hear the good news." → glad 0.442, eager 0.085, relieved 0.059. The model's distribution over words in context is exactly what pretraining optimizes; plausible but not always "correct" alternatives (lille, lyon) show it models likelihood, not truth. Executed WordPiece/special tokens: hello world → ids [101, 7592, 2088, 102] = [CLS] hello world [SEP].

docs.title: 5. Using pretrained models — the decision ladder
docs.text:
1. Frozen sentence embeddings + logistic regression/k-NN (minutes, CPU/GPU light, strong with little data).
  2. Fine-tune a small encoder (DistilBERT/MiniLM/ELECTRA-small) — best accuracy/latency trade-off for most classification, NER and pairwise tasks.
  3. Fine-tune a base/large encoder (RoBERTa, DeBERTa, XLM-R) when accuracy is critical and compute allows.
  4. Distill the large model into a small one for serving; quantize (Ch G.5).
  5. Prompt an LLM (few-shot/zero-shot) or use RAG when labels are scarce, tasks change often, or generation is needed (Section 10). Encoders (BERT-style) still excel on cost-efficient understanding tasks (classification, NER, reranking, embeddings); decoder LLMs dominate generation and flexible instruction following.

docs.title: 6. Notebook experiments (what to run and what to expect)
docs.text: nlp_2_transformers.ipynb (Colab T4): | § | Experiment | What to look for | Your result | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | WordPiece tokenization | Rare words split into pieces; matches Section N.1 outputs | run | | 2 | "bank" in finance vs river contexts at layers 0, 8, 12 | Within-sense cosine > between-sense cosine in upper layers; layer 0 (static) shows no gap. (A quick single-sentence-pair test I ran earlier gave a counter-intuitive result — finance-vs-river 0.651 > finance-vs-finance 0.600 at the last layer — because raw BERT vectors are anisotropic and sentence-specific; the notebook averages over 4+4 sentences and compares layers for a fairer test) | run | | 3 | Fill-mask + extractive QA | QA span for answerable questions; an unanswerable question still gets a span (SQuAD-v1 models can't abstain) | run | | 4 | Pretrained NER | Entities PER/ORG/LOC/MISC in a sentence | run | | 5 | MiniLM semantic search vs BM25 (precision@10 over 300 queries) | BM25 reference 0.432; dense retrieval typically helps paraphrase queries, may tie/lose on keyword-heavy short queries | run | | 6 | SST-2: TF-IDF+LR vs MiniLM+LR vs fine-tuned DistilBERT | Expect fine-tuned transformer to lead by several points | run |

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: any text understanding task with moderate labels; semantic search/dedup/clustering via sentence embeddings; domain adaptation via continued pretraining; multilingual transfer (XLM-R). Avoid: tiny CPU-only edge cases with strict latency (use TF-IDF or distilled/quantized models), very long documents without chunking/long-context encoders (Longformer, BigBird), tasks where you cannot audit bias, and "BERT for everything" when a linear baseline is within noise.

docs.title: 8. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Large accuracy gains, transfer from unlabeled data, one architecture for many tasks, rich ecosystem. − Compute/latency/memory, fixed context (512), seed variance on small data, opaque, encode biases, domain shift, catastrophic forgetting in sequential fine-tuning, tokenization mismatch pitfalls.

docs.title: 9. Implementation (version-robust skeleton; full code in the notebook)
docs.text:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification, get_linear_schedule_with_warmup
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('distilbert-base-uncased')
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained('distilbert-base-uncased', num_labels=2)
enc = tok(batch_texts, padding=True, truncation=True, max_length=128, return_tensors='pt')
loss = model(**enc, labels=labels).loss; loss.backward()          # AdamW + linear warmup/decay, grad clipping 1.0
# frozen features alternative:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
emb = SentenceTransformer('sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2').encode(texts, normalize_embeddings=True)
Practical tips: mixed precision (torch.autocast), dynamic padding, sort by length for inference, max_length ≤ model limit, freeze lower layers or use LoRA (Ch G.5) for memory, early stopping on validation F1, save tokenizer with the model.

docs.title: 10. Evaluation
docs.text: Task metrics (accuracy/macro-F1/entity-F1/EM-F1 for QA), multiple seeds, error analysis by slice, calibration, robustness (typos, paraphrase, negation — CheckList, Ribeiro et al. 2020), out-of-domain test, efficiency (latency, memory, cost), fairness. Benchmarks: GLUE/SuperGLUE (saturated), SQuAD, CoNLL-2003, XNLI, MTEB (embeddings) — use for orientation, not for deciding your product.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• What does BERT pretraining do? Masked-LM (and originally NSP) on large unlabeled corpora to learn bidirectional contextual representations.
  • BERT vs GPT? Bidirectional encoder for understanding vs causal decoder for generation.
  • Why [CLS]? A learned position whose final state summarizes the sequence for classification heads.
  • Frozen vs fine-tuned? Frozen is cheap and stable; fine-tuning gives higher accuracy at more cost.
  • Why do raw BERT vectors perform poorly for similarity? Anisotropy and no similarity objective; use Sentence-BERT-style training.
  • DistilBERT? Knowledge-distilled smaller BERT: faster, slightly less accurate.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Fine-tune three seeds of DistilBERT and report mean±std; plot layer-wise probing accuracy (e.g. POS) from frozen hidden states; compare MiniLM+LR vs TF-IDF+LR at 50/500/5,000 labeled examples (learning curves); distill a larger model into a TF-IDF linear model and compare.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Peters et al. (2018) ELMo; Howard & Ruder (2018) ULMFiT; Devlin et al. (2018) BERT; Liu et al. (2019) RoBERTa; Sanh et al. (2019) DistilBERT; Clark et al. (2020) ELECTRA; Conneau et al. (2020) XLM-R; Reimers & Gurevych (2019) Sentence-BERT; Rogers, Kovaleva & Rumshisky (2020) "A primer in BERTology"; Hugging Face NLP course.

docs.title: Chapter N.9 — Sequence-to-Sequence NLP: Machine Translation, Summarization, Question Answering and Generation Metrics
docs.text: ← NLP index · Prev N.8 · Next N.10 Evaluation & practice · Priority 🟠 · Notebook: nlp_2_transformers.ipynb §3, §7 (not run by the author; the hand-worked metric examples below were computed and verified)

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Map an input text sequence to an output text sequence of different length: translation, summarization, paraphrase/simplification, data-to-text, dialogue, question answering (extractive or generative), code generation. Defining difficulty: many valid outputs, so evaluation is hard.

docs.title: 2. Lineage
docs.text: Era Machine translation Others 1950s–80s Rule-based (direct, transfer, interlingua) Rule/template generation 1990–2013 Statistical MT: IBM Models 1–5 (Brown et al. 1993) word alignment; phrase-based (Koehn et al. 2003; Moses) Extractive summarization (TextRank 2004), IR-based QA 2014 Seq2seq encoder–decoder RNNs (Sutskever; Cho) → attention (Bahdanau 2014; Luong 2015) fixes the fixed-vector bottleneck Pointer-generator summarizers (See et al. 2017) 2016 GNMT (Wu et al.) production NMT; subword units (BPE) solve rare words SQuAD (2016) extractive QA with BiDAF 2017 Transformer (Vaswani) — parallel, SOTA 2018–20 BERT readers for QA; pretrained seq2seq BART, T5, mBART, PEGASUS for summarization/translation/generation Multilingual NMT (M2M-100, NLLB) 2020–now LLMs for translation/summarization/QA, RAG for open-domain QA (Ch G.4) Evaluation by LLM judges

docs.title: 3. Core techniques
docs.text:
• Encoder–decoder with attention: decoder step t computes attention over encoder states, c_t = Σ α_{ti} h_i, p(y_t|y_{<t},x) = softmax(W[s_t; c_t]); trained with cross-entropy and teacher forcing; exposure bias arises because at test time the model conditions on its own outputs.
  • Decoding: greedy; beam search (keep top-k partial hypotheses; length normalization; beam 4–5 typical for MT); sampling (temperature, top-p) for open-ended generation; constrained decoding. Beam search can favor generic or truncated outputs, and very large beams can reduce quality.
  • Subword vocabularies (BPE/SentencePiece) shared across languages.
  • Summarization: extractive (select sentences) vs abstractive (generate); faithfulness (hallucination) is the main risk; long inputs need chunking or long-context models.
  • QA: extractive (predict start/end span in a passage; SQuAD v1.1/v2.0 with unanswerable questions), generative (T5/LLM writes the answer), open-domain (retrieve then read; RAG), multi-hop (HotpotQA), conversational.
  • Pretraining objectives for seq2seq: denoising autoencoding (BART), span corruption (T5), gap-sentence generation (PEGASUS).

docs.title: 4. Evaluation metrics — with worked examples
docs.text: BLEU (Papineni et al. 2002): geometric mean of modified n-gram precisions (n=1..4) times a brevity penalty BP = min(1, exp(1 − r/c)). Worked example (verified). Hypothesis: the cat is on the mat (6 tokens). Reference: there is a cat on the mat (7 tokens). - 1-grams: clipped matches = {the:1 (ref has one "the"), cat, is, on, mat} = 5 of 6 ⇒ p₁ = 0.833 - 2-grams: matches "on the", "the mat" = 2 of 5 ⇒ p₂ = 0.400 - 3-grams: "on the mat" = 1 of 4 ⇒ p₃ = 0.250 - 4-grams: 0 of 3 ⇒ p₄ = 0, so unsmoothed BLEU-4 = 0 even though the sentence is a decent paraphrase — why sentence-level BLEU needs smoothing and BLEU is meant for corpus-level evaluation. - Brevity penalty: exp(1 − 7/6) = 0.846. BLEU-2 = 0.846 × √(0.833×0.400) = 0.489. ROUGE (Lin 2004; summarization): ROUGE-1 recall = unigram overlap / reference unigrams; same pair: overlap 5, so recall 5/7 = 0.714, precision 5/6 = 0.833, F1 = 0.769. ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence; ROUGE-2 bigram overlap. chrF (character n-gram F-score): robust for morphologically rich languages; METEOR (stems/synonyms); BERTScore (cosine of contextual embeddings; correlates better with humans for paraphrase); COMET/BLEURT (learned metrics trained on human judgments; best correlation for MT); QA: Exact Match and token-level F1 (SQuAD); faithfulness metrics (NLI-based consistency, QAGS/SummaC, LLM judges); human evaluation (fluency, adequacy, MQM error annotation). Pitfalls: BLEU values depend on tokenization/casing — report sacreBLEU signatures; n-gram metrics under-reward valid paraphrases and can't detect hallucinated facts; improvements of <1 BLEU are often noise (use paired bootstrap significance, Koehn 2004).

docs.title: 5. What to run (notebook §7) and your results
docs.text: T5-small English→French on six sentences with references, beam search 4: | Metric | Your result | |---|---| | Corpus BLEU (sacreBLEU) | run notebook §7 | | chrF | run notebook §7 | The notebook also reproduces the hand-computed example with sacreBLEU (unsmoothed sentence BLEU-4 = 0) and ROUGE via rouge_score. Six sentences is far too few for conclusions — use ≥500 sentences (e.g. WMT test sets) for real evaluation. Extractive QA (notebook §3): answerable questions get correct spans; the unanswerable question still returns a span — add a no-answer threshold or use a SQuAD-v2 model.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use dedicated seq2seq/NMT systems for: high-volume translation with latency/cost limits, domain-adapted translation (fine-tune on parallel data), summarization of known formats with fine-tuned models. Use LLMs when: flexible instructions/styles, low-resource tasks via prompting, multi-step transformations — with verification. Avoid: abstractive summarization of high-stakes content (legal/medical) without faithfulness checks and human review; BLEU-only evaluation; translating without handling named entities/terminology (use glossaries, constrained decoding).

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Beam size, length penalty, max length, repetition/no-repeat-ngram constraints, temperature/top-p (sampling), label smoothing, learning rate/warmup, batch size in tokens, vocabulary size, dropout; for summarization: input truncation strategy, minimum/maximum summary length.

docs.title: 8. Implementation skeleton (version-robust)
docs.text:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('t5-small'); m = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained('t5-small').eval()
enc = tok(['translate English to French: The weather is nice today.'], return_tensors='pt', padding=True)
out = m.generate(**enc, max_new_tokens=64, num_beams=4)
print(tok.batch_decode(out, skip_special_tokens=True))
import sacrebleu; print(sacrebleu.corpus_bleu(hyps, [refs]).score)
(Newer transformers releases removed some high-level task pipelines; calling generate directly is stable across versions.)

docs.title: 9. Failure modes
docs.text: Hallucinated content in summaries (faithfulness), omissions, repetition/loops, over-literal translation, mistranslated names/numbers, gender bias in translation (pronoun defaults), low-resource language quality, exposure bias, length bias (beam search favors short outputs without length normalization).

docs.title: 10. Case study (template)
docs.text: Support-ticket summarization: baseline = extractive lead-3/TextRank; model = fine-tuned BART/T5 or prompted LLM; evaluate ROUGE + faithfulness checks (entity/number consistency) + human rating of 100 samples; ship with citation of source sentences and fallbacks to extractive summaries when confidence is low.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• What is attention in seq2seq? A learned soft alignment letting the decoder look at all encoder states, removing the single-vector bottleneck.
  • What is exposure bias? Training on gold prefixes vs inference on own predictions.
  • Why does BLEU have a brevity penalty? Precision alone rewards very short outputs.
  • BLEU vs BERTScore vs COMET? n-gram overlap vs embedding similarity vs trained quality estimator.
  • Extractive vs abstractive summarization? Select vs generate; abstractive can hallucinate.
  • Beam search vs sampling? Maximization (translation) vs diversity (creative generation).

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Recompute the BLEU example with smoothing (add-1) and compare with sacreBLEU's exp smoothing; implement beam search for a toy LM; evaluate T5-small vs a larger model on 200 WMT sentences with paired bootstrap; measure ROUGE vs human faithfulness ratings on 30 summaries.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Brown et al. (1993); Koehn, Och & Marcu (2003); Bahdanau, Cho & Bengio (2014); Vaswani et al. (2017); Papineni et al. (2002) BLEU; Lin (2004) ROUGE; Post (2018) "A call for clarity in reporting BLEU scores" (sacreBLEU); Rei et al. (2020) COMET; Rajpurkar et al. (2016, 2018) SQuAD; Lewis et al. (2020) BART; Raffel et al. (2020) T5.

docs.title: Chapter N.10 — NLP Evaluation, Multilingual Issues and Production Practice
docs.text: ← NLP index · Prev N.9 · Next section: 10 — GenAI & LLMs · Priority 🔴

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text: Tie the NLP chapters together: how to choose a model, evaluate it honestly, handle languages and domains, and run NLP systems in production. This chapter is a checklist-oriented synthesis built on the executed experiments in N.1–N.7.

docs.title: 2. The model-selection ladder (use the simplest that meets the bar)
docs.text: Rung Method When it wins Evidence in this handbook 0 Rules / regex / gazetteers / lexicons Structured patterns, no data, audits N.7 (hybrid approach) 1 TF-IDF + linear / NB Small–medium labels, speed, interpretability Sentiment 0.859–0.879 vs majority 0.500 (N.2/N.3); 4-class topic 0.84–0.86 2 CRF / feature-rich linear taggers Token labeling with limited data POS 0.9705 vs baseline 0.9297; NER F1 0.787 (N.7) 3 Static embeddings (word2vec/fastText) + classifier Small labels + domain text, OOV morphology N.5 4 Frozen sentence embeddings + LR / k-NN Little labeled data, quick semantic features Notebook §5–6 5 Fine-tuned small/base encoder Production classification/NER/reranking Notebook §6, N.8 6 Seq2seq / LLM prompting / RAG Generation, flexible tasks, few labels N.9, Section 10 Move up a rung only if a measured improvement justifies the added cost, latency and maintenance. Keep the rung-1 model as a regression test and fallback.

docs.title: 3. Evaluation protocol for NLP
docs.text:
1. Define the metric from the decision: accuracy for balanced single-label; macro-F1 for imbalance; entity-level F1 (not token accuracy) for NER; EM/F1 for QA; BLEU/chrF/COMET for MT; ROUGE + faithfulness for summarization; MRR/NDCG/Recall@k for retrieval.
  2. Split correctly: by document/author/thread/time/source, never random sentences (leakage via near-duplicates; e.g. newsgroup quoted replies, product-review templates). Deduplicate before splitting.
  3. Baselines: majority, keyword/lexicon, TF-IDF+LR; report them in every table.
  4. Uncertainty: CIs by bootstrap; multiple seeds for neural models; paired tests for model comparisons. Worked example: accuracy 0.859 on 2,000 documents ⇒ standard error √(0.859·0.141/2000)=0.0078, 95% CI ≈ ±1.5 points — so 0.859 vs 0.855 (Table N.2) is not a real difference.
  5. Error analysis: sample 100 errors, tag causes (negation, sarcasm, OOV/rare entities, label noise, truncation, domain shift), fix categories not instances. Slice metrics by length, language, dialect, topic, demographic mentions.
  6. Annotation quality: measure inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ / Krippendorff's α; entity F1 between annotators); write guidelines with examples; adjudicate disagreements; the human ceiling bounds achievable scores.
  7. Robustness & behavior tests: CheckList-style tests (negation, typos, name swaps, paraphrase), adversarial/perturbation suites, out-of-domain evaluation.
  8. Calibration & abstention: reliability curves, confidence thresholds to route uncertain cases to humans (Ch 0.5).

docs.title: 4. Multilingual NLP
docs.text:
• Challenges: no whitespace (zh, ja, th), rich morphology (fi, tr, ar), scripts and normalization (Unicode NFKC, Arabic diacritics), code-switching, dialects, transliteration, low-resource languages with little unlabeled/labeled data, tokenizer fertility (more tokens per word in some languages ⇒ higher cost and shorter effective context).
  • Approaches: language-specific models where available; multilingual encoders (mBERT, XLM-R) with zero-shot cross-lingual transfer (fine-tune on English, test on others — works best for related languages and large-resource languages); translate-train / translate-test; multilingual LLMs; language ID first (fastText LID or character n-gram LMs, N.4); evaluate per language, never only on average.
  • Fairness note: performance gaps across languages and dialects are common; report them.

docs.title: 5. Bias, safety and privacy in NLP
docs.text: Embeddings and models inherit societal biases (N.5); sentiment/toxicity classifiers can mislabel dialects (e.g. African-American English flagged toxic more often — Sap et al. 2019); NER may miss non-Western names; generation can leak training data. Mitigations: audit slices, counterfactual augmentation (swap names/pronouns), de-identification (PII NER + redaction), data governance, documentation (datasheets/model cards), human oversight for high-stakes use.

docs.title: 6. Production architecture
docs.text:
raw text → language ID → normalization/cleaning → tokenization (model-matched) → model(s) → post-processing/validation → business rules → output
              │                                                                       │
          monitoring: input length, language mix, OOV rate, score distributions, latency, drift, human review samples
- Reproducibility: pin tokenizer + model versions; one shared preprocessing function for training and serving (train/serve skew is the #1 NLP bug). - Latency/cost: batch requests, dynamic padding, ONNX/TensorRT, quantization, distillation, caching of embeddings, ANN indices (Ch 2.5), truncation policies, asynchronous processing. - Drift: vocabulary and topic drift (new slang, products, events), label drift; monitor out-of-vocabulary rate, embedding-space distribution shift, performance on a rolling labeled sample; schedule retraining. - Human-in-the-loop: active learning (label the most uncertain/diverse examples), review queues, feedback capture, relabeling workflows. - Testing: unit tests for tokenization edge cases (emoji, Unicode, long inputs, empty strings), regression suite of historical failures, shadow deployment and canary releases.

docs.title: 7. Common mistakes (seen repeatedly)
docs.text: Random split of near-duplicate texts · evaluating NER with token accuracy · comparing models trained with different preprocessing · tuning on the test set · ignoring class imbalance · assuming a BERT beats a linear model without testing · forgetting max_length truncation hides the decisive sentence · lowercasing for case-sensitive models · mismatched tokenizer · reporting average over languages hiding failures · no monitoring after launch.

docs.title: 8. Project template: end-to-end text classification (reuse for any label set)
docs.text:
1. Collect and deduplicate data; define labels and guidelines; label 500–2,000 examples (stratified, with a gold subset labeled twice for agreement).
  2. Baseline: TF-IDF (word + char n-grams) + LR; macro-F1 and confusion matrix; inspect top features and errors.
  3. Candidates: sentence embeddings + LR; fine-tuned small encoder (several seeds); optionally prompted LLM on a sample.
  4. Compare under the same split and CIs; add cost/latency; choose the simplest model within tolerance of the best.
  5. Calibrate, set thresholds, define abstention; fairness/slice analysis.
  6. Package as one pipeline; serving tests; monitoring; retraining plan. Everything needed for steps 2–4 exists in code/nlp_text_basics.py and notebooks/nlp_2_transformers.ipynb; the tabular analogue is in Project 1.

docs.title: 9. Datasets and tools (starting points)
docs.text: Text classification: 20 Newsgroups, IMDB, SST-2, AG News; NER: CoNLL-2002/2003, OntoNotes, WNUT; POS/parsing: Penn Treebank, Universal Dependencies; QA: SQuAD, Natural Questions, HotpotQA; MT: WMT, FLORES; summarization: CNN/DailyMail, XSum; embeddings/retrieval: MTEB, BEIR; benchmarks: GLUE/SuperGLUE (saturated), XTREME/XNLI (multilingual). Tools: NLTK, spaCy, scikit-learn, gensim, Hugging Face (transformers, datasets, evaluate, tokenizers), sentence-transformers, seqeval, sacreBLEU. Check each dataset's license.

docs.title: 10. From NLP to LLMs (bridge to Section 10)
docs.text: LLMs subsume many pipeline stages (tokenization → subwords; representation → learned embeddings; task heads → prompts) but the same engineering questions remain: representative evaluation sets, leakage, uncertainty, error analysis, bias, drift, cost. The tokenization, language-model, embedding and transformer concepts in N.1, N.4, N.5 and N.8 are exactly what Ch G.2 builds on; retrieval metrics from N.2/N.8 feed RAG; evaluation discipline continues in Ch G.11.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• You have 500 labeled examples and need a text classifier. Plan? TF-IDF+LR baseline, sentence-embedding+LR, maybe fine-tune a small encoder with several seeds; choose by CV with CIs, then calibrate and monitor.
  • Why did your offline score not match production? Distribution shift, leakage, train/serve skew, label noise, truncation, or metric mismatch.
  • How evaluate NER properly? Strict entity-level F1 with seqeval, per-type breakdown, out-of-domain test.
  • How handle many languages? Language ID, multilingual encoder or per-language models, per-language evaluation.
  • How decide BERT vs linear? Measure on your data with CIs; consider cost/latency and maintenance.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Draft annotation guidelines for a 5-class problem and compute κ on 100 double-labeled items; run a CheckList-style test (negation, typos, name swap) on your baseline and a fine-tuned model; build a drift monitor that tracks OOV rate and score distribution; evaluate a multilingual model per language on XNLI.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Ribeiro et al. (2020) "Beyond accuracy: behavioral testing of NLP models with CheckList"; Sap et al. (2019) "The risk of racial bias in hate speech detection"; Bender & Friedman (2018) data statements; Mitchell et al. (2019) Model Cards; Hovy & Prabhumoye (2021) "Five sources of bias in NLP"; Ruder (2019–) NLP-progress and multilingual NLP resources; Chip Huyen, Designing Machine Learning Systems.

docs.title: Section 9 — Generative AI, LLMs and Agentic Systems
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Prerequisite: Section 9 — NLP

Same 16-section template as every other chapter (TEMPLATE.md). Because this field changes fast, each chapter separates durable concepts (math, architectures, trade-offs) from version-sensitive details (model names, API parameters, prices), which are flagged and dated.

docs.title: Choosing an LLM technique (decision guide, preview)
docs.text:
Need Try first Escalate to Better task behavior Clearer prompt + few-shot examples Fine-tune (LoRA) when prompts plateau and you have good data Private / fresh knowledge RAG Fine-tune for style/format, not for facts that change Strict output format Structured output / schema Constrained decoding, validation + retry Needs live data or actions Tool calling Agent loop with guardrails Fixed multi-step process Deterministic workflow (chain) Agent only if steps can't be predetermined Latency/cost too high Smaller model, caching, shorter prompts Distillation, quantization

Rule of thumb: use the simplest system that meets the eval bar — prompt → RAG → tools → workflow → agent → fine-tune, adding complexity only when measured results demand it.

docs.title: Priority within this section
docs.text: 🔴 6.1–6.4, 6.9–6.11 first (what most ML-engineer GenAI work looks like) · 🟠 6.5–6.8 next.

docs.title: Chapter 6.1 — Generative vs. Discriminative Modeling
docs.text: ← Section index · Next 6.2 Language models → LLMs · Priority 🔴 · Code: classification_family.py, genai_demos.py

docs.title: 1. The distinction
docs.text:
• Discriminative models learn p(y|x) (or a decision boundary): given the input, what is the label? Logistic regression, SVM, trees/GBMs, most neural classifiers.
  • Generative models learn p(x) or p(x,y)=p(x|y)p(y): how is the data produced? They can score likelihood, sample new data, handle missing inputs, and classify via Bayes' rule. Naive Bayes, LDA/QDA, GMM, HMM, VAEs, GANs, diffusion models, autoregressive language models. Terminology caution: "generative AI" (models that produce text/images/audio) overlaps with, but is not identical to, "generative classifiers" (modeling p(x|y) to classify). LLMs are generative models of p(text), yet are used discriminatively too (prompted classification).

docs.title: 2. Math
docs.text: Bayes: p(y|x) = p(x|y)p(y)/p(x). A generative classifier models the numerator; a discriminative one models the left side directly. For Gaussian class-conditionals with shared covariance, the generative posterior is exactly logistic in x (Ch 2.4) — the same form as logistic regression, different fitting (joint vs conditional likelihood). Generative model families by how they represent p(x): | Family | Representation | Likelihood | Examples | |---|---|---|---| | Autoregressive | Πp(x_t|x_{<t}) | Exact | n-grams, RNN/Transformer LMs, PixelCNN | | Latent variable | ∫p(x|z)p(z)dz | Bound (ELBO) | VAE, GMM, HMM | | Implicit | Sampler only | None | GAN | | Score/diffusion | Learned noise/score | Bound/ODE | DDPM, score SDE (Ch 6.7) | | Flow | Invertible transform | Exact | RealNVP, Glow | Worked example (generative classification). Priors p(spam)=0.4; word likelihoods give joint scores 0.010 (spam) vs 0.012 (ham) → posterior spam 0.4545 (Ch 2.3). The generative model also assigns p(x)=0.022 to the message — a score unavailable to a purely discriminative model.

docs.title: 3. When each wins
docs.text: Situation Prefer Plenty of labeled data, prediction accuracy is the goal Discriminative Very small labeled sets (Ng & Jordan 2001: NB approaches its asymptotic error faster) Generative may win early Missing features at test time, semi-supervised learning, anomaly detection (low p(x)) Generative Need to sample/synthesize data, simulate, augment Generative Language, image, audio, code generation Generative (autoregressive/diffusion) Calibrated class probabilities on tabular data Usually discriminative (logistic/GBM)

docs.title: 4. Evidence from this handbook (measured)
docs.text:
• Breast cancer 5-fold CV accuracy: Gaussian NB 0.939, LDA 0.954, QDA 0.956 vs Logistic 0.979, RBF-SVM 0.977 (Ch 2.x) — discriminative models ahead with ~450 training points per fold.
  • 20-newsgroups (4 classes, test accuracy): MultinomialNB 0.842 vs TF-IDF+Logistic 0.844 vs LinearSVC 0.858 — a tie in accuracy, NB far cheaper.
  • Anomaly detection (Ch 4.5) uses generative-style density/isolation scoring because anomalies lack labels.
  • Autoencoder vs PCA (Ch 5.5): the small nonlinear model did not beat the linear one with limited data — generative flexibility needs data.

docs.title: 5. Cost and risk
docs.text: Generative modeling of high-dimensional data is harder than classification (it must model everything about x, including irrelevant detail). Generated data can be wrong yet fluent (hallucination), memorize training data, and carry biases; evaluation is subjective and costly (Ch 6.11). Using a generative model as a classifier may underperform a dedicated discriminative model.

docs.title: 6. Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Generative vs discriminative? Model of how data arise vs model of the boundary/label given data.
  • Can a generative model classify? Yes via Bayes' rule; may be less accurate with large data but more sample-efficient with small data.
  • Is an LLM generative or discriminative? Generative autoregressive model of text; can be applied discriminatively by prompting or adding a head.
  • Why does Naive Bayes lose to logistic regression with more data? Its independence assumption introduces asymptotic bias.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Fit NB and logistic regression on increasing subsets of 20-newsgroups and plot learning curves; derive the logistic form of LDA's posterior; score held-out points under a GMM and use low-density points as anomalies.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Ng & Jordan (2001) "On discriminative vs. generative classifiers"; Bishop PRML Ch 4; Murphy PML Ch 20–22; Goodfellow et al., Deep Learning Ch 20; Lilian Weng's generative-model posts.

docs.title: Chapter 6.2 — Language Models → Large Language Models
docs.text:
← Section index · Prev 6.1 · Next 6.3 Prompt engineering · Priority 🔴 · Code: genai_demos.py, deep_learning_numpy.py

Version-sensitivity: architectures and training recipes here are durable concepts; model names, prices, context sizes and API parameters change quickly and are dated where quoted.

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: A language model assigns probabilities to token sequences: p(w₁…w_n)=Πp(w_t|w_{<t}). An LLM is a very large such model (Transformer decoder) pretrained on trillions of tokens, then adapted to follow instructions. Used for chat, code, extraction, reasoning, tool use, retrieval-grounded answers.

docs.title: 2. History (what each step fixed)
docs.text: Era Model Advance Limitation 1948– n-gram LMs (Shannon; Jelinek) Counts + smoothing Sparse, short context 2003 Neural LM (Bengio et al.) Embeddings generalize Small context, slow 2013 word2vec / GloVe Cheap static embeddings One vector per word, no context 2014–16 RNN/LSTM LMs, seq2seq + attention Context, translation Sequential, limited range 2017 Transformer (Ch 5.4) Parallel, long-range Quadratic attention 2018 ELMo, GPT, BERT Pretrain → fine-tune paradigm Task-specific fine-tuning 2019–20 GPT-2, GPT-3 (few-shot in-context learning), T5, scaling laws (Kaplan 2020) Scale unlocks prompting Costly, unreliable 2022 Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al.): compute-optimal ≈ more tokens per parameter (~20 tokens/param rule of thumb); InstructGPT (SFT + RLHF) Better data/compute balance, instruction following Alignment tax, hallucination 2023– Open models (LLaMA family etc.), long context, MoE, reasoning-trained models with test-time compute, tool use, multimodality Capability/efficiency Evaluation, safety, cost

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Predict the next token, trillions of times. To predict well the model must learn grammar, facts, code patterns and some reasoning heuristics. Instruction tuning and preference training then steer it into an assistant.

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text:
• Tokenization: text → subword tokens (BPE: Gage 1994; Sennrich et al. 2016; WordPiece; SentencePiece/Unigram). Vocabulary 30k–250k. Worked BPE (executed). Corpus: low×5, lower×2, newest×6, widest×3. Start from characters (+end marker). Merge the most frequent adjacent pair each step: es(9) → est(9) → est</w>(9) → lo(7) → low(7) → ne(6) → new(6) → newest</w>(6). Result: frequent words become single tokens; rare words (widest → w i d est</w>) split into pieces.
  • Loss: cross-entropy −(1/N)Σ log p_θ(x_t|x_{<t}); perplexity =exp(loss). Uniform over a 50k vocabulary gives perplexity 50,000; good LMs are far lower.
  • Sampling from logits z: p_i = softmax(z_i/T). Executed example, logits [4,3,2,1,0]: T=0.5 → [0.865,0.117,0.016,0.002,0.000] (entropy 0.66 bits); T=1 → [0.636,0.234,0.086,0.032,0.012] (1.44 bits); T=2 → [0.429,0.260,0.158,0.096,0.058] (2.01 bits). Top-k keeps the k most likely; top-p (nucleus) keeps the smallest set with cumulative mass ≥ p (p=0.9 keeps tokens {0,1,2}, mass 0.957). Greedy = T→0. Some current API models fix or reject sampling parameters — check the docs.
  • KV cache: generation reuses past keys/values. Memory per token =2·layers·kv_heads·head_dim·bytes. Executed example (fp16, 32 layers, head_dim 128, 4,096 context, batch 1): 32 KV heads → 2.15 GB; grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads → 0.54 GB; batch 16 with GQA → 8.6 GB — why serving long contexts is memory-bound.
  • Parameters: a Transformer layer ≈ 12d²; total ≈ 12Ld² + embeddings (e.g. d=4096, L=32 ⇒ ≈ 6.4B non-embedding parameters).
  • Scaling laws: loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute; compute ≈ 6·N·D FLOPs for N parameters and D tokens (a standard approximation).

docs.title: 5. Training pipeline
docs.text:
1. Pretraining (next-token, web/code/books; deduplication, filtering) →
  2. Supervised fine-tuning / instruction tuning on demonstrations →
  3. Preference optimization (RLHF/DPO, Ch 6.6) and safety training →
  4. Optionally reasoning training with reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards, and tool-use training. Inference: autoregressive decoding with KV cache, batching, quantization, speculative decoding (Ch 6.5).

docs.title: 6. Capabilities and failure modes
docs.text: In-context learning (few-shot), chain-of-thought, code, translation, tool use. Failures: hallucination (fluent falsehoods), outdated knowledge, sensitivity to prompt wording, arithmetic/logic slips, context-position effects ("lost in the middle"), prompt injection, memorization/privacy, bias. Mitigations: retrieval grounding (6.4), tools (6.9), verification, evals (6.11), constrained outputs.

docs.title: 7. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: language-heavy tasks with fuzzy rules, drafting, extraction from messy text, code assistance, semantic search (embeddings), orchestrating tools. Avoid: tasks with strict numeric/logical guarantees when a deterministic program works; high-volume simple classification where a small supervised model is cheaper and calibrated; when errors are costly and unverifiable; private data without appropriate controls.

docs.title: 8. Hyperparameters (inference and usage)
docs.text: Model choice (capability/latency/cost), temperature/top-p (where supported), max output tokens, stop sequences, system prompt, context budget, reasoning/effort setting (where supported), streaming, caching, timeouts/retries.

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
Executed: BPE and sampling in genai_demos.py; attention internals in deep_learning_numpy.py. Calling a hosted model (Anthropic Python SDK; not executed here — no API key in the authoring environment; model IDs from the SDK reference cached 2026-10-06 and may change): 

import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()               # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or a configured profile
resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
                              messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize BPE in two sentences."}])
print(resp.content[0].text, resp.usage.input_tokens, resp.usage.output_tokens)
Open models: Hugging Face transformers / vllm for local serving.

docs.title: 10. Evaluation
docs.text: Intrinsic: perplexity. Extrinsic: benchmark suites (MMLU-style knowledge, code benchmarks, reasoning sets) — contaminated and saturating, so build task-specific evals (Ch 6.11). Measure latency (time-to-first-token, tokens/s), cost per task, safety, robustness to paraphrase.

docs.title: 11. Case study (template)
docs.text: Contract-clause extraction: baseline regex + rules; LLM with a JSON schema; measure field-level F1 on 200 labeled contracts, error taxonomy (omissions, hallucinated values), cost per document; add retrieval/verification where needed.

docs.title: 12. Comparison
docs.text: Encoder-only (BERT-style): classification/embeddings, cheap. Decoder-only (GPT-style): general generation. Encoder–decoder (T5): seq2seq tasks. Small fine-tuned models often beat prompted giants on narrow, high-volume tasks on cost and latency.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why subword tokens? Open vocabulary with manageable size; rare words decompose.
  • What does temperature do? Rescales logits before softmax: lower → sharper/more deterministic; higher → flatter/more diverse.
  • Why is the KV cache important? Avoids recomputing past keys/values; but it dominates memory for long contexts.
  • What is perplexity? Exponentiated average negative log-likelihood; effective branching factor.
  • Why hallucinations? The objective rewards plausible continuations, not truth; the model lacks grounding unless given sources/tools.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Train BPE on your own text and inspect the merges; compute KV-cache memory for a model you use; implement top-p sampling and verify the nucleus mass; estimate pretraining FLOPs with 6ND.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Vaswani et al. (2017); Radford et al. (2018, 2019); Brown et al. (2020); Kaplan et al. (2020); Hoffmann et al. (2022); Ouyang et al. (2022); Sennrich et al. (2016); Jurafsky & Martin, Speech and Language Processing (LLM chapters); Karpathy's "Let's build GPT" and "Let's build the GPT tokenizer".

docs.title: Chapter 6.3 — Prompt Engineering
docs.text:
← Section index · Prev 6.2 · Next 6.4 RAG · Priority 🔴

Version-sensitivity: prompting best practices shift with each model generation. Prompts tuned for older models are often too prescriptive for newer ones; re-test when you change models. Everything below is a method for measuring prompts, not a guarantee.

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Prompt engineering is the design of model inputs (instructions, context, examples, output format) to elicit reliable behavior without changing weights. It is the cheapest and fastest adaptation lever, and the first step before RAG (6.4) or fine-tuning (6.5).

docs.title: 2. Evolution
docs.text: GPT-3 few-shot prompting (Brown et al. 2020) → chain-of-thought (Wei et al. 2022) and "let's think step by step" (Kojima et al. 2022) → self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022) → ReAct reasoning+acting (Yao et al. 2022) → tree/graph-of-thought variants → instruction-tuned models that follow plain instructions → structured outputs / schema-constrained decoding and tool calling (6.9) → reasoning models with built-in thinking and effort controls (less need for hand-written "think step by step"). Automated prompt optimization (APE, DSPy-style compilers, evolutionary search) uses eval sets to search prompts.

docs.title: 3. Anatomy of a good prompt
docs.text: Element Purpose Tip Role/context Who/what the model is working for, why State the purpose and audience, not just the task Task Exactly what to produce Say what to do, with success criteria; avoid contradictory rules Inputs The data to process Delimit clearly (XML-style tags, fenced blocks); put long documents before the question Examples Show format and edge cases 2–5 diverse, correct examples (few-shot); beware overfitting to their surface form Output spec Format/schema/length JSON schema or structured-output feature beats "please return JSON" Reasoning guidance When multi-step logic is needed Allow thinking space; for models with built-in reasoning, use the effort/thinking setting rather than long scripts Fallbacks What to do if info is missing "If the answer isn't in the context, say so" reduces fabrication

docs.title: 4. Techniques
docs.text:
• Zero-shot / few-shot: instructions alone vs instructions + examples. Few-shot helps format and borderline decisions.
  • Chain-of-thought (CoT): elicit intermediate reasoning; improves multi-step tasks on many models, but adds tokens and the visible rationale is not guaranteed to be the true cause of the answer.
  • Self-consistency: sample several reasoning paths, majority-vote. Worked example: 5 samples answer [42, 42, 40, 42, 41] → vote picks 42. Cost ×5.
  • Decomposition / prompt chaining: split into steps with checks between them (extract → validate → generate).
  • Structured output: request a schema and validate; retry on failure.
  • Role/persona and style guides: shape tone; do not rely on them for correctness.
  • Retrieval/context stuffing: supply sources (6.4); ask for quotes/citations.
  • Prefill/format control: some newer APIs no longer support assistant prefill; use structured outputs or instructions instead.
  • Prompt caching: keep the stable prefix (system prompt, tools, examples) first and dynamic content last so repeated requests reuse cached computation (provider-specific; verify cache-hit metrics).

docs.title: 5. Security: prompt injection
docs.text: Untrusted text (web pages, emails, tool results, user documents) can contain instructions that hijack the model ("ignore previous instructions…"). Mitigations: treat retrieved/tool content as data not instructions; give least-privilege tools; allow-list tool names and validate arguments in code (not by prompt); require human confirmation for destructive actions; separate trusted (system) and untrusted channels; monitor and red-team (6.11). Prompts alone are not a security boundary. A runnable demonstration of the code-level defense (allow-list + schema validation blocking a hijacked call) is in code/agent_loop_mock.py (Ch 6.9).

docs.title: 6. A systematic workflow
docs.text:
1. Write the eval set first: 30–200 representative inputs with expected outputs or a rubric; include hard cases and adversarial ones; keep a held-out test slice.
  2. Establish a baseline prompt and score it (exact match / field F1 / rubric / LLM-judge validated against humans).
  3. Change one thing at a time; log prompt version, model, parameters, scores, cost, latency.
  4. Inspect failures by category; fix categories (not single examples).
  5. Re-run on the held-out slice before shipping; re-run whenever the model or prompt changes. Template harness (illustrative; the scoring loop is plain Python — run it with your own call_model): 
    def evaluate(prompt_template, cases, call_model, score):
    results = []
    for c in cases:
        out = call_model(prompt_template.format(**c["inputs"]))
        results.append(score(out, c["expected"]))
    return sum(results) / len(results)
# Compare prompt_v1 vs prompt_v2 on the SAME cases; report the difference with a confidence interval (bootstrap), not a single run.
    LLM output is stochastic: repeat runs or fix temperature/seed where available, and report variance.

docs.title: 7. When prompting is not enough
docs.text: Signals: scores plateau despite clear prompts; need proprietary knowledge (→ RAG); need a consistent style/format at huge volume or lower latency/cost (→ fine-tune or distill, 6.5); need actions (→ tools, 6.9); need verification (→ programmatic checks).

docs.title: 8. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Zero training cost, instant iteration, no data pipeline. − Brittle to wording and model changes, non-deterministic, long prompts cost tokens/latency, hard to guarantee behavior, injection risk.

docs.title: 9. Common mistakes
docs.text: Vague success criteria · piling on contradictory rules · examples that leak the test set · evaluating on 5 cherry-picked cases · changing prompt and model simultaneously · demanding JSON in prose and parsing with regex · trusting model self-reports of confidence · neglecting cost of long prompts · copying prompts tuned for another model.

docs.title: 10. Case study (template)
docs.text: Support-ticket triage into 12 categories: baseline logistic regression on TF-IDF (Ch 2.1); zero-shot prompt with category definitions; few-shot with 2 examples/category; schema-constrained output; compare macro-F1, cost/ticket, latency; analyze confusions; decide between prompt, small fine-tuned encoder, or hybrid.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Prompting vs fine-tuning? Prompting changes inputs only (fast, cheap, brittle); fine-tuning changes weights (needs data, gives consistency/efficiency).
  • Why can CoT help? Gives the model room to compute intermediate steps in tokens; benefits vary by model and task.
  • How do you reduce hallucination? Provide sources, require citations/quotes, allow "unknown," verify with tools/checks, constrain outputs.
  • How do you test a prompt change? Same eval set, A/B with variance and held-out slice.
  • How defend against prompt injection? Architectural controls (least privilege, validation, human approval) — not just wording.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Build a 50-case eval for a task you care about and compare three prompts; add 10 adversarial cases; measure the effect of example order; write an injection test for a document summarizer.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Brown et al. (2020); Wei et al. (2022) CoT; Wang et al. (2022) self-consistency; Yao et al. (2022) ReAct; Greshake et al. (2023) on indirect prompt injection; OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications; provider prompting guides (check current versions): Anthropic, OpenAI; Khattab et al. (2023) DSPy.

docs.title: Chapter 6.4 — Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
docs.text: ← Section index · Prev 6.3 · Next 6.5 Efficient adaptation · Priority 🔴 · Code: genai_demos.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: RAG gives a language model external, up-to-date, private knowledge at inference time: retrieve relevant passages, put them in the prompt, generate an answer grounded in them (and cite them). It addresses stale knowledge, hallucination on proprietary facts, and auditability without retraining.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Keyword retrieval (TF-IDF; BM25, Robertson & Zaragoza) → latent semantic indexing (Deerwester 1990) → dense retrieval (DPR, Karpukhin et al. 2020) → RAG (Lewis et al. 2020) → retrieve-then-read pipelines with rerankers (cross-encoders, ColBERT late interaction) → hybrid sparse+dense with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack et al. 2009) → query rewriting/HyDE → contextual chunking → agentic RAG (iterative retrieval via tool calls, Ch 6.9–6.10) and long-context alternatives. Each step addresses recall, precision or flexibility; none removes the retrieval-quality ceiling.

docs.title: 3. Pipeline
docs.text:
Ingest:  documents → clean/parse → chunk (+metadata) → embed → vector index (+ BM25 index)
Query:   user question → (rewrite) → retrieve top-K (sparse + dense) → fuse → rerank → select N chunks
Answer:  prompt = instructions + question + chunks (delimited, with IDs) → LLM → answer + citations → verify
- Chunking: by structure (headings/paragraphs) with overlap (e.g. 10–20%); chunk size trades precision (small) vs context (large); attach title/section/date metadata; contextual chunk headers help. - Embeddings: bi-encoder maps text → vector; similarity = cosine/dot (Ch 0.1). Choose by retrieval benchmarks (MTEB) and your data; keep query/document prefixes if the model requires them. - Index: exact for small corpora; ANN (HNSW, IVF-PQ; Ch 2.5) for millions; metadata filters for access control. - Hybrid + fusion: RRF(d)=Σ_rankers 1/(k+rank_r(d)), k≈60. Worked example: doc A ranks 1st in BM25 and 5th in dense → 1/61+1/65=0.0318; doc B ranks 3rd and 2nd → 1/63+1/62=0.0320; B edges A since it is consistently high. - Reranking: a cross-encoder scores (query, chunk) pairs jointly — more accurate, slower; apply to top 50–100. - Generation: instruct to answer only from the context, say "not found" otherwise, cite chunk IDs; place important chunks at the start/end (long-context position effects).

docs.title: 4. Math
docs.text: BM25 score: Σ_{t∈q} IDF(t)·tf(t,d)(k₁+1)/(tf(t,d)+k₁(1−b+b·|d|/avgdl)), with IDF=ln((N−n_t+0.5)/(n_t+0.5)+1), typical k₁=1.5, b=0.75. Worked BM25 term: N=1,000 docs, term appears in 10 → IDF≈4.6; tf=3, doc length = average, k₁=1.5 → saturation factor 3·2.5/(3+1.5)=1.667; contribution ≈ 7.6. Raising tf from 3 to 30 gives 30·2.5/31.5=2.38 — diminishing returns by design. Retrieval metrics: Recall@K, Precision@K, MRR, NDCG@K. End-to-end: faithfulness (is the answer supported by the context?), answer relevance, context precision/recall, citation accuracy.

docs.title: 5. Measured retrieval comparison (executed)
docs.text: Setup: 8 newsgroup topics, ~4.5k training posts as the corpus; 300 held-out posts; query = first 12 words of a post; a retrieved document counts as "relevant" if it has the same topic (a weak, topic-level relevance proxy — not question answering). Metric: precision@10. | Retriever | P@10 | |---|---| | Random | 0.122 | | LSA-150 (dense, SVD of TF-IDF) | 0.383 | | TF-IDF cosine | 0.400 | | Hybrid RRF (BM25 + LSA) | 0.425 | | BM25 | 0.432 | Reading: lexical BM25 is a strong baseline on short, keyword-rich queries; the hybrid did not beat BM25 here (the LSA component was weaker than neural embeddings would be — LSA is only a stand-in for a dense retriever; no neural embedding model was run). Hybrid typically helps when queries mix exact terms with paraphrase; verify on your data. Always compare against BM25 before paying for embeddings and a vector DB.

docs.title: 6. Failure modes and fixes
docs.text: Failure Cause Fix Right doc never retrieved Chunking splits answer; vocabulary mismatch Better chunks, hybrid search, query rewriting, bigger K + rerank Retrieved but ignored Long/noisy context, position effects Fewer, better chunks; rerank; instruct to quote evidence Confident wrong answer from partial context Model fills gaps "Answer only from context," abstention, verification Stale/conflicting sources No metadata/versioning Date/source metadata, freshness filters, conflict handling Permission leaks Index ignores ACLs Filter by user entitlements at retrieval time Multi-hop questions Single retrieval Iterative/agentic retrieval, decomposition, graph-based RAG Prompt injection via documents Untrusted text in context Treat as data, sanitize, constrain tools (6.3, 6.11)

docs.title: 7. When to use / not (and RAG vs alternatives)
docs.text: Need Choice Private/fresh/large knowledge base, citations RAG Behavior, tone, format consistency Fine-tuning / prompting (6.5/6.3) Corpus fits in context and queries are few Long-context stuffing (+prompt caching) — simpler Structured data / exact computation Text-to-SQL, tools (6.9) Reasoning across many documents Agentic retrieval (6.10) Avoid RAG when the answer needs holistic reasoning over the whole corpus (summarization of everything) without map-reduce strategies, or when retrieval cannot be evaluated.

docs.title: 8. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Chunk size/overlap, top-K, reranker depth, hybrid weights or RRF k, similarity threshold, embedding model/dimension, query rewrite strategy, number of chunks in context, generation instructions, citation format.

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
BM25 from scratch (executed) is in genai_demos.py. Minimal template with an embedding library (not executed here): 

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import numpy as np
emb = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")                       # example open model
D = emb.encode(chunks, normalize_embeddings=True)                    # (n_chunks, dim)
def retrieve(q, k=5): s = D @ emb.encode([q], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]; return np.argsort(-s)[:k]
context = "\n\n".join(f"[{i}] {chunks[i]}" for i in retrieve(question))
prompt = f"Answer using ONLY the sources. Cite as [id]. If not found, say so.\n<sources>\n{context}\n</sources>\nQuestion: {question}"
Production: vector DB (FAISS, pgvector, Qdrant, Weaviate, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch hybrid), orchestration libraries (LlamaIndex, LangChain), or hosted retrieval tools.

docs.title: 10. Evaluation recipe
docs.text: Build a question set with gold evidence passages (50–200 questions incl. unanswerable ones). Score retrieval (Recall@K, MRR) separately from generation (faithfulness, correctness, citation accuracy); use LLM-as-judge only after calibrating against human labels (6.11). Ablate: BM25 only, dense only, hybrid, +rerank, K, chunk size. Track latency and cost per query. Monitor online with user feedback and sampled audits.

docs.title: 11. Case study (template)
docs.text: Internal policy assistant: parse PDFs by headings, chunk 300–500 tokens with titles, hybrid retrieval + cross-encoder rerank, answer with citations and abstention, ACL filters. Success = answer correctness ≥ target on the gold set, citation precision, p95 latency, and zero permission leaks in red-team tests.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• RAG vs fine-tuning? RAG injects knowledge at inference (updatable, citable); fine-tuning changes behavior/style/weights.
  • Why hybrid search? Sparse captures exact terms/IDs; dense captures paraphrase; fusion is more robust.
  • How evaluate a RAG system? Separate retrieval and generation metrics; gold evidence sets; faithfulness checks.
  • What limits RAG quality? Retrieval recall — the generator cannot use what isn't retrieved.
  • Why rerank? Cross-encoders model query–doc interaction, improving precision of the final few chunks.

docs.title: Exercises
