docs.text: Reproduce the retrieval table and add a neural embedding retriever; test chunk sizes 100/300/800 words; build 20 unanswerable questions and measure abstention; implement RRF and tune k.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Lewis et al. (2020); Karpukhin et al. (2020); Robertson & Zaragoza (2009) "The probabilistic relevance framework: BM25 and beyond"; Cormack, Clarke & Buettcher (2009) RRF; Khattab & Zaharia (2020) ColBERT; Gao et al. (2023) "Retrieval-augmented generation for LLMs: a survey"; MTEB (Muennighoff et al. 2022).

docs.title: Chapter 6.5 — Efficient Adaptation: Fine-Tuning, LoRA/QLoRA, Distillation, Quantization, Efficient Inference
docs.text:
← Section index · Prev 6.4 · Next 6.6 Alignment · Priority 🟠 · Code: genai_demos.py

PEFT/quantization libraries and recipes evolve rapidly; the mathematics and trade-offs below are stable. Library snippets are templates (not executed here — no GPU/PyTorch in the authoring environment).

docs.title: 1. Problem
docs.text: Adapt a large pretrained model to a task/domain/style, and make it cheap to train and serve. Full fine-tuning of a billion-parameter model needs gradients and optimizer states for every weight (Adam stores 2 extra copies) — typically ~12–16 bytes/parameter in mixed precision, i.e. >100 GB for a 7B-parameter model before activations.

docs.title: 2. Lineage
docs.text: Idea Landmark What it fixes Cost Full fine-tuning BERT/GPT era Max quality Memory, per-task model copies, forgetting Feature extraction / linear probe Transfer learning Cheap Limited adaptation Adapters Houlsby et al. 2019 Train small inserted modules Extra inference latency Prefix / prompt tuning Li & Liang 2021; Lester et al. 2021 Train soft prompts only Less reliable on small models LoRA Hu et al. 2021 Low-rank weight updates, mergeable (no latency) Rank/targets to choose QLoRA Dettmers et al. 2023 LoRA on a 4-bit quantized base (NF4, double quantization, paged optimizers) Quantization error, slower step Distillation Hinton et al. 2015 Small student mimics large teacher Needs teacher outputs, quality gap Quantization LLM.int8() (Dettmers 2022), GPTQ (Frantar 2022), AWQ (Lin 2023), SmoothQuant Smaller/faster inference Accuracy loss at low bits Efficient inference FlashAttention (Dao 2022), PagedAttention/vLLM (Kwon 2023), speculative decoding (Leviathan 2023; Chen 2023), GQA/MQA, MoE (Shazeer 2017; Switch Transformer 2021) Throughput/latency/memory Engineering complexity

docs.title: 3. LoRA mathematics
docs.text: Freeze W₀∈ℝ^{d×k}; learn ΔW = (α/r)·B·A with B∈ℝ^{d×r}, A∈ℝ^{r×k}, r ≪ min(d,k); init B=0 (so training starts at the pretrained model) and A~𝒩. Forward: h = W₀x + (α/r)BAx. After training merge W = W₀ + (α/r)BA. Parameter count (executed): a 4096×4096 matrix has 16.8M parameters; LoRA rank 8 trains 2·4096·8 = 65.5K (0.39%). Applying LoRA to attention projections of every layer typically trains well under 1% of the model (exact fraction depends on targets/rank). Toy experiment (executed). Learn a hidden weight update of true rank 4 on a 32×32 linear map from 200 samples (full update = 1,024 parameters): | LoRA rank | Trainable params | Final MSE | |---|---|---| | 1 | 64 | 1.0003 (cannot represent the update) | | 4 | 256 | 0.00000 | | 8 | 512 | 0.00000 | LoRA recovers the update exactly once rank ≥ true rank, using a quarter of the parameters; too low a rank cannot. Real-model updates are only approximately low-rank, so rank is tuned empirically.

docs.title: 4. Quantization mathematics
docs.text: Symmetric uniform quantization to b bits: s = max|w| / (2^{b−1}−1), q = round(w/s), ŵ = s·q. Per-row/per-channel scales cut error when rows differ in scale. Executed on a 4096×256 Gaussian matrix with row-wise scale variation: | Bits | Per-tensor RMSE | Per-row RMSE | Memory vs fp16 | |---|---|---|---| | 8 | 0.0221 | 0.0084 | 0.50× | | 4 | 0.3880 | 0.1534 | 0.25× | Takeaways: int8 is nearly lossless relative to weight scale; naive int4 error is large and per-row scaling helps ~2.5×; real 4-bit methods use group-wise scales, outlier handling, calibration data (GPTQ/AWQ) and non-uniform codebooks (NF4) to protect quality. Always evaluate task metrics after quantizing — weight error alone isn't enough. Memory arithmetic: 7B parameters ≈ 14 GB (fp16), 7 GB (int8), ≈3.5–4.5 GB (4-bit incl. overhead).

docs.title: 5. Distillation
docs.text: Student minimizes α·CE(y, p_s) + (1−α)·T²·KL(softmax(z_t/T) ‖ softmax(z_s/T)). For LLMs: train a small model on a teacher's generated outputs/reasoning (sequence-level distillation), often with filtering/verification. Check the teacher provider's terms of use before distilling from proprietary outputs.

docs.title: 6. When to adapt vs alternatives (decision guide)
docs.text: Need Try first Then Better instructions/format Prompting (6.3) Few-shot examples Private or changing knowledge RAG (6.4) Don't fine-tune facts that change Consistent style/format/domain jargon, lower latency/cost at volume LoRA / full fine-tune on curated examples Distill to a smaller model Behavior preferences/safety Preference optimization (6.6) — Serving cost/latency Smaller model, caching, batching, quantization Speculative decoding, MoE Rule: fine-tune for behavior, retrieve for knowledge. Data quality dominates: hundreds to a few thousand high-quality, diverse examples often beat tens of thousands of noisy ones.

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters
docs.text: LoRA: rank r (8–64 typical starting range), α (often 2r or r), target modules (attention q,v or all linear layers), dropout; training: LR (1e-4–2e-4 for LoRA, lower for full FT), epochs (1–3; watch overfitting), batch size, warmup, sequence length, packing; quantization: bits, group size, calibration set.

docs.title: 8. Implementation templates (not executed)
docs.text:
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig
bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True)   # QLoRA
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("your/base-model", quantization_config=bnb)
cfg = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"], lora_dropout=0.05, task_type="CAUSAL_LM")
model = get_peft_model(model, cfg); model.print_trainable_parameters()
Hosted fine-tuning services exist for some providers; availability and supported models vary — check current docs. Numerical LoRA recovery and quantization are executed in genai_demos.py.

docs.title: 9. Evaluation
docs.text: Held-out task metrics vs the prompted base model and the strongest prompting/RAG baseline; regression tests on general capability (catastrophic forgetting), safety behavior, calibration, latency/throughput, cost per 1k requests. For quantization: perplexity plus task accuracy and long-context behavior. Report variance across seeds.

docs.title: 10. Efficient inference toolbox (concepts)
docs.text: Batching/continuous batching; KV-cache management (paged); GQA/MQA to shrink the cache (executed: 2.15 GB → 0.54 GB, Ch 6.2); FlashAttention to avoid materializing the n×n matrix; speculative decoding (small draft model proposes k tokens, big model verifies in one pass; output distribution preserved); prefix/prompt caching; model routing (small model first, escalate on low confidence); MoE (sparse activation).

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why does LoRA work? Task-specific weight updates have low intrinsic rank; learning BA captures them with few parameters.
  • Why init B to zero? So ΔW=0 at the start; training begins from the pretrained function.
  • QLoRA's trick? Backprop through a frozen 4-bit NF4 base into 16-bit LoRA adapters, with double quantization and paged optimizers.
  • Fine-tune vs RAG for new facts? RAG — facts change and need citations; fine-tuning teaches behavior and is poor at reliably injecting facts.
  • Quantization trade-off? Memory/speed vs accuracy; lower bits need smarter schemes.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Compute the LoRA parameter fraction for a 7B model with r=16 on q,v; reproduce the rank-recovery experiment with noisy targets; quantize a real weight matrix per-row and per-group (size 64) and compare error; estimate serving memory for a 70B model at 4-bit.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Hu et al. (2021) LoRA; Dettmers et al. (2023) QLoRA; Houlsby et al. (2019); Hinton, Vinyals & Dean (2015); Frantar et al. (2022) GPTQ; Lin et al. (2023) AWQ; Dao et al. (2022) FlashAttention; Kwon et al. (2023) vLLM; Leviathan et al. (2023) speculative decoding; Hugging Face PEFT docs.

docs.title: Chapter 6.6 — Alignment: Instruction Tuning, RLHF, DPO, AI Feedback
docs.text: ← Section index · Prev 6.5 · Next 6.7 Diffusion · Priority 🟠 · Code: genai_demos.py · Builds on RL: Ch 6.3 (specialized)

docs.title: 1. Problem
docs.text: A pretrained LM predicts web text; it doesn't reliably follow instructions, refuse harmful requests, or match human preferences. Alignment training shapes behavior toward being helpful, honest and harmless (and policy-compliant) using demonstrations and preference signals.

docs.title: 2. Lineage
docs.text: Stage Idea Landmarks SFT / instruction tuning Train on (instruction, ideal response) FLAN (Wei et al. 2021), T0, InstructGPT SFT (Ouyang et al. 2022) RLHF Learn a reward model from human preference comparisons, optimize the policy with RL under a KL leash Christiano et al. 2017; Ziegler et al. 2019; Stiennon et al. 2020; InstructGPT 2022 (PPO) AI feedback Use model critiques/principles instead of (some) human labels Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022), RLAIF Direct preference optimization Skip the reward model and RL loop; optimize a closed-form preference loss DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023), IPO, KTO, ORPO RL with verifiable rewards Reward = checker result (unit tests, math answers) GRPO (DeepSeekMath 2024) and reasoning-model training recipes Trade-offs: SFT is simple but limited by demonstration quality; RLHF can exceed demonstrations but is complex and unstable; DPO is simpler but offline and sensitive to data quality/distribution; verifiable-reward RL is powerful where checkers exist but narrow.

docs.title: 3. Mathematics
docs.text: Reward model (Bradley–Terry): for a prompt with chosen y_w and rejected y_l: P(y_w ≻ y_l) = σ(r(y_w) − r(y_l)); loss −log σ(r_w − r_l). Worked example (executed): r_w=1.2, r_l=0.4 → σ(0.8)=0.690; loss 0.371. RLHF objective: max_π E_{x,y~π}[r(x,y)] − β·KL(π(·|x) ‖ π_ref(·|x)); optimized with PPO (Ch 6.3 specialized). The KL term prevents drifting into reward hacking/gibberish. DPO: the optimal policy of the KL-regularized objective satisfies r(x,y) = β log(π*(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)) + const, so L_DPO = −E[log σ(β[(log π_θ(y_w|x) − log π_ref(y_w|x)) − (log π_θ(y_l|x) − log π_ref(y_l|x))])]. Worked example (executed): β=0.1; log-probs policy chosen −10, rejected −12; reference chosen −11, rejected −11.5. Margin =0.1[(−10+11)−(−12+11.5)] = 0.1(1+0.5)=0.15; loss =−log σ(0.15)=0.621 (vs 0.693 at margin 0). Training increases the policy's relative preference for the chosen answer. GRPO idea: sample a group of answers per prompt, reward each (e.g. correct/incorrect), use group-normalized advantages A_i=(r_i−mean)/std — no learned value network.

docs.title: 4. Pipeline (typical)
docs.text: Pretrain → SFT on high-quality demonstrations → collect preference data (pairs ranked by humans/AI against guidelines) → reward model and RL or DPO-style optimization → safety/red-team training → evaluation → iterate. Data quality, rater guidelines and diversity matter more than algorithm choice.

docs.title: 5. Known problems
docs.text: Reward hacking/overoptimization (Gao et al. 2022: gold-reward falls as proxy-reward is over-optimized), sycophancy (agreeing with the user), verbosity bias, annotator disagreement/bias, mode collapse/reduced diversity, alignment tax (capability regressions), distribution shift between preference data and the deployed policy, evaluation difficulty. Safety training also needs adversarial testing (6.11).

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Most practitioners consume aligned models; you align yourself when you control a base model and have preference data: product-specific style/policy, domain safety rules. Prefer prompting/RAG/SFT first. DPO-style methods are the practical first step for preference tuning; RL (PPO/GRPO) when you have a reliable reward/verifier. Avoid RLHF without a clear reward spec and eval — you will optimize the wrong thing.

docs.title: 7. Hyperparameters
docs.text: β (KL strength; higher stays near reference), learning rate (very small, ~1e-6–5e-6 for full FT), epochs (often 1–3), batch size, preference-pair quality filters, PPO clip/KL target/rollout sizes, group size (GRPO), reference-model choice.

docs.title: 8. Implementation templates (not executed)
docs.text:
# DPO with Hugging Face TRL (illustrative)
from trl import DPOTrainer, DPOConfig
cfg = DPOConfig(output_dir="out", beta=0.1, learning_rate=5e-6, num_train_epochs=1)
trainer = DPOTrainer(model=model, ref_model=None, args=cfg, train_dataset=pref_ds, processing_class=tok)  # dataset: prompt/chosen/rejected
trainer.train()
The scalar loss computation is executed in genai_demos.py.

docs.title: 9. Evaluation
docs.text: Win-rate vs a reference model under blinded human or validated LLM judges (control for position and length bias), safety evals (refusal on harmful, non-refusal on benign — track both error types), capability regression tests, KL to reference, reward-model accuracy on held-out pairs (typical agreement with humans is far below 100% — preference data are noisy), red-team success rates.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Why the KL term? Keeps the policy near the reference to avoid reward hacking and degradation.
  • RLHF vs DPO? RLHF learns a reward model then runs RL; DPO optimizes a closed-form classification-style loss directly on preference pairs.
  • What is reward hacking? Exploiting reward model flaws to score high without genuinely better outputs.
  • Why sycophancy? Human raters often prefer agreeable answers, which the optimizer then amplifies.
  • Constitutional AI? Uses written principles and model self-critique to generate preference/supervision data.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Compute DPO loss for a batch by hand; simulate reward overoptimization with a noisy proxy reward; write rater guidelines for a toy task and measure inter-annotator agreement.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Christiano et al. (2017); Ouyang et al. (2022) InstructGPT; Bai et al. (2022a,b) HH-RLHF and Constitutional AI; Rafailov et al. (2023) DPO; Gao, Schulman & Hilton (2022) on scaling laws for reward-model overoptimization; Shao et al. (2024) DeepSeekMath/GRPO; Casper et al. (2023) "Open problems and fundamental limitations of RLHF".

docs.title: Chapter 6.7 — Diffusion Models
docs.text: ← Section index · Prev 6.6 · Next 6.8 Multimodal · Priority 🟠 · Code: genai_demos.py · Related: Ch 5.5

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Generative models that learn to reverse a gradual noising process. Start from pure noise and denoise step by step into an image, audio clip, video, molecule or action trajectory. Dominant for high-fidelity image/video/audio generation.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Non-equilibrium thermodynamics-inspired diffusion (Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015) → score matching with Langevin dynamics (Song & Ermon 2019) → DDPM (Ho, Jain & Abbeel 2020) → DDIM deterministic fast sampling (Song et al. 2020) → score-SDE unification (Song et al. 2021) → classifier guidance (Dhariwal & Nichol 2021) and classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans 2022) → latent diffusion / Stable Diffusion (Rombach et al. 2022: diffuse in a VAE latent space) → text-to-image systems (GLIDE, DALL·E 2, Imagen) → Diffusion Transformers (DiT, Peebles & Xie 2022) → flow matching / rectified flow (Lipman et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2022) → few-step distillation (progressive distillation, consistency models Song et al. 2023). Problems solved vs GANs: training stability, mode coverage; cost: slow multi-step sampling (addressed by fewer-step methods).

docs.title: 3. Intuition
docs.text: Add a little Gaussian noise to a photo many times until it's static. Train a network to look at a noisy image and predict the noise that was added. Then run it backwards from static: remove predicted noise a bit at a time and an image emerges.

docs.title: 4. Math (DDPM)
docs.text: Forward: q(x_t|x_{t−1}) = 𝒩(√(1−β_t) x_{t−1}, β_t I). With α_t=1−β_t, ᾱ_t=Πα_s: closed form x_t = √ᾱ_t x₀ + √(1−ᾱ_t) ε, ε~𝒩(0,I). Training loss (simplified): E_{x₀,t,ε} ‖ε − ε_θ(x_t,t)‖². Sampling step: x_{t−1} = (1/√α_t)(x_t − (β_t/√(1−ᾱ_t)) ε_θ(x_t,t)) + σ_t z. Score connection: ε_θ ≈ −√(1−ᾱ_t)·∇_x log p_t(x); the model estimates the direction toward higher data density. Worked schedule (executed): T=200, linear β from 1e-4 to 0.05: ᾱ at t=1,50,100,200 = 0.9999, 0.7309, 0.2831, 0.0061; final SNR ᾱ_T/(1−ᾱ_T)=0.0062 — the data are essentially erased at T, so starting sampling from 𝒩(0,I) is valid. Toy demonstration (executed). Data: equal mixture of two Gaussians (means −2 and +2, std 0.3). For this distribution the diffused marginal and its score are known analytically, so we plug the exact ε predictor into the DDPM sampler (no neural network needed) and sample 20,000 points from noise. Result: 50.3% of samples near −2, 49.7% near +2; fitted left-mode mean −2.00, right-mode mean 2.00, std 0.30 — the reverse process recovers the original distribution, including bimodality. A real model learns ε_θ from data; the quality of the learned predictor limits sample quality. Classifier-free guidance: ε̂ = ε_θ(x_t,∅) + w(ε_θ(x_t,c) − ε_θ(x_t,∅)); w>1 strengthens conditioning (prompt adherence) at the cost of diversity. Latent diffusion: encoder compresses images by ~8× per side (e.g. 512×512×3 → 64×64×4), diffusion runs there, decoder reconstructs — roughly 48× fewer elements to process in that example (786,432 → 16,384).

docs.title: 5. Cost
docs.text: Training: large-scale GPU compute and data. Sampling: one network evaluation per step (tens to hundreds; CFG doubles it); fast samplers (DDIM, DPM-Solver) and distillation cut to ~1–8 steps. Memory dominated by the denoiser (U-Net or Transformer) and text encoder.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: image/video/audio synthesis and editing (inpainting, super-resolution, image-to-image), data augmentation, molecular/structure generation, robotics policies (diffusion policy). Avoid: tasks needing exact likelihoods or very low latency without distillation; text generation (autoregressive models dominate, though discrete diffusion for text is researched); when provenance/IP/safety constraints aren't managed.

docs.title: 7. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • State-of-the-art fidelity and diversity, stable training, flexible conditioning (text, image, control). − Slow sampling, heavy compute, prompt-adherence/anatomy/text-rendering failures, memorization of training data in some regimes, safety/IP concerns, evaluation difficulty.

docs.title: 8. Hyperparameters
docs.text: Noise schedule (linear/cosine/shifted), timesteps T, prediction target (ε, x₀, or v), network (U-Net vs DiT), sampler and step count, guidance scale w, resolution, latent compression, EMA of weights, conditioning dropout (for CFG).

docs.title: 9. Implementation
docs.text:
Executed scalar/1-D version in genai_demos.py. Using a pretrained model (template; not executed here): 

from diffusers import AutoPipelineForText2Image
import torch
pipe = AutoPipelineForText2Image.from_pretrained("<model-id>", torch_dtype=torch.float16).to("cuda")
image = pipe("a watercolor fox in a forest", num_inference_steps=30, guidance_scale=7.0).images[0]
Check each model's license and usage policy.

docs.title: 10. Evaluation
docs.text: FID (distribution distance; sensitive to feature extractor and sample size), CLIP score (text–image alignment; limited), precision/recall of distributions, human preference studies, task-specific checks (identity preservation, object counts), safety filtering, memorization tests, latency/VRAM.

docs.title: 11. Comparison
docs.text: VAE GAN Autoregressive Diffusion Fidelity Medium (blurry) High, narrow High Very high Mode coverage Good Weak (collapse) Good Good Training stability Good Poor Good Good Sampling Fast Fast Slow (tokens) Slow (steps) → few-step

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• What does the network predict? The noise (or equivalently the clean sample/velocity) at a given noise level.
  • Why can you sample in closed form at any t during training? The forward process is Gaussian, so x_t is a direct mix of x₀ and noise.
  • What does guidance do? Pushes samples toward the condition at the expense of diversity.
  • Why latent diffusion? Much cheaper than pixel space with little perceptual loss.
  • Diffusion vs GAN? Slower but more stable, better coverage.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Implement the closed-form forward process and visualize x_t for a 1-D dataset; train a tiny MLP ε_θ(x,t) on the two-mode mixture and compare with the exact-score sampler; sweep guidance scale on a pretrained pipeline and plot CLIP score vs diversity.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Ho et al. (2020) DDPM; Song et al. (2021) score-based SDEs; Ho & Salimans (2022) classifier-free guidance; Rombach et al. (2022) latent diffusion; Peebles & Xie (2022) DiT; Lipman et al. (2022) flow matching; Lilian Weng "What are diffusion models?"; Hugging Face Diffusion Models course.

docs.title: Chapter 6.8 — Multimodal Models (Vision-Language, Audio, Video)
docs.text: ← Section index · Prev 6.7 · Next 6.9 Tool calling · Priority 🟠 · Code: genai_demos.py, deep_learning_numpy.py

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: Models that process and/or generate more than one modality — text, images, audio, video, documents, charts, sensor data — in a shared representation. Tasks: image captioning, visual question answering, document/chart understanding (OCR-free), speech recognition and synthesis, video understanding, text-to-image/video, GUI/computer-use agents.

docs.title: 2. Evolution
docs.text: Stage Idea Landmarks Limits Separate unimodal models + glue Captioning CNN→LSTM (Show and Tell 2015), VQA models — Weak alignment Contrastive alignment Embed image and text in one space CLIP (Radford et al. 2021), ALIGN Global embedding; poor fine detail/counting Vision encoder + LLM Project image features into the LLM's token space Flamingo (2022), BLIP-2 (2023), LLaVA (2023), later commercial multimodal LLMs Hallucinated visual details Natively multimodal training One Transformer over interleaved text/image/audio tokens Recent frontier systems (details vary by vendor) Compute, data, evaluation Speech Whisper (2022: weakly supervised ASR at scale), neural TTS (VITS, VALL-E-style codec LMs) Accents/noise, latency Generation Text-to-image (diffusion, Ch 6.7), text-to-video, audio generation Consistency, control, safety Any-to-any / agents Unified models; screen/GUI understanding for computer use Reliability

docs.title: 3. Core mechanisms
docs.text:
• Vision Transformer tokenization: split an image into patches, embed linearly, add position → Transformer (Ch 5.4). Executed arithmetic: 224×224 image with 16×16 patches → 196 tokens (+1 CLS); 336×336 with 14×14 patches → 576 tokens. Higher resolution multiplies visual tokens (and cost/latency); many systems tile or resize large images.
  • Contrastive pretraining (CLIP): batch of N (image, caption) pairs; similarity matrix S_ij = cos(v_i,t_j)/τ; symmetric cross-entropy pulls matching pairs together. InfoNCE worked example in Ch 5.7 (loss 0.1446).
  • Zero-shot classification: embed class prompts ("a photo of a {class}") and pick the highest cosine similarity. Worked example: image embedding (0.8, 0.6); text embeddings "cat" (0.9, 0.436), "dog" (−0.5, 0.866) normalized → cosines ≈ 0.98 vs 0.12 → "cat".
  • Connectors: linear/MLP projector or cross-attention/Q-Former mapping vision features into LLM embedding space; the LLM then treats image tokens like words.
  • Audio: waveform → log-mel spectrogram (or learned codec tokens) → encoder; ASR decoders output text; speech LMs predict codec tokens.
  • Video: frames sampled over time + temporal modeling; token cost grows with frames×patches — sampling strategy is critical.

docs.title: 4. When to use / not
docs.text: Use: documents with layout/tables/charts, screenshots, product photos, medical or industrial imagery (with domain validation), voice interfaces, video moderation/search, accessibility. Prefer a dedicated model when you need precision at scale: OCR engines for exact text, object detectors for counting/boxes, ASR specialists for noisy audio. Avoid trusting multimodal LLMs for exact counting, small text in low resolution, fine spatial reasoning, medical diagnosis without clinical validation.

docs.title: 5. Strengths / weaknesses
docs.text: • Unified interface, zero-shot flexibility, handles messy documents, reduces pipeline glue. − Hallucination about image content, resolution/token trade-offs, bias, privacy (faces, documents), adversarial images/typographic attacks, high cost per image/frame.

docs.title: 6. Hyperparameters / usage choices
docs.text: Image resolution and tiling, number of frames, audio chunking, modality-specific prompts (ask for coordinates/quotes), output schema, which encoder/connector (when training), temperature, max tokens; for retrieval: embedding model, index per modality.

docs.title: 7. Multimodal RAG
docs.text: Embed images/page screenshots (CLIP-style or document-page embeddings) alongside text; retrieve pages; pass images (or OCR'd text + layout) to a multimodal LLM. Evaluate retrieval separately (Recall@K on page-level gold) and answer faithfulness (Ch 6.4).

docs.title: 8. Implementation templates (not executed)
docs.text:
Calling a hosted multimodal model with an image (Anthropic Python SDK; check current docs for supported media types/limits): 

import anthropic, base64
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
img = base64.standard_b64encode(open("invoice.png", "rb").read()).decode()
msg = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
    {"type": "image", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "image/png", "data": img}},
    {"type": "text", "text": "Extract vendor, date and total as JSON."}]}])
Local CLIP zero-shot (Hugging Face transformers.CLIPModel) and Whisper (openai/whisper-* checkpoints) are common open baselines.

docs.title: 9. Evaluation
docs.text: Task benchmarks (VQA, DocVQA/ChartQA, MMMU-style multi-discipline, video QA) — useful but contaminated/saturating; build your own labeled set from real inputs (scans, phone photos, screenshots) with field-level accuracy; measure hallucination rate (unsupported claims), robustness to rotation/blur/compression, latency/cost per image, subgroup performance, privacy compliance. For ASR: word error rate by accent/noise condition.

docs.title: 10. Case study (template)
docs.text: Invoice processing: baseline OCR + regex/layout rules; multimodal LLM with a JSON schema; compare field-level exact-match on 300 labeled invoices across scan quality tiers; add validation (totals must equal line-item sums), human review for low-confidence cases; track cost per page.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• How does CLIP enable zero-shot classification? Shared embedding space trained contrastively; classify by similarity to text prompts.
  • How are images fed to an LLM? Patch-tokenized, encoded by a vision Transformer, projected into the LLM's embedding space as extra tokens.
  • Why is video expensive? Tokens scale with frames × patches; sampling and compression are essential.
  • Failure modes? Hallucinated details, counting errors, small-text misreads, bias, prompt injection through images.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Compute visual token counts for several resolutions/patch sizes; build a 50-image labeled set and compare an OCR pipeline vs a multimodal LLM; implement CLIP-style retrieval with an open model and measure recall@5.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Dosovitskiy et al. (2020) ViT; Radford et al. (2021) CLIP; Alayrac et al. (2022) Flamingo; Li et al. (2023) BLIP-2; Liu et al. (2023) LLaVA; Radford et al. (2022) Whisper; Yin et al. (2023) "A survey on multimodal LLMs".

docs.title: Chapter 6.9 — Tool Calling (Function Calling)
docs.text:
← Section index · Prev 6.8 · Next 6.10 Agents · Priority 🔴 · Code: agent_loop_mock.py (executed, scripted model)

Version-sensitivity: API field names and model behavior change. The SDK snippets below follow the Anthropic Python SDK reference as of late 2026 (model IDs cached 2026-10-06) and were not executed here (no API key in the authoring environment). The control-flow code in agent_loop_mock.py was executed against a scripted stand-in model with the same message shapes. Verify against current provider docs before shipping.

docs.title: 1. Identity & problem
docs.text: LLMs only emit text. Tool calling lets a model request actions — look up data, call an API, run code, query a database — by emitting a structured call that your application executes; the result is fed back and the model continues. It converts a text generator into a component that can fetch fresh facts, compute exactly, and act.

docs.title: 2. History
docs.text: Toolformer (Schick et al. 2023: models learn when to call APIs), ReAct (Yao et al. 2022: interleave reasoning and acting), WebGPT (2021), plugins (2023) → provider function-calling APIs (2023) with JSON-schema tool definitions → parallel tool calls, strict schema adherence/structured outputs, server-hosted tools (search, code execution) → Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard introduced by Anthropic (Nov 2024) for exposing tools/resources to models across applications → agent frameworks (Ch 6.10). Improvement chain: prompt-parsing hacks → schema-validated calls → standardized tool servers.

docs.title: 3. The protocol (provider-agnostic)
docs.text:
App → model:  messages + tool definitions (name, description, input JSON schema)
Model → app:  assistant turn containing tool_use block(s): {id, name, input}   [stop_reason = "tool_use"]
App:          validate input → execute the function → capture result or error
App → model:  user turn with tool_result block(s): {tool_use_id, content, is_error?}  (ALL results of a turn in ONE message)
Model:        continues; repeats until it answers (stop_reason = "end_turn")
Key facts: the model never executes anything; tool_use_id links result to call; parallel calls in one turn should be answered together; failures should be returned as error results so the model can recover; the loop needs a step cap.

docs.title: 4. Designing tools
docs.text: Principle Why Few, clear, non-overlapping tools; name and describe like documentation for a new teammate Selection accuracy falls as tools multiply and overlap Precise JSON schema: types, enums, required fields, additionalProperties: false Fewer malformed calls; some APIs offer a strict: true mode that guarantees schema-valid arguments Return concise, relevant, human-readable results (not raw 10k-token dumps); paginate Context is a budget Make errors informative ("city 'Pariss' not found; did you mean Paris?") Enables self-correction Idempotent/safe by default; separate read tools from write tools; confirm destructive actions Limits blast radius Many tools? Tool search / deferred loading, routing to sub-tools Keeps the prompt small Tool choice: auto (model decides) is the common mode; some newer models reject forced tool_choice (any/specific tool) — steer via instructions, strict schemas or structured outputs instead; check the current model notes.

docs.title: 5. Executed demonstration (scripted model)
docs.text:
agent_loop_mock.py implements the loop with a deterministic fake model that (a) issues three parallel calls, (b) is "hijacked" by an instruction hidden in a tool result and requests a forbidden tool, (c) makes a malformed call, then (d) corrects itself and answers. Output: 

(0, 'get_weather', 'ok')            (0, 'get_weather', 'ok')            (0, 'read_note', 'ok')
(1, 'delete_all_files', "error: tool 'delete_all_files' is not allowed")
(1, 'add', "error: arg 'a' must be number")
(2, 'add', 'ok')
results per user turn: [3, 2, 1]    # all parallel results returned together in one user message
final: Paris 18C rain, Rome 26C sun. The note mentions a 5pm meeting. 2+3=5. (I did not run the destructive tool.)
What it shows: allow-listing and schema validation in code blocked the injected destructive call and the bad argument type, errors were returned to the model as is_error results, and the step cap bounds runaway loops. Real models behave differently — this verifies your harness, not the model.

docs.title: 6. Provider SDK usage (templates, not executed)
docs.text:
Tool runner (the SDK runs the loop for you; Anthropic Python SDK, beta helper): 

import anthropic
from anthropic import beta_tool
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

@beta_tool
def get_weather(location: str, unit: str = "celsius") -> str:
    """Get current weather for a location.

    Args:
        location: City and state, e.g., San Francisco, CA.
        unit: Temperature unit, either "celsius" or "fahrenheit".
    """
    return f"72°F and sunny in {location}"        # your implementation

runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, tools=[get_weather],
                                          messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Paris?"}])
for message in runner: print(message)
Manual loop (full control; same protocol as Section 3): 
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_input}]
while True:
    response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, tools=tools, messages=messages)
    if response.stop_reason == "end_turn": break
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
    results = [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": execute_tool(b.name, b.input)}
               for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
(Production code should also handle pause_turn, max_tokens, refusals, validation, timeouts and is_error results as in the executed harness.) Server-hosted tools (web search, code execution, etc.) run on the provider's infrastructure and arrive as result blocks without your execution code. Always parse tool inputs as JSON, never by string matching.

docs.title: 7. Security checklist
docs.text: Validate every argument in code · allow-list tool names · least-privilege credentials per tool · sandbox code execution · rate-limit and log every call · human approval for irreversible actions (payments, deletes, external messages) · treat tool results as untrusted data (prompt injection; see 6.3/6.11) · avoid giving the model secrets · defend against SSRF/path traversal/SQL injection in tool implementations (the model is an untrusted caller).

docs.title: 8. Evaluation
docs.text: Tool-selection accuracy (right tool), argument accuracy (exact/semantic match), task success end-to-end, number of calls/latency/cost per task, invalid-call rate, recovery rate after errors, safety tests (injection, forbidden tools). Use recorded traces for regression tests; mock tools for determinism.

docs.title: 9. Common mistakes
docs.text: Vague descriptions causing wrong tool choice · returning enormous outputs · swallowing exceptions instead of returning errors · splitting parallel results across messages · no step/budget cap · letting tool results contain instructions the model follows · assuming the model's JSON is valid without checking.

docs.title: 10. Case study (template)
docs.text: Customer-support assistant with tools lookup_order, refund (requires approval), search_kb. Metrics: correct-tool rate, refund policy violations (must be 0), resolution rate, average calls, p95 latency. Start with workflow-style routing; add autonomy only if evals show benefit (Ch 6.10).

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Who executes the function? Your application; the model only proposes a call.
  • Why return errors to the model? It can retry with corrected arguments.
  • Parallel tool calls? Independent calls in one turn; return all results together.
  • How do you make tool calling reliable? Clear schemas, strict mode/validation, few well-described tools, evals, retries.
  • What is MCP? An open protocol for exposing tools/resources/prompts to AI applications through standardized servers.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Extend agent_loop_mock.py with a rate limiter and an approval gate for a send_email tool; write a schema for a SQL-query tool with a read-only allow-list; build an eval of 30 tool-selection cases.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Yao et al. (2022) ReAct; Schick et al. (2023) Toolformer; Model Context Protocol specification (modelcontextprotocol.io); provider tool-use documentation (Anthropic, OpenAI); OWASP LLM Top 10 (excessive agency, insecure tool use).

docs.title: Chapter 6.10 — Agents and Agentic AI
docs.text:
← Section index · Prev 6.9 · Next 6.11 Evaluation, safety, LLMOps · Priority 🔴 · Code: agent_loop_mock.py

Fast-moving area. The patterns (workflow vs agent, ReAct loop, memory, guardrails) are durable; frameworks, model capabilities and platform products change monthly. Product-specific statements are dated and should be re-checked.

docs.title: 1. Definitions
docs.text:
• Workflow: LLM calls and tools orchestrated by predefined code paths (you decide the control flow).
  • Agent: the LLM dynamically directs its own process — deciding which tools to use, in what order, and when it is done — in a loop with environmental feedback.
  • Agentic AI: systems with goal-directed autonomy over multi-step tasks, often with memory, planning, tool use, and sometimes multiple cooperating agents. Autonomy is a spectrum; most production value today comes from workflows and constrained agents.

docs.title: 2. Lineage
docs.text: Symbolic agents/planners (STRIPS, BDI) and RL agents (Ch 6.3 specialized) → LLM prompting patterns: ReAct (Yao et al. 2022: Thought → Action → Observation), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023: verbal self-feedback), plan-and-execute, tree search → tool-use fine-tuning and APIs (6.9) → open frameworks (AutoGPT 2023 hype, LangChain/LangGraph, LlamaIndex, AutoGen, CrewAI, provider agent SDKs) → coding agents and computer-use agents → standard tool protocols (MCP) and managed agent platforms. Anthropic's "Building effective agents" (Dec 2024) popularized the workflow-vs-agent distinction and the guidance to use the simplest design that works.

docs.title: 3. Patterns (from simplest to most autonomous)
docs.text: Pattern Control flow Use when Single LLM call (+retrieval/tools) One step Most tasks Prompt chaining Fixed sequence with gates/validation between steps Task decomposes cleanly (extract → check → write) Routing Classifier sends input to specialized handler Distinct categories, different prompts/models Parallelization Sectioning (independent subtasks) or voting (same task, many samples) Speed or confidence Orchestrator–workers Central LLM decomposes dynamically, workers execute Unpredictable subtasks (e.g. multi-file code changes) Evaluator–optimizer One generates, another critiques, loop Clear criteria, iteration improves results Autonomous agent Open-ended loop with tools until done/budget Open-ended problems, can't predict steps, trusted environment, can verify results Multi-agent Several agents with roles/handoffs/shared state Parallel exploration, context isolation, large jobs — adds cost and failure modes

docs.title: 4. The agent loop
docs.text:
goal + context ─▶ [LLM: plan / choose action] ─▶ tool call ─▶ observation ─┐
          ▲                                                                 │
          └──────────────── update state (messages, memory, scratchpad) ◀───┘
          stop when: goal met · budget/step cap · needs human · error threshold
The executable skeleton (message protocol, parallel results, validation, step cap) is in agent_loop_mock.py (Ch 6.9). Components: - Model + instructions (system prompt: goal, constraints, tool guidance, when to stop/ask). - Tools (read vs write separation; sandboxes; Ch 6.9). - Memory: short-term = conversation/scratchpad (context window; summarize or compact when long); long-term = files, databases, vector stores, notes the agent reads/writes; retrieval of past experience. - Planning/reflection: explicit plans, TODO lists, self-critique, verification steps (run tests, validate outputs). - Guardrails & oversight: permissions, approval gates, budgets, timeouts, logging, kill switch. - Context management: keep it small (summaries, compaction, tool-result trimming, sub-agents with isolated contexts).

docs.title: 5. Math/engineering intuition: compounding error and cost
docs.text: If each step succeeds independently with probability p, an n-step task succeeds with pⁿ. Worked example: p=0.95, n=10 → 0.599; n=20 → 0.358; p=0.99, n=20 → 0.818. Hence: shorten chains, verify intermediate results, add retries/checkpoints, make steps recoverable. Cost/latency scale with steps × context length; a loop that re-sends long history each turn is expensive — use caching and compaction. Token budget example: 15 steps × average 20k input tokens = 300k input tokens per task before caching.

docs.title: 6. When to use / not
docs.text: Use agents when: the path can't be hardcoded, outcomes are verifiable (tests, checks, ground-truth lookups), errors are recoverable, value justifies cost/latency, and you have sandboxing. Good fits: coding with test suites, research with source checking, data analysis in notebooks, IT/ops runbooks with approvals. Avoid when: a deterministic workflow suffices, errors are irreversible or costly, outputs can't be verified, latency is critical, or you can't monitor behavior. Start simple: single call → workflow → agent, and add autonomy only when evals prove the benefit.

docs.title: 7. Failure modes and mitigations
docs.text: Failure Mitigation Loops / no progress Step and token caps; detect repeated actions; escalate to human Wrong tool / bad args Clear tools, validation, error feedback Compounding errors Checkpoints, verification, smaller steps Prompt injection from tool results/web Data-vs-instruction separation, least privilege, approval for risky actions Excessive agency / unsafe actions Permission model, dry-run, allow-lists, audit logs Context overflow / forgotten goal Compaction, notes/plan files, re-stating goal Cost blowups Budgets, caching, cheaper sub-agents for reading-heavy work Hallucinated completion ("done" without doing) Programmatic completion checks, tests, independent verifier

docs.title: 8. Platform options (verify current docs)
docs.text: Build with: the model API + your loop (max control); an SDK tool-runner helper (loop automated, your tools, you host); a batteries-included agent SDK (built-in file/shell tools, you host); or a managed agent service where the provider runs the loop and hosts a sandbox (persisted agent definitions, sessions, event streams). Pick by who should own the loop and the sandbox. Multi-agent coordination, scheduled/autonomous runs, outcome-graded sessions and memory stores are emerging platform features; details vary and change rapidly.

docs.title: 9. Evaluation
docs.text: Evaluate tasks end-to-end with verifiable outcomes (unit tests passed, correct final answer, state of database) not just the final text; benchmarks: SWE-bench (software issues), WebArena/BrowserGym, τ-bench (tool-agent-user interaction), GAIA, OSWorld — useful but narrow and contaminated; build in-house suites from real tasks. Track: success rate, steps, cost, latency, human interventions, safety incidents, variance over repeated runs (agents are stochastic: run each task several times and report pass@1 and pass^k). Review traces, not only outcomes. Use sandboxed replays of tools for determinism.

docs.title: 10. Case study (template)
docs.text: Data-analysis agent: tools run_sql (read-only), python_sandbox, plot; workflow-first design (plan → query → validate row counts → analyze → draft). Add an evaluator step that re-computes headline numbers independently. Success criteria: numeric answers match analyst-verified ground truth on 50 questions, zero writes, median cost < target. Roll out with human review, then relax.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• Agent vs workflow? Model-directed control flow vs code-directed.
  • When not to use an agent? When a fixed pipeline works or outcomes can't be verified/recovered.
  • What is ReAct? Interleaving reasoning traces with tool actions and observations.
  • Why do agents fail on long tasks? Compounding per-step errors, context bloat, drift from the goal.
  • How secure an agent? Least privilege, sandboxing, approval gates, input/output validation, logging, red-teaming.
  • Single vs multi-agent? Multi-agent helps with parallelism and context isolation, at the cost of coordination complexity and tokens.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Turn the mock harness into a ReAct loop with a scratchpad and a stopping check; measure success probability vs steps with injected random tool failures; design an approval policy for a finance agent; write an eval of 20 tasks with programmatic checkers.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Yao et al. (2022) ReAct; Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion; Anthropic (2024) "Building effective agents"; Wang et al. (2023) "A survey on LLM-based autonomous agents"; Jimenez et al. (2023) SWE-bench; Yao et al. (2024) τ-bench; Model Context Protocol docs; OWASP LLM Top 10 (excessive agency); provider agent documentation (check current versions).

docs.title: Chapter 6.11 — Evaluation, Safety and LLMOps
docs.text:
← Section index · Prev 6.10 · Back to Roadmap · Priority 🔴

Evaluation is the bottleneck of every chapter in this section: you cannot improve prompts, retrieval, fine-tunes or agents faster than you can measure them.

docs.title: 1. Why LLM evaluation is hard
docs.text: Open-ended outputs (many valid answers), stochastic generation, benchmark contamination and saturation, sensitivity to prompt wording, no single metric for "good," and high cost of human labeling. Offline scores often mispredict production behavior.

docs.title: 2. Evaluation layers
docs.text: Layer Question Methods Unit/component Does each piece work? Retrieval Recall@K, tool-argument accuracy, parser success, schema validity Task Is the output correct for the job? Exact match, field-level F1, unit tests, executable checks, rubric scoring System/e2e Does the whole pipeline succeed? Task success on realistic scenarios, human review, agent traces Safety Can it be misused or hurt users? Red-teaming, jailbreak/injection suites, policy tests, bias audits Operational Is it fast/cheap/reliable? Latency percentiles, cost/task, error rate, availability Online Do users benefit? A/B tests, retention, escalation rate, thumbs, complaint review

docs.title: 3. Building a task eval (workflow)
docs.text:
1. Collect real inputs (logs, tickets, documents) and cover rare/hard cases; 50–300 to start; keep a held-out slice and never tune on it.
  2. Define the success criterion (programmatic if possible; otherwise a written rubric with examples).
  3. Label expected outputs/rubric scores; measure inter-annotator agreement.
  4. Automate scoring; log model, prompt version, parameters, cost, latency.
  5. Report uncertainty: bootstrap CI. Worked example: 80 items, 64 correct → 80% accuracy; normal-approx standard error √(0.8·0.2/80)=0.0447, 95% CI ≈ 80% ± 8.8 points → [71%, 89%]. A new prompt scoring 84% on the same 80 items is not distinguishable from 80% — use paired comparisons (McNemar/bootstrap on per-item differences) and more items.
  6. Re-run on every model, prompt or retrieval change (regression suite); add every production failure as a new test.

docs.title: 4. LLM-as-judge
docs.text: Use a strong model to grade outputs against a rubric or compare two answers. Known biases (Zheng et al. 2023, MT-Bench): position bias (prefers first/second), verbosity bias, self-preference, sensitivity to rubric wording. Practices: randomize order and average both orders, require reasoning then a score, use pairwise comparisons for subjective quality, give reference answers when available, calibrate against human labels (report agreement/Cohen's κ) on a sample, and never use the same model/prompt being tuned as the sole judge. Judges are for scale, not a substitute for ground truth.

docs.title: 5. Metric cheat-sheet
docs.text: Output type Metrics Classification/extraction Accuracy, macro-F1, field exact-match, schema validity Code pass@k on unit tests (Chen et al. 2021: pass@k = 1 − C(n−c,k)/C(n,k)) Summarization/translation ROUGE/BLEU/chrF (weak), BERTScore, rubric/judge, human preference RAG Retrieval Recall@K/MRR, faithfulness/groundedness, answer correctness, citation precision Agents Task success, steps, cost, safety violations, pass^k consistency Safety Attack success rate, refusal rate on harmful, over-refusal rate on benign Worked pass@k example: n=10 samples, c=3 correct, k=1: 1 − C(7,1)/C(10,1) = 1 − 7/10 = 0.30; k=5: 1 − C(7,5)/C(10,5) = 1 − 21/252 = 0.9167.

docs.title: 6. Safety and security
docs.text:
• Threats: prompt injection (direct/indirect), jailbreaks, data exfiltration via tools, insecure output handling (XSS/SQL from model text), excessive agency, training-data leakage/PII, model denial-of-service (huge inputs), supply-chain risks (malicious models/tools), bias and harmful content, over-reliance. See OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and NIST AI RMF.
  • Defenses (layered): least privilege and sandboxing; validate/escape model outputs before using them as code, SQL, HTML; allow-lists and schemas for tools; human approval for high-impact actions; separate trusted/untrusted content; input/output moderation and classifiers; rate limits; secrets never in prompts; audit logs; incident response plan; red-team before launch and continuously. Prompt wording alone is not a control.
  • Privacy/compliance: data minimization, retention settings, vendor data-use terms, PII redaction, regional requirements; documentation (model cards/system cards, risk assessments).
  • Responsible-use checks: subgroup evaluation, harm review, user disclosure, escalation paths.

docs.title: 7. LLMOps (running LLM systems)
docs.text: Concern Practice Versioning Version prompts, tool schemas, retrieval indexes, models and eval sets together; pin model versions; staged rollouts Observability Trace every request (prompt, retrieved chunks, tool calls, outputs, tokens, latency, errors); sample for review; dashboards and alerts Cost control Prompt caching (stable prefix first), shorter context, right-size models (route simple requests to smaller models), batch APIs for offline jobs, output caps, budgets per user/task Reliability Timeouts, retries with backoff, fallbacks across models/providers, rate-limit handling, graceful degradation, circuit breakers Quality over time Drift monitoring (inputs, retrieval hit rates, user feedback), periodic re-evaluation, handling model deprecations and changing behavior Governance Access control, approvals for prompt/tool changes, audit trails Cost arithmetic (illustrative; prices change — check current pricing): with an example list price of $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens (a current frontier-tier rate as cached 2026-10-06), a request with 2,000 input and 500 output tokens costs 2,000·4/1e6 + 500·20/1e6 = $0.008 + $0.010 = $0.018; 1M such requests ≈ $18,000. Cached input tokens are billed at a fraction of the normal input price on providers that support prompt caching, so stable prefixes (system prompt, tools, reference documents) placed first can cut input cost substantially — verify the cache-hit counters in usage metadata rather than assuming.

docs.title: 8. Release checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Eval suite with CI gate (no regression on critical slices)
  • [ ] Safety/red-team results reviewed; known limitations documented
  • [ ] Monitoring, tracing, alerts, cost budgets in place
  • [ ] Human fallback / escalation path; kill switch
  • [ ] Data handling reviewed (PII, retention, vendor terms)
  • [ ] Rollout plan: shadow → canary → gradual; rollback tested
  • [ ] Post-launch review cadence and ownership

docs.title: 9. Common mistakes
docs.text: Shipping on vibes from 5 examples · tuning on the test set · using a judge model without human calibration · ignoring variance from sampling · measuring only accuracy and not cost/latency/safety · benchmark chasing instead of task evals · treating prompts as unversioned config · no tracing so failures can't be reproduced · assuming model upgrades are drop-in.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
• How would you evaluate a RAG chatbot? Gold questions with evidence passages; retrieval metrics + faithfulness + correctness; human-calibrated judge; online feedback.
  • Pitfalls of LLM-as-judge? Position/verbosity/self-preference bias; calibrate with humans.
  • Why CIs on eval scores? Small eval sets give wide intervals; use paired tests to compare variants.
  • How reduce cost? Caching, routing to smaller models, shorter prompts, batching, output limits, distillation (Ch 6.5).
  • How handle prompt injection? Architectural controls: least privilege, validation, approvals, data/instruction separation, monitoring.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Compute CI and a paired bootstrap for two prompts on the same 100 items; write a rubric and measure human–judge agreement on 30 outputs; build an injection test suite of 20 attacks for a RAG app; implement a cost dashboard from usage logs.
